decls.summary: **The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem in `C(X, Y)`.** An equicontinuous family of continuous maps whose values at each point lie in a common compact set has relatively compact range in the compact-open topology. No assumption on the topology of `X` is needed.
If `K` is bounded, then `holomorphicHull Ω K` is bounded.

**Holomorphic hull on `ℂ` equals the polynomial hull.** For any nonempty index type `ι` (in particular `ι = Fin 1`, where `Function.const (Fin 1)` is `⇑(ContinuousLinearEquiv.funUnique (Fin 1) ℂ ℂ).symm`) and any bounded set `K ⊆ ℂ`, the entire holomorphic hull `holomorphicHull univ K` equals the preimage of `RiemannMasullo.External.TauCeti.polynomialHull (Function.const ι '' K)` under `Function.const ι`.
For any nonempty index type `ι` and any bounded `K ⊆ ℂ`, `K` equals its entire holomorphic hull `holomorphicHull univ K` if and only if `Function.const ι '' K` is polynomially convex.

**The local `Lᵖ` translation estimate**: for a `C¹` function and `1 ≤ p ≤ ∞`, if every segment `[x, x + h]` starting in `K` lies in the measurable set `T`, then
**The `Lᵖ` translation estimate**: a `C¹` function moves in `Lᵖ` at most linearly in the translation, at the rate given by the `Lᵖ` seminorm of its derivative,

**The powered segment estimate in the direction of the increment.** For a `C¹` function and `r ≥ 1`, the `r`-th power of `‖u(x + h) - u(x)‖` is bounded by the integral along `[x, x + h]` of the `r`-th power of the directional derivative `Du · h`.

A `C^n` map which agrees outside a ball with a map whose order-`n` derivative is bounded there has a bounded order-`n` derivative: on the closed ball the derivative is continuous, and outside it the two derivatives coincide.

A `C^k` function on `E × F` satisfies, for `x` in a compact set and `ξ` in a ball, the estimate `‖D^k f(x, ξ)‖ ≤ C (1 + ‖ξ‖ ^ 2) ^ (r / 2)` for every real `r`: the derivative is bounded there, and the weight is bounded below.
Over `ℝ` the Riesz isomorphism is a linear isometry, so the gradient of a `C^{m+1}` function is `Cᵐ`, just as its Fréchet derivative is.

**Asymptotic bounds on the derivatives of `exp ℓ - 1`.** Along a filter on which the weight `ρ` is bounded, the derivative of order `n` of `y ↦ exp (ℓ y) - 1` is `O(ρ)` for a `Cⁿ` map `ℓ` whose derivatives of order at most `n` are `O(ρ)`.

The case `(c, v) ↦ c.smulRight v` of `ContinuousLinearMap.isBigO_iteratedFDeriv_of_bilinear`: along any filter, if the derivatives of order at most `n` of `f` and `g` are `O(ρ₁)` and `O(ρ₂)`, then the order-`n` derivative of `y ↦ (f y).smulRight (g y)` is `O(ρ₁ ρ₂)`.

**Asymptotic bounds on the derivatives of `exp ℓ`.** Along any filter, the derivative of order `n + 1` of `y ↦ exp (ℓ y)` is `O(ρ)` for a `C^(n + 1)` map `ℓ` once the derivatives of `ℓ` of orders `1` to `n + 1` are `O(ρ)` and those of `exp ℓ` of order at most `n` are bounded: it is the order-`n` derivative of `exp ℓ • Dℓ`, which `ContinuousLinearMap.isBigO_iteratedFDeriv_of_bilinear` bounds.
**The translation estimate in `∫⁻` form**: for a `C¹` function and `1 ≤ r`, `∫ ‖u(x + h) - u(x)‖ ^ r dx ≤ ‖h‖ ^ r ∫ ‖Du‖ ^ r`.
Rescaling the variable by `c` with `1 ≤ ‖c‖` multiplies uniform bounds for the derivatives of order at most `N` by at most `‖c‖ ^ N`.

**Leibniz bound for a product with uniform constants.** If the derivatives of order at most `N` of `f` and `g` are bounded by `C` and `D` everywhere, those of `f * g` of order at most `N` are bounded by `2 ^ N * (C * D)`.
**Landau-type interpolation inequality.** If `f` is `C^(k+2)` with `‖D^k f‖ ≤ M₀` and `‖D^(k+2) f‖ ≤ M₂`, then `‖D^(k+1) f x‖ ≤ 2 M₀ / ε + M₂ ε` for every `ε > 0`.

For a map which is `C²` over a larger field `𝕜'`, the second derivative over `𝕜` is the second derivative over `𝕜'`. In particular, the real second derivative of a holomorphic map is complex bilinear.
The pointwise form of `ContDiff.gradient_right`: over `ℝ`, the gradient of a function that is `C^{m+1}` at `x` is `Cᵐ` at `x`.
For a `C²` map, the conjugate Wirtinger derivative `y ↦ \bar∂g(y) u` in a fixed direction `u` is differentiable, with derivative built from the second derivative of `g`.
At a twice continuously differentiable point, `fderiv 𝕜 g` is differentiable, with derivative the second derivative of `g`.

The bound on the derivative at `q`, applied to `(1, w)`, of a cut-off `(t, x) ↦ χ (s • x) * φ (t, x)`: the cut-off does not increase the derivative of `φ`, and the derivative of `χ`, applied to `s • w`, contributes at most `B * D * (1 + ‖w‖)`, where `B` bounds `φ` and `D` bounds the derivative of `χ`; so the bound is `(C + B * D) * (1 + ‖w‖)`.

The partial derivative in the second variable of a map that is `C¹` on an open set `U` is continuous on every set `K` with `{a} × K ⊆ U`.
On an open set `s`, the second directional derivative `x ↦ D(Dg(·) v)(x) v` of a `C²` map `g` in a fixed direction `v` is continuous.
On a compact subset `K` of `s`, the derivatives within `s` of order at most `n` of a map that is `C^n` on `s` are bounded by a single constant.
A function `C^k` on `U ×ˢ univ`, for an open set `U`, agrees with a function `C^k` on the whole product at every point `(y, η)` with `y` near a compact set `K ⊆ U`, for all `η`.
On a compact subset `K` of an open set `s`, the derivatives of order at most `n` of a map that is `C^n` on `s` are bounded by a single nonnegative constant.

On a compact set `K`, the order-`n` derivative of `z ↦ L z (φ (τ z))` is bounded by a constant multiple of any common bound `δ` for the derivatives of `φ` of order at most `n` along `τ '' K`. The constant depends on `L`, `τ`, `K` and `n` but not on `φ`.

**A compact component of a level set has a neighbourhood with compact levels.** In a locally compact Hausdorff space, if the connected component of `x` in the level `f⁻¹(f x)` of a continuous map `f` to a Hausdorff space is compact, then it has an open neighbourhood `W` which meets every level `f⁻¹(c)` of `f` in a compact set.

Composing on the left with a continuous linear map `L` preserves a bound `‖D^k g x‖ ≤ C w x` on the `k`-th derivative of a `C^k` map `g` by a multiple of a weight `w`.

For a continuous linear map `Φ` with a continuous linear left inverse `Ψ`, the derivative of `Φ ∘ k` at `y` is `Φ` composed with the derivative of `k` at `y`, for every `k` (no differentiability assumption).

For a continuous linear map `g` with a continuous linear right inverse `s`, the derivative of `h ∘ g` at `x` is the derivative of `h` at `g x` composed with `g`, for every `h` (no differentiability assumption).
The usual bilinear derivative rule holds globally when the second factor is supported inside the open set where the first factor is differentiable. Outside this set all terms vanish.
The inverse of `c • f` is `c⁻¹ • f.inverse`. This holds for every scalar: both sides vanish when `c = 0` or when `f` is not invertible.

**Asymptotic bounds on the derivatives of `L ∘ f`.** Along any filter, if the derivative of order `n` of a `Cⁿ` map `f` is `O(ρ)`, then so is that of `y ↦ L (f y)` for a continuous linear map `L`, by `ContinuousLinearMap.norm_iteratedFDeriv_comp_left`.

**Asymptotic bounds on the derivatives of a bilinear expression.** Along any filter, if the derivatives of order at most `n` of `f` and `g` are `O(ρ₁)` and `O(ρ₂)`, then the order-`n` derivative of `y ↦ B (f y) (g y)` is `O(ρ₁ ρ₂)`, by the Leibniz bound `ContinuousLinearMap.norm_iteratedFDeriv_le_of_bilinear`.
An endomorphism is invertible, that is, a continuous linear equivalence, exactly when it is a unit of the ring of continuous endomorphisms.

A continuous linear map `T : M₁ × M₂ → M₁ × M₃` which preserves the first coordinate is block lower triangular, `T (a, b) = (a, C a + K b)`, so it is invertible exactly when its diagonal block `K = snd ∘ T ∘ inr : M₂ → M₃` is.
The product `f.prodMap g` of two continuous linear maps is invertible exactly when both factors are.
Multiplying a continuous linear map by a nonzero scalar does not change its invertibility.
On a topological semifield, the continuous linear map `a ↦ a • c` is invertible exactly when `c ≠ 0`.

Scaling the identity by a nonzero scalar `c` is invertible, with inverse scaling by `c⁻¹`. The scalars need not commute with operators: for example, multiplication by a nonzero complex number is an invertible real-linear map of `ℂ`.
**The determinant is bounded by the operator norm** over an `RCLike` field: `‖det f‖ ≤ ‖f‖ ^ n` for a linear endomorphism `f` of a normed space of finite dimension `n`.

For a real-linear map `ℓ : E →L[ℝ] ℂ`, the `n`-th derivative of `x ↦ exp (ℓ x)` has norm at most `‖exp (ℓ x)‖ ‖ℓ‖ ^ n`. For a purely imaginary `ℓ`, such as the phase `x ↦ 2πi ⟪x, w⟫` of a character, this is `‖ℓ‖ ^ n`.

**Leibniz bound with uniform constants.** If the derivatives of order at most `N` of `f` and `g` are bounded by `C` and `D` everywhere, those of `x ↦ B (f x) (g x)` of order `p ≤ N` are bounded by `2 ^ p * (C * D)`, for a bilinear map `B` of norm at most one.
A norm bound `‖T x‖ ≤ r` for a continuous linear map on a set `s` extends to the closed real convex hull `closure (convexHull ℝ s)`.
For a real-linear map `Ψ` preserving the symplectic form `Im ⟪·, ·⟫`, the complex-linear part `P` and the complex-antilinear part `A` satisfy `‖P z‖² = ‖z‖² + ‖A z‖²`.
The operator norm of a continuous linear map on an inner product space is at most the sum of the norms of its values on the vectors of an orthonormal basis.
The squared operator norm of a continuous linear map on an inner product space is at most the number of vectors of an orthonormal basis times the sum of the squared norms of its values on them.
The real-linear operator underlying the complex-linear part is `½ (Ψ - i ∘ Ψ ∘ i)`.
Multiplying by a nonzero scalar is composing with the corresponding scalar equivalence.

A critical point of a map yields a critical point of its slice along a level set of a functional `φ`. Precisely, let `(φ, ρ)` be jointly injective on `F`, let `γ` parametrize a family of points along which `φ ∘ f` is locally constant, and let `φ ∘ Df` be nonzero at `γ z`. If `ρ ∘ f ∘ γ` has surjective derivative at `z`, then `Df` is surjective at `γ z`; equivalently, if `γ z` is critical for `f`, then `z` is critical for the slice `ρ ∘ f ∘ γ`.

`ContinuousLinearMap.complexAntilinearPartL` is the algebraic complex-antilinear part `RiemannMasullo.External.TauCeti.complexAntilinearPart` for the complex structures given by multiplication by `i`.
A continuous group isomorphism into a second-countable locally compact group is nonsingular for any Haar measures on its source and target.
An entry `H ![b i, b j]` of a bilinear map on an orthonormal basis `b` has norm at most the operator norm.
A bilinear map whose entries `H ![b i, b j]` on an orthonormal basis `b` are bounded by `B` has operator norm at most `(card ι)² B`.
The operator norm of a continuous multilinear map on inner product spaces is at most the sum of the norms of its values on tuples of vectors of orthonormal bases, one for each argument.

**Inverses of maps out of compact sets are continuous.** If `f` is continuous on a compact set `K` with values in a Hausdorff space, injective on `U ⊆ K`, and no point of `K \ U` has the same image as a point of `U`, then the inverse `invFunOn f U` of `f` on `U` is continuous on `f '' U`.

**Lifting a map which is the identity near a point.** Let `f` be continuous on `Q`, with values in a `T₁` space, and injective on `P` with inverse continuous on `f '' P`. Let `k` be continuous on `f '' Q` and the identity near `y` within `f '' Q`. Suppose that `k ∘ f` maps `Q \ f⁻¹(y)` into `f '' P`, and that every point of `Q \ f⁻¹(y)` mapped into `f '' P` lies in `P`. Then there is a map `g`, continuous on `Q`, with `f ∘ g = k ∘ f` on `Q`, which fixes `Q ∩ f⁻¹(y)` pointwise, maps `Q \ f⁻¹(y)` into `P`, and is injective on every `R ⊆ Q` such that `k` is injective on `f '' R` and `f` is injective on `R \ f⁻¹(y)`.

**Lifting a map of the target through a map injective off one fibre.** Let `f` be continuous on a compact set `K` with values in a Hausdorff space, and injective on `K` away from the fibre `K ∩ f ⁻¹' {y}`. Let `k` be continuous and injective on `f '' K`, equal to the identity on `f '' K` near `y`, and mapping `f '' K` into `f '' (K ∩ U)` for a set `U` containing the fibre. Then there is a map `g`, continuous and injective on `K`, which maps `K` into `K ∩ U`, satisfies `f (g x) = k (f x)` on `K`, and fixes every point `x` of `K` with `k (f x) = f x`.
Under a measure positive on nonempty open sets, an almost everywhere inequality on an open set `U` between functions continuous on `U` into an order-closed space holds at every point of `U`.
A convex set containing the ball `ball x r` and a point `y` contains the ball of radius `(1 - t) * r` about `x + t • (y - x)` for every `0 ≤ t ≤ 1`.
For a closed real-convex set `K ⊆ Ω`, the `Ω`-holomorphic hull of `K` is `K` itself.
For a closed real-convex set `K ⊆ ℂ`, the `Ω`-holomorphic hull of `K` is `K ∩ Ω`.
Every entire function `f : ℂ → ℂ` can be approximated uniformly on any bounded set `K ⊆ ℂ` by polynomials in `Polynomial ℂ`.

**Difference quotients converge uniformly.** If `u` is differentiable with a uniformly continuous derivative, then for every direction `v` the difference quotients `t⁻¹ (u(x + t v) - u(x))` converge to `Du(x) v` uniformly in `x` as `t → 0`.
A function differentiable at `y` is differentiable in its `i`-th variable: the slice `x ↦ f (update y i x)` is differentiable at `y i`.
For complex differentiable `g`, the conjugate Wirtinger derivative vanishes: this is the Cauchy–Riemann equation `\bar∂g = 0`.

A function that satisfies the Hölder bound with constant `K` and exponent `r` between points of `s` at distance less than `δ > 0`, and whose values on `s` lie within distance `D` of each other, is Hölder on `s` with constant `K + D δ^(-r)`. This passes from Hölder bounds on the pieces of a cover of `s` to a Hölder bound on `s`, with `δ` a Lebesgue number of the cover (`lebesgue_number_lemma_of_metric`).
A curve on a set `S` of times with `d(u s, u t)² ≤ c |s - t|` is `1/2`-Hölder continuous on `S` with constant `c ^ (1 / 2)`.

A function that satisfies the `β`-Hölder bound with constant `K` between points of `s` at distance less than `δ > 0`, and whose values on `s` lie within distance `D` of each other, is `γ`-Hölder on `s` for every `γ ≤ β`, with constant `K δ^(β - γ) + D δ^(-γ)`: the `β`-Hölder bound is used at distances less than `δ` and the bound `D` at larger distances. A small scale makes the coefficient of `K` small at the price of a large coefficient of `D`. For `β = 1` the hypothesis is a Lipschitz bound between nearby points, as given by a derivative bound on balls of radius `δ`. Compare Mathlib's `HolderOnWith.of_le`, which bounds the domain instead of the values.
A pointwise limit on `s` of maps that are `r`-Hölder on `s` with a common constant `C` is `r`-Hölder on `s` with constant `C`.
The difference of two Hölder functions on a set has the same exponent and the sum of their Hölder constants.
**Boundedness of the top derivative.** If `f` is `C^(k+2)` with `‖D^k f‖ ≤ M` and `D^(k+2) f` is globally Hölder, then `‖D^(k+2) f‖` is bounded above.
Precomposition with a `1`-Lipschitz map preserves a global Hölder bound, with the same constant and exponent.

**Absorbed interpolation inequalities for the first two derivatives.** If `f` is `C²` with `‖f‖ ≤ M`, and `D²f` is globally `α`-Hölder with constant `H`, then for every scale `0 < ε ≤ 1` both `‖Df x‖` and `‖D²f x‖` are at most `(34 / ε + 32 / ε²) M + 2 H ε^α`.
**Interpolation inequality.** If `g` is differentiable with `‖g‖ ≤ M` and its derivative is globally `α`-Hölder with constant `H`, then `‖fderiv ℝ g x‖ ≤ 2 M / ε + H ε^α` for every `ε > 0`.

**Absorbed interpolation inequality for the top derivative.** If `f` is `C^(k+2)` with `‖D^k f‖ ≤ M` and `D^(k+2) f` is globally `α`-Hölder with constant `H`, then `‖D^(k+2) f x‖ ≤ 32 M / ε² + 2 H ε^α` for every `ε > 0`.

**Absorbed interpolation inequalities with one constant.** If `f` is `C^(k+2)` with `‖D^k f‖ ≤ M` and `D^(k+2) f` is globally `α`-Hölder with constant `H`, then for every scale `0 < ε ≤ 1` both `‖D^(k+1) f x‖` and `‖D^(k+2) f x‖` are at most `(34 / ε + 32 / ε²) M + 2 H ε^α`.

**Absorbed interpolation inequality for the intermediate derivative.** If `f` is `C^(k+2)` with `‖D^k f‖ ≤ M` and `D^(k+2) f` is globally `α`-Hölder with constant `H`, then `‖D^(k+1) f x‖ ≤ 34 M / ε + 2 H ε^(1 + α)` for every `ε > 0`.
**Interpolation inequality for iterated derivatives.** If `‖D^k f‖ ≤ M` and `D^(k+1) f` is globally `α`-Hölder with constant `H`, then `‖D^(k+1) f x‖ ≤ 2 M / ε + H ε^α` for every `ε > 0`.

**Interpolation inequality.** If `g` has derivative `g'` everywhere, `‖g‖ ≤ M`, and `g'` is globally `α`-Hölder with constant `H`, then `‖g' x‖ ≤ 2 M / ε + H ε^α` for every `ε > 0`. With `α = 1` this is the Landau-type inequality `‖g' x‖ ≤ 2 M / ε + L ε` for a derivative that is Lipschitz with constant `L`.
A pointwise limit of maps that are `r`-Hölder with a common constant `C` is `r`-Hölder with constant `C`.
A finite sum of Hölder functions with a common exponent is Hölder, with the sum of the constants.
A homeomorphism maps a connected component onto the connected component of the image point.
Two points are joined by a path exactly when their images under a homeomorphism are.
A homeomorphism induces a bijection of the sets of path components.
The image of a clopen subset under `ConnectedComponents.mk` is clopen in `ConnectedComponents X`.
A clopen subset is saturated for the connected-components equivalence relation: pulling its image in `ConnectedComponents X` back along `ConnectedComponents.mk` recovers `s`.
A connected component of a closed set is closed.

**A compact component of a closed set is cut out by an open set.** In a locally compact Hausdorff space, if the connected component of `x` in a closed set `F` is compact, then it has an open neighbourhood `V` with compact closure whose frontier misses `F`.
For an open set `Ω` and closed `K` in a locally connected pseudometric space, `RiemannMasullo.External.TauCeti.fillIn K Ω` is closed.
For a closed set `K` in a locally connected space, if the frontier of a connected component of `Ω \ K` lies in `interior Ω`, then it lies in `K`.
The frontier of the bounded complementary components of a closed set lies in the set itself. In particular, filling introduces no new boundary points.
If `K ⊆ Ω` is closed in `ℂ`, then `holomorphicHull Ω K` is closed in `ℂ`.
Filling a closed set preserves closedness in a locally connected space.
The bounded complementary components of a closed set form an open set in a locally connected space. No Jordan-curve or finiteness assumption is needed.
For `t ≥ 0`, the outer parallel set `K + t • closedBall 0 1` of a compact set `K` is the closed `t`-thickening of `K`.
**Connected components of a compact set are compact.** The connected component of a compact set `K` at a point is closed in `K`, hence compact; it is empty at a point outside `K`.
In a finite-dimensional topological vector space, the convex hull of a compact set is compact.
A compact set contained in an open set admits a smooth cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of the compact set.

A compact set contained in an open set admits a smooth cutoff that is eventually equal to one near every point of the compact set: the form of `IsCompact.exists_contDiff_cutoff` that is used pointwise.
A compact set contained in an open set admits a smooth cutoff whose value and gradient are bounded by a common nonnegative constant.

**Uniform approximation by functions piecewise constant in the first variable.** A function `K` continuous on a product `s ×ˢ t` of compact sets and zero outside it is within `ε` of a function that is piecewise constant in the first variable on a finite measurable partition of `s`, equal on the piece `P i` to the slice `K (c i)` at a point `c i ∈ s`: the difference is at most `ε` on `s ×ˢ t` and vanishes outside it.

**Local Hölder bounds near a compact set are uniform on a thickening.** If `f` is `α`-Hölder on a ball around each point of a compact set `K`, with radii and constants depending on the point, then on some open thickening of `K` the function `f` is `α`-Hölder with one constant and is bounded.

**Neighbourhoods in a compact set are read through a continuous injection.** Let `f` be continuous and injective on a compact set `K` with values in a Hausdorff space. For `x ∈ K` and a neighbourhood `s` of `x`, there is a neighbourhood `t` of `f x` such that every point of `K` that `f` maps into `t` lies in `s`.
**Compact cofinality in the interior.** Every compact subset `K ⊆ interior Ω` lies inside `interior (filledExhaustion Ω n)` for some `n`.
A family that eventually lies in a compact set `s` along an ultrafilter converges along it to a point of `s`.

**Limits read back through an injective map.** Let `f` be continuous and injective on a compact set `K`, with values in a Hausdorff space, and let `x i` be maps from a space `T` with values in `K` on a set `Ω ⊆ T`. If the maps `f ∘ x i` converge pointwise on `Ω` to a map `g` continuous on `Ω`, then `g = f ∘ y` on `Ω` for a map `y` continuous on `Ω` with values in `K`, and the `x i` converge pointwise on `Ω` to `y`.
In a proper real normed space, filling a compact set `K` inside an open set `Ω` produces a compact set.
If `K ⊆ Ω` is compact, then `holomorphicHull Ω K` is compact.
For compact `K ⊆ ℂ`, the `Ω`-holomorphic hull of `K` lies in its ordinary convex hull `convexHull ℝ K`.

**A continuous injection on a compact set maps components onto components.** If `f` is continuous and injective on a compact set `K` with values in a Hausdorff space, and `A ⊆ K`, then `f` maps the connected component of `A` at a point `x ∈ K` onto the connected component of `f '' A` at `f x`. Both sides are empty when `x ∉ A`.
Compactness of `U ∩ S` for a compact set `U` may be checked on open pieces of `U` around each of its points.
The points of a compact set `C` that a map continuous on `C` sends into a closed set `K` form a compact set.
**A continuous injection on a compact set embeds it.** If `f` is continuous and injective on a compact set `K` with values in a Hausdorff space, then its restriction to `K` is a closed embedding.

**The filled hull of a compact set is compact.** In a locally compact Hausdorff, locally connected space with no compact connected component, a compact set `K` together with the connected components of `Kᶜ` having compact closure is compact. This set is the filled hull of `K` for the bornology of relatively compact sets; points of `K` belong to it because their component in `Kᶜ` is empty.

**Polynomial Runge theorem**: a compact set `K ⊆ ℂ` has connected complement `Kᶜ` if and only if every holomorphic function on an open neighbourhood `U ⊇ K` can be approximated uniformly on `K` by polynomials `p : Polynomial ℂ`.
For compact `K ⊆ ℂ`, the complement `Kᶜ` is connected if and only if the image of `K` in `Fin 1 → ℂ` under the diagonal embedding is polynomially convex.
Every compact subset of the real locus `ℝⁿ ⊆ ℂⁿ` is polynomially convex.
On a compact set, `‖x‖⁻¹` is `Lʳ` for every exponent `r < dim E`.
For compact `K ⊆ Ω`, membership in `holomorphicHull Ω K` is equivalent to the supremum bound `‖f z‖ ≤ sSup ((‖f ·‖) '' K)` for every `Ω`-holomorphic `f` (including `K = ∅`, where `sSup ∅ = 0`).
For compact `K ⊆ Ω`, every `Ω`-holomorphic function `f` satisfies `‖f z‖ ≤ sSup ((‖f ·‖) '' K)` at each point `z ∈ holomorphicHull Ω K`.
If an `Ω`-holomorphic function `f` is strictly smaller in modulus at every point of a compact set `K ⊆ Ω` than at `z`, then `z` is not in `holomorphicHull Ω K`.
If a polynomial is strictly smaller in modulus at every point of a compact set `K` than at `z`, then `z` is not in the polynomial hull of `K`.
**Coincidences of two maps form a compact set.** For maps `f`, `g` into a Hausdorff space, continuous on compact sets `s` and `t`, the pairs `(x, y) ∈ s ×ˢ t` with `f x = g y` form a compact set.
In a T₀ space, a compact closed subset `S` is contained in an open subset `U` as soon as every closed point in `S` belongs to `U`.

**Convergence in a compact set is read through a continuous injection.** Let `f` be continuous and injective on a compact set `K` with values in a Hausdorff space, and let `g` eventually take values in `K`. If `f ∘ g` tends to `f x` for some `x ∈ K`, then `g` tends to `x`.

At a local extremum `w` of `‖ψ‖`, the Fréchet derivative of `ψ` is orthogonal to `ψ w`. This covers a map whose norm is constant near `w`: the derivative of a map into a sphere is tangent to the sphere. At nondifferentiable points, the Fréchet derivative is zero by definition.
**Maximum-principle inclusion.** In an open plane set `Ω`, if the connected component `C` of `z` in `Ω \ K` has compact closure contained in `Ω`, then `closure C` lies in `holomorphicHull Ω K`.
Almost-everywhere equal open sets have the same closure for a measure positive on nonempty open sets. The open sets themselves need not be equal.
In an open plane set `Ω`, every connected component of `Ω \ K` whose closure is compact and contained in `Ω` lies in `holomorphicHull Ω K`.
A nonempty bounded open set in a nontrivial real normed space has positive diameter.

**A smooth decomposition of unity of an open set, with cutoffs.** Every open set `U` of a finite-dimensional real normed space carries smooth compactly supported functions `ζ j` and `χ j`, `j : ℕ`, with topological supports in `U`, such that `χ j = 1` on the topological support of `ζ j`, and every point of `U` has a neighbourhood on which `χ j` vanishes and `∑ j ∈ Finset.range N, ζ j = 1` for all large `j` and `N`. The functions `ζ j` are nonnegative and every partial sum `∑ j ∈ Finset.range N, ζ j` is at most one.

**Filled compact exhaustion.** Every open set `Ω` of a proper real seminormed space is the union of compact sets `K n` with `K n ⊆ interior (K (n + 1))`, each of which is filled in `Ω`: no connected component of `Ω \ K n` is relatively compact in `Ω`.
**Compact cofinality.** Every compact subset `K` of an open set `Ω` lies inside `filledExhaustion Ω n` for some `n`.
Every compact subset `K` of an open plane set `Ω` lies inside the interior of a compact `L` forming a Runge compact pair `(Ω, L)`.
**Compact cofinality (strict).** Every compact subset `K` of an open set `Ω` lies inside `interior (filledExhaustion Ω n)` for some `n`.
A continuous function on the closure of an open set `U` is determined by its values at almost every point of `U`, for a measure which charges every nonempty open set.
For `K ⊆ Ω` with `Ω` open, the fill-in of `K` in `Ω` (`K` together with all relatively compact connected components of `Ω \ K` in `Ω`) lies inside `holomorphicHull Ω K`.
If the connected component of `x` in `Ω \ K` has closure contained in an open set `Ω` of a locally connected space, then its frontier lies in `closure K`.
For an open set `Ω`, the stages `filledExhaustion Ω n` have union `Ω`.

**A closed ball minus a thickening of `Ωᶜ` is filled in `Ω`.** In a real seminormed space, for any open set `Ω`, radius `0 ≤ r`, and `δ : ℝ`, no connected component of `Ω \ (closedBall a r \ thickening δ Ωᶜ)` has compact closure contained in `Ω`.
Every stage `filledExhaustion Ω n` of an open set `Ω` in a real seminormed space is filled in `Ω`.
The `Ω`-holomorphic hull of any set is filled in an open set `Ω`.
Every stage of `RiemannMasullo.External.TauCeti.filledExhaustion Ω` forms a Runge compact pair with an open `Ω ⊆ ℂ`.
For an open set `Ω ⊆ ℂ` and compact `K ⊆ Ω`, `holomorphicHull Ω K` forms a Runge compact pair with `Ω`.

**Points of a component of an open set are joined inside it.** In a locally path-connected space, the connected component of `x` in an open set `U` is open and connected, hence path connected, so it joins `x` to each of its points.
An open set contained almost everywhere in another set is contained in its closure. No measurability assumption on either set is needed.

A subset `U` of a topological space `X` is *path-homotopy-trivial* if any two paths in `X` whose images lie in `U` and which share endpoints are homotopic in `X`. This is the form of "`U` is simply connected" used in the universal-cover construction: it is weaker than `IsSimplyConnected U` because the homotopy is not required to lie inside `U` (`IsSimplyConnected.isPathHomotopyTrivial`).
A loop in a path-homotopy-trivial set is nullhomotopic.
A preconnected open set `u`, disjoint from an open set `v`, is a connected component of `u ∪ v`: it is the component in `u ∪ v` of each of its points.
Two points of a preconnected subset of `s` represent the same connected component of `s`.
A preconnected set disjoint from a bounded `K` that meets its filled hull has diameter at most `diam K`. No regularity is required of `K`.

**A proper component of a cut set reaches the cut.** Let `U` be preconnected and let `U \ S` be open in a locally connected space. If the connected component of `z` in `U \ S` misses some point of `U`, then its closure meets `S ∩ U`.
**A preconnected set that meets both a set and its complement meets its frontier.** If `S` is preconnected and contains a point of `V` and a point outside `V`, then `S` meets `frontier V`.
A preconnected subset of `s` lies in the ambient carrier of any component of `s` containing one of its points.

**Trapping a preconnected set in a component of an open set.** Let `U` be open in a locally connected space and let `C` be the connected component of `x ∈ U` in `U`. A preconnected set `A` through `x` lies in `C` as soon as it meets the closure of `C` only inside `U`. This weakens the hypothesis `A ⊆ U` of `IsPreconnected.subset_connectedComponentIn`.

**A preconnected set that a set cuts off from infinity lies in its filled hull.** If `S` is preconnected and disjoint from `K`, then `S` lies in a single connected component of `Kᶜ`; meeting the filled hull says that component is bounded, so all of `S` is in the hull.
**A preconnected set missing the frontier lies in the interior or in the exterior.** If `S` is preconnected and disjoint from `frontier V`, then `S ⊆ interior V` or `S ⊆ (closure V)ᶜ`.
A preconnected set that meets `V` and misses its frontier lies in `V`: otherwise it would straddle `V` and so meet `frontier V`.
The `δ`-thickening of a preconnected set in a real seminormed space is preconnected.
The union of two σ-compact sets is σ-compact.
**A simply connected set is path-homotopy-trivial.** Two paths with the same endpoints whose ranges lie in a simply connected set are homotopic in the ambient space.
Postcomposition with an isometry preserves a Hölder bound on a set, with the same constant and exponent.
Postcomposition with an isometry preserves a global Hölder bound, with the same constant and exponent.
Postcomposition with an isometry neither creates nor destroys a global Hölder bound: `g ∘ f` is Hölder with constant `C` and exponent `r` exactly when `f` is.
In a totally disconnected space, points joined by a path are equal.
Pointwise a.e. formula for `LinearIsometry.compLpₗᵢ`.
Postcomposing `Lᵖ` classes with a semilinear isometry `f : E →ₛₗᵢ[σ] F`, bundled as a semilinear isometry `Lp E p μ →ₛₗᵢ[σ] Lp F p μ`.
Postcomposition with a linear isometry commutes with `indicatorConstLp`.
A pointwise continuous family of linear isometries acts jointly continuously on `X × Lp E p μ` for `1 ≤ p < ∞`.
The continuous linear map underlying `LinearIsometry.compLpₗᵢ` is `ContinuousLinearMap.compLpL`.
Pointwise a.e. formula for `LinearIsometryEquiv.compLpₗᵢ`.
Postcomposing `Lᵖ` classes with a semilinear isometric equivalence `e : E ≃ₛₗᵢ[σ] F`, bundled as a semilinear isometric equivalence `Lp E p μ ≃ₛₗᵢ[σ] Lp F p μ`.
Postcomposition with a linear isometric equivalence commutes with `indicatorConstLp`.
A pointwise continuous family of linear isometric equivalences acts jointly continuously on `X × Lp E p μ` for `1 ≤ p < ∞`.
Every linear isometry self-equivalence of a finite-dimensional real normed space pushes every additive Haar measure forward to itself.
Every linear isometry self-equivalence of a finite-dimensional real normed space preserves every additive Haar measure on that space.
A real-linear map out of the complex plane is evaluated in the real basis `(1,I)`.
If a real-linear map out of the complex plane sends `I` to `A (L 1)`, where `A` squares to `-1`, then so does its precomposition with multiplication by any `b`: `L (b * I) = A (L b)`.
A real-linear map between complex modules that commutes with multiplication by `I`, as a complex-linear map.

Rotating `L 1 + I • L I` by the conjugate of `e` gives the derivative of `L` along `e` plus `I` times its derivative along `I * e`: the map `e ↦ L e + I • L (I * e)` is conjugate-linear. For `L` the derivative of a map `u` at `w + r e^{iθ}` and `e = e^{iθ}`, these are the radial derivative and `r⁻¹` times the angular derivative of `(r, θ) ↦ u (w + r e^{iθ})`.
A real-linear map out of the complex plane with `L I = A (L 1)`, where `A` squares to `-1`, vanishes as soon as it vanishes at a single nonzero point.

A real-linear map `L` out of the complex plane intertwines multiplication by `I` with an endomorphism `A` squaring to `-1` exactly when `L 1 + A (L I) = 0`: the value at `I` is then determined by the value at `1`.
A real-bilinear map on the complex plane is unchanged by conjugating both arguments exactly when `B 1 I = B I 1 = 0`.
A real-linear map out of the complex plane is unchanged by conjugating its argument exactly when it vanishes at `I`.
A real-linear map between complex modules that anticommutes with multiplication by `I` is conjugate-linear: `u (z • v) = conj z • u v`.
A bounded Lipschitz map is Hölder for every exponent at most one, without a bounded-domain assumption. The scale-one estimate uses the Lipschitz constant plus twice the value bound.
A function that is Lipschitz on `s` is locally Lipschitz on `s`.
The inclusion of a subset into a larger subset is `1`-Lipschitz.
A locally Lipschitz map composed with a function locally Lipschitz on `s` is locally Lipschitz on `s`.

If `f` is locally Lipschitz on a separable set `s` in an extended pseudometric space (for instance any set in a second-countable space, by `TopologicalSpace.IsSeparable.of_separableSpace`), then `s` can be covered by countably many open sets `U n` such that `f` is Lipschitz on each `s ∩ U n`.
If `u` is locally Lipschitz on `s`, then so is `ψ (c (u - t))` for the smooth transition function `ψ`.

**Integral bounds from an exhaustion.** Let `φ` cover `μ`-almost everything along `l`, and let `f` and `g` be almost everywhere nonnegative, with `g` integrable and `f` integrable on each `φ i`. If eventually `∫_{φ i} f ≤ ∫_{φ i} g + e i` with errors `e i → 0`, then `f` is integrable and `∫ f ≤ ∫ g`.
An almost everywhere strongly measurable function is in `L²` exactly when the lower integral of its squared extended norm is finite.
Translation is continuous in the `L¹` distance from a fixed translate.
An integrable function whose norm is almost everywhere at least one can only be carried by a finite measure.

Scalar multiplication by a finite product of multiplicative indicators preserves integrability, when each factor is a constant on a null-measurable set and `1` off it. Neither a finite measure nor disjoint sets are required.
An integrable function times a multiplier bounded on a set containing its support is integrable.
Convergent shifts of an integrable function converge in `L¹`.
The derivative of an improper tail integral is the negated integrand at each continuity point strictly inside the integrable ray.
At a continuity point strictly inside an integrable ray, the tail integral has derivative equal to the negated integrand.
At a continuity point strictly inside an integrable ray, the tail integral is strictly differentiable with derivative equal to the negated integrand.

For `g` integrable on `(x, ∞)`, with tail integral `Ψ v = ∫ u in Ioi v, g u`, the integral of `g * Ψ ^ k` over `(x, ∞)` is `Ψ x ^ (k + 1) / (k + 1)`. This identity is behind the factorial decay of the Picard increments of Volterra integral equations on a half-line.

For a continuous integrand on an integrable ray, the derivative of order `n + 1` of its tail integral is the negated derivative of order `n` of the integrand at each interior point. The identity concerns total iterated derivatives and does not assume higher smoothness.
If `g` is integrable on `(x, ∞)`, with tail integral `Ψ v = ∫ u in Ioi v, g u`, then `v ↦ g v * Ψ v ^ k` is integrable on `(x, ∞)`.
The norm of a nonnegative real `L¹` function is its integral.
A sequence of scalar L² functions with summable squared L² norms is the coordinate family of a single square-integrable function with values in ℓ².
The outer product of two scalar L² functions has L² norm equal to the product of their norms.
The integral of the squared pointwise norm is the square of the L² norm.

A representative `g` of a real `L∞` class `f` agrees almost everywhere with its truncation to `[-‖f‖, ‖f‖]`. The truncation is bounded everywhere by `‖f‖` (`RiemannMasullo.External.TauCeti.abs_max_min_le`).
An `L∞` function is bounded almost everywhere by its norm.
If `u` and `v` are almost everywhere `g` and `h`, then `u + v` is almost everywhere `g + h`.
The equivalence is almost everywhere precomposition by `f`.
The inverse equivalence is almost everywhere precomposition by `g`.
`Lp.imCLM` takes the imaginary part almost everywhere.
If `u` is almost everywhere `g`, then `-u` is almost everywhere `-g`.
`Lp.normLp f` equals `x ↦ ‖f x‖` almost everywhere.
`Lp.ofRealLI` casts representatives from `ℝ` to `𝕜` almost everywhere.
`Lp.reCLM` takes the real part almost everywhere.
If `u` is almost everywhere `g`, then `c • u` is almost everywhere `c • g`.
If `u` and `v` are almost everywhere `g` and `h`, then `u - v` is almost everywhere `g - h`.

The map underlying `MeasureTheory.Lp.compMeasurePreservingₗᵢ` is `MeasureTheory.Lp.compMeasurePreserving`: the unapplied form of `MeasureTheory.Lp.compMeasurePreservingₗᵢ_apply`, for statements about the map itself, such as its monotonicity or its fixed points. Together with Mathlib's simp lemma `LinearIsometry.coe_toContinuousLinearMap` it also normalizes the continuous linear map the isometry induces.
For ordered values, precomposition by a measure-preserving map is monotone on `Lp`.
For ordered values, precomposition by a measure-preserving map sends nonnegative `Lp` classes to nonnegative ones.
Precomposition of the `Lp` class of a continuous function by a measure-preserving continuous map is the `Lp` class of the composite continuous function.
**The `L^p` isometric equivalence induced by an almost-everywhere inverse pair of measure-preserving maps.**
The application lemma for `MeasureTheory.Lp.compMeasurePreservingₗᵢ`.
Translation of a fixed `Lᵖ` class depends continuously on the translation parameter when `p < ∞`.

**Gluing `Lᵖ` classes along a finite cover.** For `1 ≤ p`, let finitely many sets `u i` cover `s`. If each `f i ∈ Lᵖ(u i)` agrees almost everywhere on `u i` with one function `g`, then some class in `Lᵖ(s)` agrees almost everywhere on `s` with `g` and has norm at most `∑ᵢ ‖f i‖`.
Every `Lp` function strongly measurable for the sigma algebra generated by a measure-preserving map lies in the range of its pullback.
On a σ-finite measure space, every nonnegative `c < ‖A‖` is witnessed by a single vector `u : E` and a measurable set `t` with `0 < μ t < ∞` on which `c * ‖u‖ < ‖A x u‖`.
Pointwise imaginary-part operator `Lp 𝕜 p μ →L[ℝ] Lp ℝ p μ`.
Multiplying by `RCLike.I` scales the real part by `RCLike.im (RCLike.I : 𝕜)` in the imaginary coordinate.
When `RCLike.im (RCLike.I : 𝕜) = 1`, `Lp.imCLM` recovers `g` from `I • ofRealLI g`.
When `(RCLike.I : 𝕜) = 0`, `Lp.imCLM` is the zero operator.
Imaginary part vanishes on `Lp.ofRealLI`.
Over `ℝ`, `Lp.imCLM` is the zero operator.
On the zero measure, `Lp E p 0` has `0` as its unique element.
On a finite measure space, the `L¹` norm of an `Lᵖ` function, `1 ≤ p`, is at most `μ(univ)^{1 - 1/p}` times its `Lᵖ` norm.
For `0 < p < ∞`, the integral of the `p`-th power of the pointwise norm of an `Lᵖ` function is the `p`-th power of its `Lᵖ` norm.
The integral of the squared pointwise norm of an `L²` function is its squared `L²` norm.
If `f` and `g` are measure-preserving and `f ∘ g` is the identity almost everywhere, then precomposition by `g` is a left inverse of precomposition by `f` on `Lp`.
Every nonnegative level strictly below the `L∞` norm of `f` is exceeded by `‖f‖` on a set of nonzero measure.
The range of a measure-preserving pullback consists exactly of the `Lp` classes with an almost-everywhere strongly measurable representative for the comap sigma algebra.
Pointwise norm `x ↦ ‖f x‖` bundled as an element of `Lp ℝ p μ`.
`Lp.normLp f` vanishes if and only if `f` vanishes.
`Lp.normLp` is invariant under negation.
`Lp.normLp f` is nonnegative in `Lp ℝ p μ`.
Taking `Lp.normLp` after `Lp.ofRealLI` gives `|f|`.
On `Lp ℝ p μ`, `Lp.normLp` agrees with the lattice absolute value `|f|`.
`Lp.normLp` pulls scalar multiplication out as multiplication by `‖c‖`.
`Lp.normLp` is invariant under the pointwise `star` involution.
`Lp.normLp` sends `0` to `0`.
The norm of an element of `Lᵖ(ν)` is the `Lᵖ` norm of any of its representatives.
On a finite measure space, a function dominated pointwise by `K ‖f‖` for an `Lᵖ` function `f`, `1 ≤ p`, has norm of its integral at most `K μ(univ)^{1 - 1/p} ‖f‖`.
The norm of an `Lᵖ` function dominated pointwise by a two-term combination of two other `Lᵖ` functions obeys the same bound in norm.
**Multiplication by a bounded function.** If `‖ψ‖ ≤ C` almost everywhere and `v = ψ • u` almost everywhere for `u, v ∈ Lᵖ`, then `‖v‖ ≤ C ‖u‖`.
If the measure is positive on nonempty open sets, a representative of an `L∞` class is bounded by its norm at every point where it is continuous.
Taking `Lp.normLp` preserves the `Lᵖ` norm.
An almost everywhere bound on an `L∞` function bounds its norm, whatever the measure. Compare `MeasureTheory.Lp.norm_le_of_ae_bound`, which needs a finite measure.
Isometric scalar inclusion `Lp ℝ p μ →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Lp 𝕜 p μ` for an `RCLike` scalar field `𝕜`.
Every `f : Lp 𝕜 p μ` decomposes into real and imaginary parts in `Lp ℝ p μ`.
Over `ℝ`, `Lp.ofRealLI` is the identity linear isometry.
Pointwise real-part operator `Lp 𝕜 p μ →L[ℝ] Lp ℝ p μ`.
Multiplying by `RCLike.I` sends the real part to minus the imaginary part.
Real part vanishes on `I • ofRealLI g`.
Real part is a left inverse to `Lp.ofRealLI`.
Over `ℝ`, `Lp.reCLM` is the identity continuous linear map.
For an `L²` function `f` on `t`, the integral of `‖f‖²` over a subset `s ⊆ t` is at most the squared `L²` norm of `f`.
In a nontrivial finite-dimensional space, comparing the measures of two concentric balls is comparing their radii, as long as the first radius is nonnegative.
Closed and open balls agree up to a null set in a nontrivial finite-dimensional space.
At nonzero radius, closed and open balls agree up to a null set even in a trivial space.
The measure of `y + r • S`, relative to that of a closed ball of radius `r > 0`, is the measure of `S` relative to that of the closed unit ball.

For a ball of radius `r > 0` in dimension `n`, the ratio `μ (ball 0 1) * (diam (ball x r)) ^ (n + 1) / μ (ball x r)` of real measures is at most `2 ^ (n + 1) * r`. This is the constant of the Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality on a convex domain, evaluated on a ball.
The real measure of a ball of positive radius is the corresponding power of the radius times the real measure of the unit ball.
A real power of the real measure of a ball of radius `r > 0` is `r ^ (n e)` times the same power of the real measure of the unit ball, where `n` is the dimension.

For a ball of radius `r > 0` in dimension `n`, the ratio `μ (ball 0 1) ^ (1 - 1/n) * (diam (ball x r)) ^ n / μ (ball x r)` of real measures is at most `2 ^ n / μ (ball 0 1) ^ (1/n)`, whatever the radius. This is the constant of the localized Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality on a convex domain, evaluated on a ball.

The part of the ball `ball y s` outside the ball `ball z s` of the same radius `s > 0` has measure at most `((s + dist y z)ⁿ - sⁿ)` times the measure of the unit ball, the measure of the shell between the spheres of radii `s` and `s + dist y z` about `z`. Here `n` is the dimension.
A closed ball of radius `R ≤ c r` has at most `cⁿ` times the real measure of a closed ball of radius `r > 0`, whatever their centres, where `n` is the dimension.
The closed ball of radius `c r`, for `c ≥ 0` and `r > 0`, has `cⁿ` times the real measure of the open ball of radius `r` with the same centre, where `n` is the dimension.
The shell between the open ball of radius `r > 0` and the concentric closed ball of radius `s ≥ r` has real measure `(sⁿ - rⁿ)` times the real measure of the unit ball, where `n` is the dimension.

If a set `s` has density at least `c > 0` in `closedBall y ε`, in the sense that `c μ(closedBall y ε) ≤ μ(closedBall y ε ∩ s)`, then for `0 ≤ r ≤ 2 ε` a closed ball of radius `r` has at most `2ⁿ / c` times the `μ.restrict s`-measure of `closedBall y ε`, whatever its centre, where `n` is the dimension.

In a nontrivial finite-dimensional space, `{x | μ (ball 0 ‖x‖) < m}` is the centered open ball of `μ`-measure `m` when `m` is finite, and the whole space when `m = ∞`; in both cases its measure is `m`.
A null-measurable set inside a closed ball of radius `r`, with the measure of some closed ball of radius `r`, agrees up to a null set with the ball containing it.
Translation by `h` is almost everywhere precomposition by addition of `h`.
Translation of a fixed `Lᵖ` class depends continuously on the translation parameter when `p < ∞`.

Hölder's inequality on a ball: for `p₀ ≤ p`, the `L^{p₀}` norm on `B(x₀, R)` is at most the `L^p` norm times `(Rⁿ |B(0, 1)|)^{1/p₀ - 1/p}`, where `n` is the dimension. For `R > 0` this factor is `|B(x₀, R)|^{1/p₀ - 1/p}`; for `R ≤ 0` the ball is empty, so the inequality holds trivially and the factor need not be the volume.
The `Lᵖ` extended norm of a translation increment is its pointwise `eLpNorm`.
Every finite nonnegative value is the measure of a centered ball in a nontrivial finite-dimensional real normed space.
For a ball of radius `r > 0` in dimension `n`, `n / r` times its real measure is `n rⁿ⁻¹` times the real measure of the unit ball, the derivative in `r` of its measure.
Two Haar measures on a second-countable locally compact group are positive finite multiples of each other, so they compare sets the same way.
The real measure of the ball of radius `ρ` about `x`, as a function of `ρ`, has derivative `n rⁿ⁻¹` times the real measure of the unit ball at every `r > 0`, where `n` is the dimension.
Every finite Haar measure on a locally compact group is invariant under inversion.

A left-invariant measure on a second-countable locally compact group that is finite on compact sets and agrees with a Haar measure on a single set of positive finite Haar measure coincides with that Haar measure.
A left-invariant measure with the same total mass as a finite Haar measure on a locally compact group coincides with it.
Every finite Haar measure on a locally compact group is right-invariant.
A homothety of nonzero ratio `r` pushes an additive Haar measure to its multiple by `|r ^ n|⁻¹`, where `n` is the dimension.
**Image of an additive Haar measure under an invertible affine map.** The image of `μ` under `x ↦ c + A x` is `μ` scaled by the reciprocal absolute determinant `|det A|⁻¹`.

A power of the distance to a point is not integrable for an additive Haar measure on a nontrivial finite-dimensional space, for every real exponent: integrability near the point needs `-finrank < p` and integrability away from it needs `p < -finrank`.

If a set `s` has density at least `c` in `closedBall x r`, `r > 0`, in the sense that `c μ(closedBall x r) ≤ μ(closedBall x r ∩ s)`, then the `μ.restrict s`-measure of the ball is at least `c rⁿ μ(closedBall 0 1)`, where `n` is the dimension.
A product of two finite product measures is determined by its coordinate rectangles.
In a nontrivial finite-dimensional space, restricting an additive Haar measure to a closed ball or to the open ball of the same radius gives the same measure.
At nonzero radius, restricting an additive Haar measure to a closed ball or to the open ball of the same radius gives the same measure, even in a trivial space.
A closed ball in which a set `s` has density at least `c > 0`, in the sense that `c μ(closedBall y ε) ≤ μ(closedBall y ε ∩ s)`, charges `μ.restrict s`.

Hölder's inequality on a ball, in scale-invariant form: for `0 < p₀ ≤ p`, `R > 0` and `f` in `L^p` on `B = B(x₀, R)` in dimension `n`, `R^(-n/p₀) ‖f‖_{L^{p₀}(B)}` is at most `|B(0, 1)|^(1/p₀ - 1/p) R^(-n/p) ‖f‖_{L^p(B)}`.

A function bounded by `B` almost everywhere on the ball `B(x₀, R)` of radius `R > 0`, in dimension `n`, has scale-invariant `L^p` norm there at most a constant times `B`: `R^(-n/p) ‖f‖_{L^p(B(x₀, R))} ≤ |B(0, 1)|^(1/p) B`. For `p ≤ 0` the `L^p` norm vanishes.

In a finite-dimensional real normed space, the points whose centered norm-radius ball has measure strictly below that of the centered radius-`r` ball form exactly that ball. No sign condition on `r` is needed.
The square root of the real measure of a ball of radius `R` is `R ^ (n / 2)` times that of the unit ball, where `n` is the dimension.
Translations by vectors tending to zero of `Lᵖ` classes converging to `g` converge to `g`, when `p < ∞`.
Translation by `h` on `Lᵖ`, as a linear isometric equivalence: almost everywhere it sends `f` to `f (· + h)`, and its inverse is translation by `-h`.
Translating by `h₁ + h₂` is translating by `h₂` and then by `h₁`, so these equivalences give a left action even when addition is not commutative.
The inverse of translation by `h` is translation by `-h`.
Translation by zero is the identity on `Lᵖ`.
A function in `Lᵖ` with `p ≠ 0` is finite almost everywhere.
The translate of the `Lᵖ` class of `f` by `h` is almost everywhere `f (· + h)`.

An `Lᵖ` function remains `Lᵖ` after translation on any set whose translate lies in the original domain. This is the restricted-domain counterpart of precomposition by `MeasureTheory.Measure.translateLp`.
For a positive real order `p` and an almost everywhere nonnegative `g` in `Lᵖ`, the `p`-th power of its `eLpNorm` equals `ENNReal.ofReal` of its Bochner `p`-th moment.
For `0 < q < ∞`, the `q`-th power of the `L^q` norm of `f` is the norm of the integral of `‖f‖ ^ q`.
The `L²` seminorm of a square-integrable function is the square root of the integral of its squared pointwise norm.
For a function `g` in `L²(t)`, the squared distance `‖g - c‖²` to a constant `c` is integrable on every subset `s ⊆ t` of finite measure.
A function in `Lᵖ(t)`, `1 ≤ p`, is integrable on every subset `s ⊆ t` of finite measure.
For a positive real order `p`, if `g` lies in `Lᵖ` then `g ^ p` is integrable.
On a finite measure space, the `L¹` norm of a function in `Lᵖ`, `1 ≤ p`, is at most `μ(univ)^{1 - 1/p}` times its `Lᵖ` norm. This is `MeasureTheory.Lp.integral_norm_le_mul_norm` for a representative.
For a positive real order `p` and an almost everywhere nonnegative `g` in `Lᵖ`, the lower integral of `ENNReal.ofReal (g y) ^ p` equals `ENNReal.ofReal` of the Bochner `p`-th moment.

On a set `s` of finite measure, a function in `Lᵖ(s)`, `1 ≤ p < ∞`, bounded almost everywhere on `s` by `M` has `Lᵖ(s)` norm at most `μ(s)^{1/p} M`. Unlike `MeasureTheory.Lp.norm_le_of_ae_bound`, no sign condition on `M` is needed.
On a finite measure space, a function in `Lᵖ` bounded almost everywhere in norm by `C ≥ 0` has `Lᵖ` norm at most `measureUnivNNReal μ ^ p.toReal⁻¹ * C`.
The squared `L²` norm of the class of a square-integrable function is the integral of its squared pointwise norm.
A function in `Lᵖ` on each of finitely many sets is in `Lᵖ` on every set they cover.

Hölder's inequality for the `L²` mass on a ball: for `2 ≤ q` and a function `g` in `L^q(t)`, the integral of `‖g‖²` over a ball `B(x, r) ⊆ t` of radius `r > 0` is at most `‖g‖²_{L^q(t)} |B(0, 1)|^{1 - 2/q} r^{n (1 - 2/q)}`, where `n` is the dimension.

**Hölder's inequality for the `L²` mass on a subset.** For `2 ≤ q` and a function `g` in `L^q(t)`, the integral of `‖g‖²` over a subset `s ⊆ t` of finite measure is at most `‖g‖²_{L^q(t)} μ(s)^{1 - 2/q}`.
Translation increments of an `Lᵖ` function tend to zero as the translation tends to zero.
The `Lp` class of a pointwise finite sum `fun x ↦ ∑ i ∈ s, f i x` of `Lᵖ` functions is the sum of their `Lp` classes.
The `Lp` class of a finite sum of `Lᵖ` functions is the sum of their `Lp` classes.
Integrating against a complex density measure multiplies the integrand by the density.

If a kernel agrees product-almost everywhere with a continuous function of two separately measurable parameters, then the agreement holds almost everywhere on the diagonal at which the kernel is jointly continuous.
On a discrete space, a measure positive on nonempty open sets charges every point, so almost everywhere means everywhere.
If `f` is nonnegative on `(a, ∞)` and integrable on `(x, ∞)` for every `x > a`, then its tail integral `x ↦ ∫ v in Ioi x, f v` is antitone on `(a, ∞)`.
A pointwise continuous linear family of integrable functions on a first countable barrelled space depends continuously on its parameter in the L¹ norm.
**Subadditivity of `eLpNorm` in the measure.** For `1 ≤ p`, `eLpNorm f p (μ + ν) ≤ eLpNorm f p μ + eLpNorm f p ν`.

The `p`-th power of the `Lᵖ` seminorm is subadditive under adding measures. For `p = 0` or `p = ∞`, `p.toReal = 0` and the bound reduces to `1 ≤ 1 + 1`. No measurability is assumed: if the function is not almost everywhere strongly measurable for one of the measures, its seminorm there is `∞`. The codomain needs a pseudometrizable topology and an extended norm.

**Monotone convergence for the `Lᵖ` seminorm.** The `Lᵖ` seminorm of the pointwise supremum of an almost everywhere increasing sequence of almost everywhere measurable functions with values in `[0, ∞]` is the supremum of their `Lᵖ` seminorms.
If `∫ ‖k‖ ^ q ≤ t ^ q` then `‖k‖_q ≤ t`.
If `‖k x‖ ^ q ≤ t ^ (q - p) ‖f x‖ ^ p` pointwise, where `t = ‖f‖_p`, then `‖k‖_q ≤ t`.

**Subadditivity of `eLpNorm` over a finite union.** For `1 ≤ p`, the `Lᵖ` seminorm of `f` on a finite union of sets is at most the sum of its `Lᵖ` seminorms on the pieces. The sets need not be measurable or disjoint.
**Subadditivity of `eLpNorm` over a finite cover.** For `1 ≤ p`, the `Lᵖ` seminorm of `f` on a set covered by finitely many sets is at most the sum of its `Lᵖ` seminorms on the pieces.

Scaled comparisons of `Lᵖ` seminorms on each summand pass to a countable sum of measures, for every exponent, including `0` and `∞`. The functions may have different codomains with extended norms, and no measurability assumptions are needed.
The pointwise supremum over a nonempty finset of integrable functions with values in a normed lattice is integrable.
Multiplication by an almost everywhere measurable real coefficient preserves integrability exactly when its absolute value does, without assuming measurability of the vector-valued `f`.
Splitting a finite set of integration variables into two disjoint parts separates a function on one block from a product of functions on the other block.

For a positive real order `p`, an `eLpNorm` bound between almost everywhere nonnegative real-valued functions with `v ∈ Lᵖ` yields the corresponding Bochner `p`-th moment inequality; no separate `MemLp` or measurability hypothesis on `u` is needed.
The integral of a pointwise continuous linear family of integrable functions on a first countable barrelled space is a continuous linear functional.
For `p ≠ 0, ∞`, the integral of `‖f‖ₑ ^ p` is the `p`-th power of the `Lᵖ` seminorm of `f`.
If `‖f‖_q ≤ M` for `M ≠ 0, ∞`, then `∫ M ^ (r - q) ‖f‖ ^ q ≤ M ^ r` for every real `r`.
The `Lᵖ` norm of a function depends only on its almost everywhere class.
The `Lᵖ(ν)` norm of a function agreeing `ν`-almost everywhere with an element of `Lᵖ(ν')`, for `ν ≤ ν'`, is at most the norm of that element.
**Monotonicity of `lpNorm` in the measure.** If `f ∈ Lᵖ(μ)` and `ν ≤ μ`, then `lpNorm f p ν ≤ lpNorm f p μ`.
**Comparing `lpNorm` across a cutoff.** If `ψ = 1` on a measurable set `t` and `ψ • f ∈ Lᵖ(μ)`, then the `Lᵖ` norm of `f` on `t` is at most that of `ψ • f`.

**Subadditivity of `lpNorm` over a finite cover.** For `1 ≤ p`, the `Lᵖ` norm of `f` on a set covered by the sets `s i`, `i ∈ t`, is at most the sum of its `Lᵖ` norms on the pieces, provided `f` is in `Lᵖ` on each piece.

If an almost-everywhere strongly measurable function `f : α → 𝕜` into a normed division ring satisfies `ε ≤ ‖f x‖` almost everywhere for some `ε > 0`, then its pointwise inverse `x ↦ (f x)⁻¹` is essentially bounded (`MemLp · ∞ μ`).

If an almost-everywhere strongly measurable function `f : α → 𝕜` into a normed division ring satisfies `ε ≤ ‖f x - z‖` almost everywhere for some `ε > 0`, then `x ↦ (z - f x)⁻¹` is essentially bounded (`MemLp · ∞ μ`).
If `H`, `S` and `T` are disjoint, with `S` and `T` measurable, then the integral of `f` over `S` is bounded by its integrals over `H ∪ (S ∪ T)`, `H` and `T`.
A function that is nonzero at an atom of infinite mass is not integrable.
An integral over `T` splits along finitely many pairwise disjoint measurable sets `A i ⊆ T` into the integral over the rest `T \ ⋃ i, A i` plus the sum of the integrals over the `A i`.
The pairing of an integrable function `f` on `Ω` with a function `g` bounded by `S` on `V ⊆ Ω` is at most `S ∫_Ω |f|`.
The Lebesgue integral of `‖f‖ₑ ^ 2` over `A` is the `ENNReal.ofReal` of the Bochner integral of `‖f‖ ^ 2`, when `‖f‖ ^ 2` is integrable on `A`.
A bound on the Bochner integral of `‖f‖ ^ 2` over `A` bounds the Lebesgue integral of `‖f‖ₑ ^ 2`.
Integrability with respect to a measure on a type with measurable singletons implies summability of the singleton masses weighted by the norms of the function values.
L² convergence implies convergence of the integral of the squared norm, for any measure and any normed additive group of values.
**The extended Hölder seminorm of a composition.** If `f` is `α`-Hölder and `g` is `β`-Hölder, then the `α β`-Hölder seminorm of `f ∘ g` is at most `eHolderNorm α f * eHolderNorm β g ^ α`.

**The Hölder seminorm of a composition.** If `f` is `α`-Hölder and `g` is `β`-Hölder, then the `α β`-Hölder seminorm of `f ∘ g` is at most `nnHolderNorm α f * nnHolderNorm β g ^ α`. For a `K`-Lipschitz `g` (`β = 1`) the factor is at most `K ^ α`.
The difference of two `r`-Hölder functions is `r`-Hölder. Compare `MemHolder.add`.
For a locally finite measure that is positive on nonempty open sets, closed balls of small positive radius around a point have positive finite measure.
From any point `x ∈ closure s` in a real seminormed space, the ordinary distance to `frontier s` equals the ordinary distance to `sᶜ`.
For a nonempty set in a pseudometric space, the extended distance to it equals a nonnegative real number exactly when the real distance does.
From any point `x ∈ closure s` in a real seminormed space, the extended distance to `frontier s` equals the extended distance to `sᶜ`.
In a proper space, a measure that is positive on nonempty open sets and finite on compact sets gives every ball of positive radius positive real measure.
In a proper space, a measure that is positive on nonempty open sets and finite on compact sets gives every closed ball of positive radius positive real measure.
If sets `A i` approach a closed set `Z` in the Hausdorff extended distance, then every limit of points `y i ∈ A i` lies in `Z`.

For any subsets `S` and `T` of a pseudometric space, the infimum over `z ∈ S` of the ordinary distance `infDist z T` equals `(⨅ z ∈ S, ⨅ ζ ∈ T, edist z ζ).toReal` (evaluating to `0` on both sides when `S` or `T` is empty).
If sets `A i` approach `B i` and `B i` approach `Z` in the Hausdorff extended distance, then `A i` approach `Z`.
A vector lies in the real span of a complex basis exactly when its coordinates are real.
**Multilinear maps in coordinates.** For finite bases `b i` of the modules `M i`, `f m = ∑ s, (∏ i, (b i).repr (m i) (s i)) • f (fun i ↦ b i (s i))`.
Sending every variable to `X` is surjective onto `R[X]` when there is at least one variable.
For the substitution `Tᵢ ↦ aᵢ X` of `R[Tᵢ : i ∈ σ]` into `R[X]`, the coefficient of `X` in the image of `p * Tᵢ` is `aᵢ` times the constant coefficient of `p`.
A nonzero polynomial is nonzero on a dense set, even with infinitely many variables. Only the perfect T1 topology on the coefficient domain is needed.
A polynomial whose evaluation equals `c` on a neighbourhood of some assignment is the constant polynomial `C c`, even with infinitely many variables.
Evaluating the diagonal specialization `aeval (Function.const σ Polynomial.X) p` at `w` equals evaluating `p` at the constant tuple `Function.const σ w`.
Renaming every variable to `X_c` is the map sending every variable to `X`, followed by `X ↦ X_c`.
A rational upper bound on the ratio `α / r`, expressed as a comparison of powers.
For a base greater than one, real powers are ordered exactly by their exponents.
**Reciprocal radius interval dictionary.** For a base `c > 1`, the interval `c ^ (-α/a) ≤ c ^ (-r) ≤ c ^ (-α/b)` is equivalent to `a ≤ α / r ≤ b` when `r`, `a`, and `b` are positive.
A rational lower bound on the ratio `α / r`, expressed as a comparison of powers.

A set `K ⊆ ℂⁿ` is polynomially convex if it contains its polynomial hull. **Polynomial polyhedron neighbourhoods.** A compact polynomially convex set `K ⊆ ℂⁿ` with an open neighbourhood `U` has a polynomial polyhedron neighbourhood `P = closedBall 0 R ∩ ⋂_{p ∈ s} {|p| ≤ 1}` inside `U`, for a radius `R > 0` and a finite set `s` of polynomials, such that `K` lies in the open subset `ball 0 R ∩ ⋂_{p ∈ s} {|p| < 1}` of `P`. decls.summary: , with Proposition 10.2.2.2, pp. 446–447. For the strip jets themselves and their biorthogonal vectors: the vectors form a normalized family and one constant bounds the products of the norms of a jet and of its biorthogonal vector, if and only if the norms of the jets have a common upper bound and one constant bounds those products. So, granted the bound for the products that p. 451 asks for, the lower bound for the biorthogonal vectors in (10.4.2.24) is exactly the upper bound of Proposition 10.2.2.2. This is the one place after §10.2 where that upper bound, and with it the multiplicity bound (#7220) and the finiteness of the lines (#7453), is used, and it disappears when each jet is divided by its norm (`spectralStripMarkushevichBasis_unitNormalized_primal_normalized_iff`).

decls.summary: Take a spectral Markushevich basis whose functionals are the strip jets. Dividing each functional by the norm of its jet, and multiplying its vector by that norm, gives a spectral Markushevich basis again. Its functionals are the jets divided by their norms, they have norm one, and for every index the product of the norms of the vector and of the functional is the same as before.

decls.summary: , and (10.4.2.24), p. 463. Divide each strip jet by its norm and multiply its biorthogonal vector by that norm. The vectors so obtained form a normalized family, in the sense of Terminology 10.2.1.2, if and only if one constant bounds the products of the norms of a jet and of its biorthogonal vector. Their norms are at least one in any case. So for the jets divided by their norms, the bounds of (10.4.2.24) are the bound that p. 451 asks for, and no upper bound for the norms of the jets enters.

decls.summary: , with Remark 10.2.1.5, p. 444, and (10.4.2.24), p. 463. There is a spectral Markushevich basis of the strip quotient whose functionals are the strip jets divided by their norms, hence of norm one, and whose vectors have norm at least one. So the functionals form a normalized family and the vectors a regular family, with no hypothesis on the zeros. What is not proved, and what the multiplicity bound (#7220) and the finiteness of the lines (#7453) would not give either, is an upper bound for the norms of the vectors.

decls.summary: In the trace class of a Hilbert space, a family whose finite sums are bounded in trace norm (a weakly unconditionally Cauchy family) is unconditionally summable, so its finite sums away from a large finite set are small. Proved here directly, by a gliding-hump argument in the trace class (#7459). Classically, by the theorem of Bessaga and Pełczyński (Studia Math. 17 (1958), 151–164; Albiac–Kalton, *Topics in Banach Space Theory*, Theorem 2.4.11) this holds in every Banach space containing no copy of `c₀`. The trace class contains none: it has cotype 2 (N. Tomczak-Jaegermann, Studia Math. 50 (1974), 163–182), and it is weakly sequentially complete as the predual of `B(H)` (Takesaki, *Theory of Operator Algebras I*, Ch. III §5). Only countably many members of such a family are nonzero, and the countable case is the cited one.

On the trivial rational component with no finite places, a = 1/2 and s = 2, let γ be the first positive ordinate of a critical-line zeta zero. The vector v(x) = exp(-iγx)/(1+x²) is orthogonal to theta by the Mellin zero. Use the nonzero half-weighted theta profile G of (3u² - 2πu⁴) exp(-πu²) with integer indicators at finite places. The inner products of the translates v(x-t) with G cannot vanish for all t > 0. Up to a phase they convolve G(x) exp(iγx)(1+x²) with 1/(1+x²). That convolution is real analytic and its Fourier multiplier is nowhere zero. A nonnegative test bump near a positive t with nonzero inner product still pairs nontrivially, and a sufficiently large fixed symmetric cutoff preserves a nonzero part of its geometric projection. Every right PW projection kills v.

Use the trivial rational isotype, no finite places, a = 1/2 and s = 2. As the radial test translates to positive log-norm, its convolution after a fixed spatial cutoff has trace norm tending to zero. The claimed scalar convergence would give the same decay for the cut spectral trace. A Schwartz filter in the translation parameter isolates a certified critical-line ordinate. Its rank-one trace has constant nonzero modulus for a suitably large cutoff, contradicting the decay.
Every point of the full global finite-place orbit admits a full-idele transporter into the half-open section, unique up to embedded local valuation-ring units. See ERRATA R1.

Over ℚ take the norm section with real coordinate t and finite coordinates 1, and take x to be the 2-adic-zero base point. Both 1 and the idele with 2-adic coordinate 2 and all other coordinates 1 fix x at the included left endpoint. Their ratio is outside the embedded local valuation-ring units.
The global norm-one orbit map is a quotient map for the adelic subspace topology on the target. See ERRATA R12.

Over ℚ, let U be the norm-one orbit points with real component zero and all finite components in the local unit groups. The preimage of U is open because the real-zero base point is isolated among the base points and the integral finite ideles form an open subgroup. Replacing the p-coordinate of the real-zero base point by p gives points outside U that tend to that base point. They are norm-one translates via ideles with real coordinate p.
The global norm-one orbit union is locally compact in the adelic subspace topology. See ERRATA R13.

Over ℚ, take the real-zero base point. In any basic neighbourhood choose infinitely many distinct unrestricted primes p₁, p₂, … and replace the components at p₁, …, pₙ by p₁, …, pₙ. These are norm-one translates using ideles with real coordinate p₁⋯pₙ. Their limit in the adeles has infinitely many finite nonunit components and lies outside the orbit union. A compact neighbourhood would be closed in the ambient Hausdorff space and contain this limit.

Over ℚ use the real Gaussian, the indicator of `1 + 3ℤ₃` at 3 and the indicators of ℤₚ at every other prime. This is Schwartz–Bruhat. At the adelic point with real coordinate 0, 3-adic coordinate 1 and other finite coordinates 0 it has value 1. Changing the 3-adic coordinate to −1 gives value 0. Every product allowed in the printed decomposition is invariant under this change, because an additive subgroup is invariant under negation.

Over ℚ take the norm section through the real place, any norm-one domain (it contains one), Kᵥ = ℤᵥ at every prime, and f∞ a smooth bump on ℝ equal to one on [−1, 1] and zero outside (−2, 2). For an integer N ≥ 1 the idele g with g∞ = 1 and diagonal finite components N is allowed. The left sum is a finite sum over ξ ∈ N⁻¹ℤ − {0} and is at least N, from ξ = k/N with 0 < k ≤ N, while the right side does not depend on N.

Over ℚ, take g = 1 and let f be a real smooth bump supported in `(1/2, 3/2)` with f∞(1) = 1, times `1_{1+3ℤ₃}` at 3 and `1_{ℤₚ}` elsewhere. Including the zero terms, the left side sums f∞ over the integers congruent to 1 modulo 3 and gives 1. The printed Fourier sum equals the sum of the corrected Fourier transform of f with its finite inputs negated. By Poisson summation for the corrected character, this sums f∞ over integers congruent to −1 modulo 3 and gives 0.
With the displayed projective tensor topology, multiplication of the two factors realizes the tensor product as a closed subspace of adelic Schwartz functions.

Over ℚ choose a basis of the finite test space and flat real functions supported in (2,3). In the ambient locally convex direct sum one continuous seminorm can use derivative order j on basis coordinate j. Projective continuity would bound all those orders by one continuous archimedean seminorm with a separate constant per coordinate. A fixed bump times exp(i n x) contradicts this bound.
The theta image of the printed unrestricted archimedean-flat tests is a nonzero closed subspace contained in the zero-moment theta image.

Over ℚ with the trivial character, tensor a nonnegative nonzero smooth bump supported in (2,3) with the indicator of the finite integral adeles. The test is archimedean-flat and its Fourier value at zero is its strictly positive integral. That value survives on the trivial homogeneous theta quotient, so no zero-moment test represents the same class.

Let S be stationary in ω₁ with stationary complement and let X = S ∪ {ω₁} have the subspace topology from ω₁ + 1. Take E = C(X, ℂ) with compact convergence and F = ℂ. The space X is zero-dimensional and Lindelöf, so every seminorm bounded on bounded sets is controlled by a compact support. Its completion is C(S, ℂ) × ℂ with compact convergence on S. Each continuous function on S is eventually constant. The norm of its eventual value is a seminorm bounded on bounded sets, since countably many stabilization ordinals have a countable supremum. It is discontinuous, since one can set the function to zero on any prescribed compact set and to one on a tail.

Both radial moments vanish by integration by parts, and all nontrivial norm-one characters vanish by orthogonality. On the critical line translation multiplies each Mellin value by a phase, so absolute convergence bounds the capped zero sum uniformly in `X`. Write `J = ∫ f(u) exp(u/2) du > 0`. The polar sum is `(π/4) J exp(X/2) + O(exp(−X/2))` by the norm-one Tamagawa volume. The archimedean term is `O(exp(−X/2))`. On each finite shell of norm `qᵐ > 1`, the term in (13.3.1.5) before the minus sign is `log(q) · q^(−m/2) · f(m log q − X)` times the integer-unit mass. That mass is one off the prime above two, whose contribution is `O(exp(−X/2))`. The prime ideal theorem and partial summation give `J exp(X/2) + o(exp(X/2))` for the finite sum. Thus the printed right side grows in magnitude like `(1 − π/4) J exp(X/2)` for large `X`.
The common test subspace for all the character jets in (13.3.1.2) is claimed to have codimension `[F : ℚ]`.

Take `F = ℚ`, the section with positive real component and finite components one, and identify the norm-one classes with `ℤ̂ˣ`. Let `ω` be the nontrivial character of `(ℤ/4ℤ)ˣ`, pulled back along the projection from `ℤ̂ˣ`. For a smooth compactly supported bump `b` with integral one, the tests `b(log t)` and `b(log t) · conj (ω(k))` on `(t,k)` have, respectively, moment pairs `(1,0)` and `(0,1)` for the trivial character and `ω`, by Haar orthogonality. The common kernel therefore has codimension at least two.
For every compactly supported continuous multiplier in the target variable, smoothening the multiplied kernel gives the pointwise product of the multiplier with the smoothened kernel.
The pointwise identity is refuted by the counterexample above: at the identity the two sides are one and zero.
The printed choice `δ = α η(|T - t₀|)` is claimed to place the entire contour inside the region specified by the width `η`.

Take `t₀ = 0`, `t = 2`, `T = 4`, and `c = 1`. At the top left corner the shifted height is 6. Take the trivial character over the rationals and any genuine logarithmic zero-free width from Proposition B.6.1.1, shrinking its numerator to ensure the range condition. For every such width, `η(6) / η(4) < 1`. Choose `α` strictly between that ratio and one.
The last sentence asserts that at every pair in the group product, regularity for the indented lift is equivalent to regularity of the quotient pair for the original kernel.

Use additive `G = ℤ × ℝ`, `H = ℤ × {0}`, counting times Lebesgue measure, `D = {0} × ℝ`, and `U n = {0} × (−2⁻ⁿ, 2⁻ⁿ)`. Put `a(t) = 3/4 + sgn(t) min(1, |t|^(1/8))/4`. The indentation is `a(t)` on the integer slice 0, `1 − a(t)` on slice 1, and zero on the others. On the quotient use the rank-one kernel `u(t,s) = g(t) χ(s)`, where `χ(t) = max(0, min(1, 2 − |t|))` and `g(t) = χ(t) sgn(t) |t|^(−1/4)` for `t ≠ 0`, with `g(0) = 0`. At the origin the quotient averages are zero by oddness, but the lift averages over squares of radius `r = 2⁻ⁿ` are `r^(−1/8)/7` and diverge. For the truncation extension, Xⁿ converges to zero for every fixed coefficient maximum, while the sum of absolute coefficients is continuous in the finest locally convex topology and has value one on each Xⁿ. For any extension p, scale Xⁿ by λₙ = ((n + 1)(1 + max_{k ≤ n} pₖ(Xⁿ)))⁻¹. All pₖ tend to zero on λₙXⁿ, while the seminorm summing absolute coefficients with weights 1/|λₙ| takes value one on each λₙXⁿ. The same argument applies to Theorem 5.3.2.5(1), p. 246.
Take one normal coordinate, no tangential coordinates and N = 0. The zero multi-index is the sole slot and supplies the coefficient for the point mass at zero. The printed count is 0¹.

Reading “of order” as the least order, a distribution of order N with compact support contained in the coordinate plane admits coefficients in (5.3.2.4) of exact order N − |α|, each with compact support. The repaired statement is `distribution_coordinatePlane_decomposition`. See ERRATA F48.

Take one normal coordinate, no tangential coordinates, N = 1 and T = δ₀ + δ₀′. A compactly supported test equal to one near zero forces the zero-index coefficient to send one to one. Every distribution on a point has order at most zero, while the formula requires exact order one for that coefficient.
