If V has dense image in the quotient and its intersection with the kernel is dense in the kernel, a normalized quotient Schauder basis has a Schauder lift in V that is stable under kernel perturbations.

Take complex ℓ², E₀ = 0, and V the dense subspace of finitely supported sequences. Choose an orthonormal basis starting with the normalization of (2⁻ʲ)ⱼ. Its first lift would have to equal that vector by biorthogonality, but the vector has infinite support.

A normalized Schauder or Markushevich quotient basis has bounded biorthogonal lifts forming a normalized Schauder basis of their closed span, stable under small perturbations in the kernel. The Banach-space Markushevich condition uses point separation by the dual family, equivalently weak-star density of its span.

In complex ℓ² take E₀ = 0 and V = E. With its standard unit vectors eⱼ, choose x₂ₖ = e₂ₖ and x₂ₖ₊₁ = (e₂ₖ + dₖ e₂ₖ₊₁)/sqrt(1 + dₖ²), where dₖ = 1/(k+1). The inverse change of coordinates on each two-dimensional block gives continuous biorthogonal functionals whose common kernel is zero. The partial-sum projection up to x₂ₖ sends e₂ₖ₊₁ to −(k+1)e₂ₖ, so these projections are unbounded. Biorthogonality forces the lift to be x itself.
In dimension one take rₙ = 1 + 2⁻ⁿ. Every ball and cube contains the point with coordinate 1, so none is contained in the neighborhood (−1, 1) of zero.

Take the trivial discrete group `Unit` with counting Haar measure, `U k = {1}` for all `k`, `C = 2`, `F = ∅` and `B = ∅`. The hypotheses hold, and there can be no selected center. The only possible family is empty, whose mass would have to be strictly above zero.

Take the rational field, the trivial character, and the places consisting of infinity and the prime above two. Both sign conditions apply at index zero, so `T 0 = 0`. The only finite factor in the denominator is then `|1 - 2^0| = 0`.

Take F = ℚ, S consisting of the real place, and the quadratic character modulo 3. The idele with component −1 at 3 and 1 everywhere else is a unit outside S and has norm one. Its S-projection is the identity, while the global character takes value −1 there.

Take the logarithmic profile `f(x) = χ(exp x) exp(-x)`, with `χ(t) = Real.smoothTransition (t - 1)`. It vanishes for `x ≤ 0` and is Schwartz in `x`. Its zero extension in the `t` coordinate equals `1/t` for `t ≥ 2`, so the weight `t²` makes it unbounded.

For each unramified quasi-character at a finite place, there exists a unique eigendistribution taking value one on the integer-unit indicator. The shell indicator is the difference of the integer-ring indicator and its translate by any uniformizer. The repaired statement is `finiteEigendistribution_unitShell`. See ERRATA F45.

Take the 3-adic place of ℚ and the trivial quasi-character. Every invariant functional takes the same value on the integer-ring indicator and its translate by 3. By linearity its value on their difference is zero, so no functional satisfies the asserted normalization.

Choose a nonreal critical-line zero `1/2 + iγ` of the Riemann zeta function by Hardy's theorem. Over the rational field, the unitary character `χ = |·|^(iγ)` has finite L-function `ζ(s + iγ)` on `Re s > 1`. Take its meromorphic normal form on the plane, setting the value at `1 - iγ` to zero. At `σ = 1/2` it has positive order. The idelic norm is onto the positive reals, so `γ ≠ 0` implies `χ ^ 2 ≠ 1`.

Over the rational field take `χ = |·|^i`. Its square is nontrivial because the idelic norm is onto. The finite L-function of its square equals `ζ(s + 2i)` on `Re s > 1`. Use the meromorphic normal form on the plane, setting the value at `1 - 2i` to zero. The germ there still has a simple pole, so this continuation is not entire.
In the completion of `ℚ` at two, the values at `2^n` are `-n`. They are unbounded as the arguments tend to zero, so no value at zero gives even a continuous representative.

At the place 3 of ℚ take f to be the indicator of 1 + 3ℤ₃. The differences for the uniformizers 3 and −3 give values −1 and 0 at 3. The function f vanishes at zero. For any uniformizer π, an equation f = Pᵥ(h) forces h(x) = Σ_{j ≥ 0} f(π^(-j)x) for x ≠ 0 by telescoping and compact support. It follows that h(πʲ) = 1 and h(2πʲ) = 0 for all j ≥ 0, contradicting local constancy at zero.

Over ℚ take the even quadratic idele class character modulo 5, S consisting of the infinite place and 5, and the unitary local character at 5 as d. Its abscissa is zero. The standard test is its conjugate on the integer units, so the integrand is their indicator and the integral is their positive mass.

At a finite rational place take a nonnegative test supported on nonzero elements of absolute value less than one and equal to one at a uniformizer. The principal value is positive, whereas the printed integral with its sign is nonpositive.

Use the smooth cutoff `χ(t) = Real.smoothTransition (t - 1)`, zero for `t ≤ 1` and one for `t ≥ 2`. The logarithmic profile of `φ(t) = χ(t)/t` is Schwartz. For `x ≥ log 2` its `j`-th derivative is `(-1)^j exp(-x)`, and the zeroth derivative fails the rate `exp(-2x)`.

and p. 310. As printed: the pair of residues maps the middle term, obtained by intersecting the shifted completed zeta ideal with the entire Schwartz–Bergman space, onto ℂ². The Euler multiplier accounts for removal in (6.3.2.25); its empty product recovers (6.3.2.8). This is right exactness of the displayed middle term. See `globalConverse_normTwist_meromorphic_exact`, `globalPrincipalValueConverse_normTwist_divided_exact` and ERRATA F81.

and p. 310. Take ℚ, the trivial character, t₀ = 0 and no removed primes. Every element of the printed middle term is entire and both of its residues are zero. In particular (1, 0) has no preimage. The standard Gaussian's Mellin transform has poles at 0 and 1.
and p. 310.

and p. 310. Over ℚ let E be the trivial standard Gaussian and T its translation operator for the idele with real component 2 and all finite components 1. The test `(T-1)(T-2)E` is polar-free, and its untwisted transform is `(2^s-1)(2^s-2)Z(E,s)`, nonzero near zero. For sufficiently small nonzero t₀ its shifted transform at `s=it₀` is nonzero, although the printed generator vanishes there. This also applies with an empty removal set. The unshifted generator in (6.3.2.20) forces a zero at any completed zeta zero ρ, while the same test's shifted transform is nonzero at ρ for a choice of t₀ avoiding its discrete zero set.

and p. 310. As printed: the two displayed terminal maps onto ℂ² are surjective for every character. The formulas are evaluated on test representatives, which cover the respective theta spaces. This is the right-exactness part. See `globalConverse_nontrivial_exact`, `globalPrincipalValueConverse_nontrivial_exact` and ERRATA F78.

and p. 310. Take F = ℚ and the even quadratic idele class character modulo 5, which is nontrivial on the norm-one classes. The Kronecker delta is zero, so both coordinate maps are identically zero for every removal set.

Take F = ℚ(i) and the class of the trivial standard Gaussian E. Both normalized generators take value 1 there. The complex factor is `(2π)⁻¹ exp(-2π|z|²)`, so E(0) = (2π)⁻¹. Its complex integral against `2 dx dy` is also `(2π)⁻¹`, and the product of the finite integer-ring masses is 1/2. The Fourier evaluation is therefore `(4π)⁻¹`.

Over ℚ take the quadratic Hecke character of the odd Dirichlet character modulo 3, twisted by the squared idelic norm. Take f with a nonnegative real bump near 1, finite factor `1_{1+3ℤ₃}` at 3, and `1_{ℤₚ}` elsewhere. Its zeta integral is nonzero by the local integrals and the absolutely convergent Euler product. The printed transform is the corrected transform multiplied in its argument by the idele with real coordinate 1 and finite coordinates −1. The dual character takes value −1 on this idele, so the right side acquires a minus sign by change of variables and meromorphic continuation.

For a test vanishing at the identity, the global spectral kernel of Definition 10.4.3.2 divided by its input weight is claimed to fail square integrability against the product of the two positive Sobolev measures. The print writes `k^spec_{φ,a,s}(x,y)`, without a tilde, and does not say which variable carries the weight; it is the input variable, as in (10.4.3.30).

Take the zero test over the rationals with twist one and Sobolev degree four. Theorem 10.4.3.4(2) makes the weighted spectral kernel the Hilbert–Schmidt kernel of spectral projection after convolution, so it is square integrable. For the zero test that operator is zero and its kernel has squared norm zero.

Take ℚ, the trivial character, no removal, and the entire multiplier `exp(s^4)`. On `s = 2 + it` its modulus is `exp(t^4-24t²+16)`. The Euler product bounds the ordinary zeta modulus below by `ζ(4)/ζ(2)` and Stirling's formula gives only exponential decay of the gamma factor. The resulting product grows on the vertical line and violates the Schwartz–Bergman condition.

Take ℚ, the trivial character and remove 2. The factor `1 - 2^{-s}` cancels the first pole for every test, so (1, 0) has no preimage. For the test with real component `(1-2πx²) exp(-πx²)` and integer indicators at every finite place, the value at zero is one and the Fourier value there is zero. The removed transform has two zero residues and takes value `-log 2` at zero. If a polar-free test had the same removed transform, cancelling the Euler factor would equate its entire transform with the original transform having residue -1 at zero.

Take ℚ, remove 2, and set t₀ = π/log 2 in the pure norm twist. Use (1-2πx²) exp(-πx²) at infinity and the integer indicators at finite places. Its polar values are (1,0), and the rational class mass is 1. The printed Euler factors are 2 and 3/2, so the printed pair is (-2,0). The full Mellin continuation has Euler factors 0 and 1/2 at the two shifted poles and hence residue pair (0,0). Injectivity of the terminal isomorphism gives the contradiction.

Take F = ℚ, the standard Gaussian at infinity, the indicator of ℤ̂ at the finite places, and χ induced by the quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor 5. At s = 0 the character has modulus one and takes the value −1 at the norm-one idele with component 2 at 5 and 1 elsewhere. At norm t, the theta sum is Σ_{n ≠ 0} exp(−πn²t²) ∼ 1/t as t tends to zero, so its integral against dt/t diverges.

Take `F = ℚ(i)` and the theta class of the trivial-character standard adelic Gaussian `E`. The complex Gaussian factor is `(2π)⁻¹ exp(−2π|z|²)`, and the finite factors are the integer-ring indicators. Both normalized eigendistributions take value `1` on the class. Evaluation at zero gives `1/(2π)`. Fourier evaluation at zero gives `1/(4π)`, since the complex integral against `2 dx dy` is `1/(2π)` and the finite integer rings have product additive mass `1/2`.
The range of the extended principal-value map is asserted to be closed for degree at least twice the set size.

Take ℚ, S₀ = {2}, degree 2 and the trivial isotype. The functions `exp (-ε * |log ‖g‖|)` are nonzero approximate invariants for the uniformizer translation. The resulting principal-value differences contradict the closed-range bound for the injective extension. See ERRATA.md F162 for the obstruction reported by Refine and Naslund.
At every twist and nonnegative degree the completed PV map is a closed embedding whose image equals the completion of its test image.
The case a = 0, s = 2, F = ℚ and S = {2} already has nonclosed image.
At the simple zero of the rational two-prime Euler product, a first logarithmic moment can be nonzero on the principal-value image.
As printed, the global Sobolev completion in the proposition uses theta functions of all Schwartz–Bruhat tests. The proposed completion requires their weighted square integrability.

For ℚ, set a = s = 0 and I = {0}. The real Gaussian times the characteristic functions of the finite integer rings has theta(t) = Σ_{n ≠ 0} exp(-πn²t²), asymptotic to 1/t at zero on each norm-one fibre, so its square is not integrable.
The interval norm is finite on every weighted global polar-free theta function for every closed interval with interior.

At zero weight and order, take the closed half-line [0,∞). A norm-two dilation difference of a bump near the archimedean identity is polar-free and has nonzero theta at some positive log norm. The endpoint weights on [0,b] force the Sobolev norm to be infinite.
, (10.1.1.14). The product of the global homogeneous quotient maps factors isometrically through the Hilbert sum. The factors carry the norm of their weighted homogeneous functions.

Take ℚ(ζ₃), a = s = 0 and I = {0}, so the weight is one. The isometry gives ‖θ‖² = Σ_ω ‖θ_ω‖² for every test function. By Bessel's inequality for the characters of the norm-one classes, the right side is at most vol(C¹)²‖θ‖², and vol(C¹) = π/(3√3) < 1. So every theta function would vanish, but a nonnegative archimedean bump times the indicator of the finite integers has nonzero theta. (The printed counterexample over ℚ(i), with norm-one mass π/4, works the same way.)

Take F = ℚ and the self-dual test exp(−πx²) times the indicator of the finite integer adeles. On the idele with real component t > 0 and finite components 1, its inverted theta value is asymptotic to t as t tends to infinity. Every global theta function decays there by `adelicTheta_decay_large`, so the inverted function cannot represent a global theta class.

The convergence assertion is made for each realization of the printed completion, since on an unbounded base the displayed norm can be infinite. See ERRATA F144.

Use the positive reals with identity module, trivial character, I = [−1,1] and s = 0. In log coordinates use g(x) = exp(−x²/4)/√(4π) and φ = −g′. Their Mellin transforms are exp(z²) and z exp(z²). Zero is the unique zero of the latter and is simple. The compact interval weighted L² model realizes the completion. For every positive T the range is the kernel of evaluation at zero. That functional takes value 1 on the vector of g, so continuity rules out convergence of its projections to g.
At the singleton base and nonnegative even degree an equivalent Hilbert metric makes all left translations conformal. The parallelogram identity expresses the requirement that the norm be Hilbertian.

Take F = ℚ and s = 2. The powers of a class of logarithmic norm one and of its inverse have polynomial norm bounds, so its dilation factor in any equivalent conformal norm must equal one. On the indicator of the log-norm band [0, 1], the norms of the translates by positive powers grow without bound in the weighted Hilbert norm.

On the positive reals with identity module and Haar measure dt/t, take I = [0, ∞), s = 0 and a nonzero smooth bump in log coordinates supported in (−2, −1). There the endpoint twists are uniformly bounded as the nonnegative exponent grows. The left translate by exp 3 is supported in (1, 2) in log coordinates, where the norms for [0, b] grow without bound as b tends to infinity.

On the positive reals with identity module and Haar measure dt/t, take a = b = 0, s = 2 and the operator norm seminorm. The space is nonzero, since a nonzero smooth compact log-profile lies in it. At g = 1 the translate is the identity, so the bound reads 1 ≤ 0.

At index zero, the bound forces the rational completed zeta logarithmic derivative to vanish along the horizontal segment at height `T 0`. Such an accumulating set of zeros contradicts its simple pole at one.

At the real place of `ℚ`, take the trivial local character, `a = 2`, and a smooth logarithmic bump supported in `(-1,1)` with value one at zero. On `x > 1` the two samples vanish, so the upper truncation is exactly `log R` for `R > 1`.

At the real place of `ℚ` with trivial character and `s = 2`, the printed and actual digamma arguments agree. The constant is `-log(π)/2` from the gamma prefactor, while the printed constant is `+log(π)/2`. Independently, the primitive quadratic character modulo three has local sign at the real place. It has the same exponent on positive reals as the trivial character, but its gamma argument is `(s + 1)/2` in place of `s/2`.

At a complex place, the trivial character and the angular character of weight two have the same radial exponent. The printed centered integrals coincide. The corrected digamma kernels on a Gaussian differ by a strictly positive integral.

The rational character `g ↦ |g| ^ i` has simple poles at `-i` and `1 - i`. For the Gaussian logarithmic test, each shifted Mellin sample has modulus strictly smaller than the corresponding positive real sample at zero or one.

Take the completed rational zeta function, `a = 2`, and a nonzero nonnegative smooth compactly supported logarithmic bump `f₀` with Mellin transform `Φ₀`. Use `f(x) = exp(-n) f₀(x - n)` for sufficiently large `n`. Its Mellin transform is `exp(n(s - 1)) Φ₀(s)`. Each zero has real part less than one, so absolute summability for `Φ₀` gives a zero sum tending to zero as `n` grows. The pole sample at one remains `Φ₀(1) > 0` and the sample at zero tends to zero. The two sides therefore have real parts of opposite signs for large `n`.

The poles of the rational character `g ↦ |g| ^ i` give the centered samples at `-1/2 - i` and `1/2 - i`. Their moduli on a Gaussian test are strictly smaller than the printed samples at `-1/2` and `1/2`.

Take `F = ℚ(√5)`, `χ = 1`, and `t₀ = 0`. With `φ = (1 + √5) / 2`, the ideal-counting limit is the zeta residue `2 log φ / √5`, equal to the norm-one volume by (A.3.2.1). The norm of the different is five, so the display instead gives `2 log φ / 5`.
The printed bound uses a full weight at integer cutoffs with the error terms for the half-weight Perron formula.

Over the rationals take the trivial character, `t₀ = 0`, `s = 1 + i`, `x = 2` and `c = 1`. The integral tends to the half-weight sum as `T → +∞`. The full sum differs by `log(2) / (2 · 2^s) ≠ 0`, whereas the printed error tends to zero.

On and to the right of the 1-line, excluding the pole of a pure norm character, the printed second equality subtracts `H_x` from the ordered prime-power tail. Its left side sums over primes in norm order, taking all positive powers at each prime.

Over `ℚ` take the trivial character, `x = 3`, and ordinate `2π / log 2` on the 1-line. The grouped tail includes all powers of two with exponent at least two, whose sum is `log 2 - 1/2 > 0`. The prime tail omits them and the printed subtraction counts them twice.
At the pole ordinate the printed value of the normalized oscillatory term is minus one.
With `t₀ = 0` and `n = 2`, the quotient off the pole has limit `log 2` at `s = 1`, giving normalized value one.
Use the trivial character of `ℚ`, a finite place, `m = 1`, `a = 2`, and `f(x) = exp(-x²)`. The prime-power sample is nonzero, and Mellin inversion gives a factor `2π` in the raw integral.

Use the trivial character of `ℚ`, a finite place, `m = 1`, `a = 2`, and `f(x) = exp(-x²)`. The reciprocal sample is nonzero. The reflected integral gives `2πi` times the inverse prime power, since reversing the endpoints cancels the change of differential.
Under the dense-image hypothesis in the Hilbert case the lift can be chosen with closed span isomorphic to the kernel's orthogonal complement, and small kernel perturbations preserve this conclusion.
In ℓ² with zero kernel take V to be c₀₀ and start an orthonormal basis with the normalization of (2⁻ʲ)ⱼ. Its first quotient vector has no representative in V.
As printed, inversion in the idele class group defines a continuous linear automorphism of the same ambient Sobolev space for every compact nonempty interval.

Take ℚ, I = {1} and s = 0. The indicator of |g| < 1 is square integrable for t² dt/t in the norm coordinate t, while its inverse pullback is the indicator of |g| > 1, which has infinite squared integral.

For F = ℚ and n = 2, the norm band contains every principal idele (2^k). The 2-adic norm at that place is a continuous map sending the band into ℝ; it sends the principal ideles to ‖2‖^k with 0 < ‖2‖ < 1, which tends to 0. A compact image would be closed and thus contain 0, but the norm of the component of a unit is strictly positive.

The pointwise absolutely convergent identity on every idelic test includes one term for each zero quasi-character and divides the archimedean principal values by the local unit masses. A norm section indexes each quasi-character exactly once. This isolates the scalar identity from the additional assertion of convergence in the strong dual. See `idelicExplicitFormula` and ERRATA F43.

Translate a nonnegative radial rational test supported in norm greater than two. Subtract the two formulas and multiply by the square root of the translating norm. The real principal value then stays between two fixed positive constants. The spectral side is an exponential series on the rational zeta zeros. Its Laplace transform continues across zero as a sum of Cauchy kernels, although the positive lower bound forces divergence there.

Take the real place of `ℚ`, with completion `ℝ` and local absolute value `|x|`. The preimage of `[1/2, 2]` consists of the positive and negative copies of that interval. The Tamagawa measure `dx/|x|` gives it mass `4 log 2`, whereas canonical Haar measure gives it mass `2 log 2`, since its pushforward under `|x|` is `dt/t`.

, 302. Over ℚ at the archimedean stage, take the trivial character, the identity representative and the real Gaussian `exp(-πx²)`. Its unweighted logarithmic profile is a positive constant times `exp(-π exp(2t))`, which has a nonzero limit as t tends to negative infinity.

Fatou's lemma gives divergence since the approximant tends to `t^(-2)`.
The two printed archimedean families have holomorphic limits along a chosen cofinal cutoff sequence on the interior of the specified compact set.

Use an order-four character modulo five over the rationals with value `i` at two and let `u` have local unit two at five and components one elsewhere. At norm two and parameter two, the radial value is nonzero for all sufficiently late approximants. Right translation by `u` multiplies the displayed test by `i`, while the asserted conjugate weight would multiply it by `-i`.

Take the standard integral factors at the finite places and an even real bump supported at absolute values in (3, 4), positive near 7/2. Subtract an even bump below absolute value 1/2, supported away from zero, to cancel the Fourier value at zero. For norms near 7/2 only the terms ±1 contribute. This gives positive norm mass in the lower half-line integral outside the bounded cutoff band.

Take `F = ℚ`, `S` consisting of the real place, and `χ = 1`. Use `p(s) = exp(s²)` on the right half-plane. The factor `π^((1−2s)/2) Γ(s/2) / Γ((1−s)/2)` has a simple pole at zero, where `p(1) = e`. The product is unbounded as `s` approaches zero through positive real arguments, so no holomorphic output exists on the reflected half-plane.

Take `F = ℚ`, `S` consisting of the real place, the positive-real section, and `χ = 1`. Use `f(t) = exp(−1/t) / t`. For every `a < 1`, the twist `t^a f(t)` is Schwartz in `log t`, since the power at infinity is `a−1 < 0` and the exponential dominates at zero. The radial image is `exp(−t)`. Its weight-zero twist tends to `1` as `t` tends to zero, and hence is outside the target with weights `a < 1`.

Take `F = ℚ`, `S` consisting of the real place, the positive-real section, and `χ = 1`, so both Mellin transforms have shift zero. Set the first input to zero and the second to the inverse Mellin image of `Q(s) = exp((s−2)²)` on the right half-plane. At `s = 1/4`, `Q(1/4)` and `Q(3/4)` differ and `ρ(1/4) ≠ 0`. Both arguments are in the overlap and the two paths give different values there.
For two unitary base points of the same component, the new base is asserted to be the pure imaginary norm twist specifying the chart translation.

Over a universe lift of ℚ with only the archimedean place, use the same nontrivial imaginary norm character as both basepoints. The first printed identity expresses this character as the pure norm twist. Substituting it into the second identity at exponent zero forces the character to be one. Its value at norm exp(π) is −1, giving a contradiction.
The coordinate insertions into the S-idèle quotient are closed embeddings.
For ℚ with only the real place, the two real units 1 and −1 give the same class.
, strictness in (11.1.2.6). The printed claim requires a strictly smaller closed cutoff stage along a subsequence of every increasing exhaustion by radii, for each cutoff choice.

, strictness in (11.1.2.6). Take F = ℚ, the trivial character, S with no finite places, s = 2, the empty index and the singleton at 2. Use bounded cutoffs with radii k + 2. On the logarithmic line the principal value is I − T, where T translates by log 2 up to sign. The theta test space is translation invariant. Applying I − T to a finite sum of translates of a test gives the test minus a distant translate, which tends to zero after cutting off to any bounded window. Thus the two closed stages are equal at every radius in the sequence.

The printed functional equation inserts an additional epsilon factor in the ratio of the original and Fourier Euler products. The two basic products use the same normalization, so their common scalar cancels.

For ℚ(i) with the complex place and the place over 2, take the trivial unitary base and its standard Gaussian tensor. At exponent 1/4 the zeta integral is nonzero and the epsilon factor is not one. The ratio already contains epsilon, so the proposed identity fails on a neighborhood of that exponent.
The printed lexicographic orders on the real and complex cutoff tuples make the no-pole spaces a decreasing filtration.

For F = ℚ(√2) and the trivial character on the archimedean stage, (0,2) is lexicographically below (1,0). Both real places have the poles of Γℝ. Apply the Euler differential polynomial s²(s+2)² in the Mellin variable to the product Gaussian. Its double pole at −4 remains, while the poles at 0 and −2 are canceled. Its class is in the stage (1,0) and outside (0,2).

On the signed Laurent convention of Definition 7.1.2.1, the displayed positive-index coefficients (7.3.4.4) form a finite independent spanning family for the annihilator. On representatives after finite PV this says the finite array is onto and its common kernel is the no-pole stage, characterized by vanishing of the negative coefficients.

For the rational archimedean stage and trivial character take a nonnegative nonzero even bump in the annulus two to three. Its Mellin transform is entire, and its derivative at zero integrates the bump against a strictly positive logarithm. The coefficient of exponent one therefore fails to annihilate the zero-cutoff stage.

Over ℚ with only the real place, take the trivial character, `A = 1/2`, and a real Gaussian. Both sums are empty and theta has a positive limit at norm zero. For the finite-place overlap take ℚ with finite places 2 and 3, the trivial character, and `A = 1/2`. At the finite places use the integer-ring indicators. At the real place take a positive log-profile obtained by convolving a nonzero nonnegative smooth bump in (0,1) with the indicators of [0, log 2] and [0, log 3]. The zeta function is a positive constant times `6^s H(s)/s^2`, where H is the Mellin transform of the original bump in the log coordinate. The origin is its only pole. Each finite-place series contributes the printed logarithmic coefficient `-a₁`, whereas the inverse Mellin transform has coefficient `-a₋₂`. The ratio 2a₁/a₋₂ is the bump-weighted mean of (u + log 6)³/3, which exceeds one on (0,1).

Comparing the two Weil identities for its common global insertion shows that the printed transition formula would force the added place's integer-unit Tamagawa mass to be one. That mass is strictly smaller than one at a place dividing the different.

On the reading that the listed poles occur with their multiplicities, every point of (5.3.4.13) is a pole after applying all finite principal values to any S-adelic test. This isolates occurrence from the multiplicity formula. The repaired statements are `sLocalIdelicZFunction_principalValue_pole_bound` and `exists_sLocalIdelicZFunction_principalValue_attaining_poles`. See ERRATA F58.

For ℚ with only the real place, take the trivial character at s = 0 and a nonzero even, nonnegative smooth bump supported on 1 < |x| < 2. There are no finite principal values to apply. The Mellin transform is entire, while the real Euler factor Γℝ(s) has a simple pole at zero.

Take ℚ(√2), only its two real places, the trivial character, and at each place `x² exp(-πx²)`. The zeta transform is a nonzero constant times Γℝ(s + 2)². At A = 2 its norm on the vertical line is of order `|Im s|⁻²` near −2.

Use ℚ, S = {∞, 2}, χ = 1, Λ = 1 and a = s = 0. The test (H(u) - H(2u)) times the 2-adic integer indicator from the absolute-level counterexample also lies in the invariant region. , with Definition 7.3.2.3, p. 355. The invariant levels formed with the printed unit factors exhaust the homogeneous theta space sequentially, both for unrestricted and for zero-moment tests. Applying principal value to the inserted integer indicators realizes the printed unit factors.

, with Definition 7.3.2.3, p. 355. Take F = ℚ, S = {∞}, S₀ = {p}, and the trivial character. All inserted tests vanish near 0 at p, so their Mellin transforms have no pole at 2πi/log p. The middle-term surjectivity consequence on each component takes the whole homogeneous theta space onto all meromorphic sections with the full divisor bound. Those sections are expressed as meromorphic functions in a component chart.

, and Theorem 7.2.1.1(1), p. 334. The literal nonnegative subscript in §7.1 denotes the coefficient of the positive power, including the constant at index zero.
At a common pole, the phases at two places over the same rational prime differ by a unique integer multiple of the period for that prime. The integer norm of the rational place is p.

Take F = ℚ(∛2), p = 5, and S consisting of the places over 5 together with the archimedean places. Modulo 5, X³ - 2 factors as (X - 3)(X² + 3X + 4), with irreducible quadratic and discriminant of X³ - 2 prime to 5. The local residue sizes are 5 and 25. With T = 2π/log 5 and χ = |·|^(3iT/4), take the common pole c = 1. The local phases are 3T/4 and T/4, so their difference is T/2.

Each listed coefficient is called an eigendistribution of its center. The finite sets S and T specify the finite parts of the printed S and S₀, both of which contain all infinite places. Pullback to tests expresses the weight equation.

For ℚ take S = {∞,2,3}, S₀ = {∞,2}, and c = 1. The real Gaussian times the integer indicators has a triple pole with leading coefficient 2/(log 2 · log 3). Dilation of norm 2 multiplies the zeta germ by 2^s and changes the selected second-order coefficient by (log 2) times the leading coefficient.
Both printed quotients require the primary principal-value image of the given zero-moment level to lie inside the level divided by the product of residue sizes.

Over ℚ start with no finite places and add one prime of residue size N > 4. Take the product cutoff Y = 3. On the trivial component, principal value acts as the identity minus translation by an idele of norm 1/N. The translated Fourier theta vanishes on [1, 2], where the original test has a nonzero Fourier theta value. The printed target cutoff 3/N is below 1.

For both printed quotient levels every enumeration of either restricted family gives an unconditional strong-dual basis, and the ambient biorthogonals lift to an absolute basis. The containment expresses existence of the quotients in (7.3.3.5)–(6). In (7.3.3.7) the small-stage multiplicity counts contributing places in S, and the Laurent subscript is the signed exponent of Definition 7.1.2.1.

Over the rationals with one added prime and trivial character, the index contains the order-zero jet at the trivial center. It evaluates the Fourier zeta integral at norm power one, a nonzero multiple of evaluation at zero by Fourier inversion. Its restriction vanishes on each zero-moment level, contradicting the unit biorthogonal pairing. The same obstruction persists with the proof's intersection denominator.
, 355. Inside each printed test level the common kernel of the two evaluations has codimension two.
, 355. For one added rational prime every inserted test vanishes at zero, so at most one independent moment remains on the test space.
, 355. On a test at either level the cited transition is asserted to insert unit indicators.

, 355. Over the rationals add one prime and choose an inverse Fourier bump with positive integral. At the zero tuple integer insertion gives its nonzero value at zero, while unit insertion gives zero.

The diagram of inclusions and restrictions of the continuous ambient PV operator commutes at the printed cutoffs and is equivariant for the large-norm semigroup. The containments define the restrictions, so both paths have the same ambient value.

Over ℚ take one old finite place and add a prime of residue size N. Choose a test with Fourier support in a box of size B and nonzero Fourier theta at a norm in [1, 2]. With X = B/N and Y = X², the bottom box has size B and the bottom product cutoff is B²/N. Choosing N > B² puts this cutoff below 1. The Fourier theta evaluation separates the two closed levels after cancelling the common unit insertion.

The printed tensor product with full multiplicative factors off the primary fibre embeds as a closed subspace of the additive tests with its projective tensor topology.

Use a nonzero smooth real test supported in (1, 2), the indicator of ℤ₂, and the multiplicative 3-adic test h(3ᵏu) = exp(−k²) for k ∈ ℤ and u ∈ ℤ₃ˣ. At a point where the real test is nonzero and the 2-adic coordinate is 1, the zero extension of the product fails local constancy at the 3-adic origin. See ERRATA R11.

Take F = ℚ, S with just the finite place over 2, p = 2, and c = 1. The local numerator has a simple pole and the reflected denominator is regular and nonzero at c, giving signed order −1. The primary count is 1.

Every closed rectifiable contour bounding the indicated domain gives the coefficient. Rectifiable contours are integrated in Lipschitz parametrizations, available by arclength reparametrization. Both directions of traversal are allowed.

Over ℚ with only the real place, a nonnegative nonzero even bump on 2 < |x| < 3 has positive first Mellin derivative at zero and zero integral in the formula for index one on a small circle. Each coefficient descends to the homogeneous theta quotient and is an eigendistribution of weight equal to its center.

For ℚ at the real place, translate a nonzero nonnegative even bump supported in 2 < |x| < 3 by dilation by 2. At the trivial center its first Mellin derivative increases by log(2) times the positive constant coefficient. With the polar reading of (7.2.1.8), use the Gaussian times the integer indicator over ℚ at ∞ and p. The top coefficient is 2/log p, so translation by p changes the residue by −2 at the trivial character.
Reading the subscript according to Definition 7.1.2.1 gives a nonnegative exponent.

With the leading-pole interpretation specified in (7.2.1.19), the unscaled product still omits the factor from Fourier and Gaussian normalization.

Multiply a real Gaussian by a finite compact-open test equal to one at zero, and use a smooth profile equal to one through radius one and zero from radius two. Any nonzero common finite-coordinate period h would identify the values at (2/‖h‖,0) and (2/‖h‖,h). The first is nonzero, while the product-norm cutoff makes the second zero.

For ℚ and the set consisting of the real place, the local unit −1 maps to the identity of the S-idele quotient because it is the diagonal S-unit −1. The local sign character takes value −1 there and so lies outside the image.

Take ℚ(i) with only its complex place and the character `(z/|z|)^4`, which descends through the four units. The printed list includes zero, but the numerator Γℂ(s + 2) and the denominator Γℂ(3 − s) are regular and nonzero there.

Take F = ℚ(i), S consisting of the complex place, the trivial character, k = 0 and σ = 1. The factor is `(2π)^(1 - 2s) Γ(s) / Γ(1 - s)`, of modulus `|τ| / (2π)` for nonzero τ by the Gamma recurrence and conjugation. The printed bound would give `O(|τ|^(1/2))`.

Over ℚ the odd Dirichlet character modulo 4 has real factor Γℝ(s + 1) and a pole at −1, while there are zero complex places. The proof obtains an odd character by separating the sign idele with any one finite place included.

Over ℚ add one prime to the archimedean stage. In ball coordinates the target is a locally convex direct sum of real Schwartz spaces, where the seminorm `∑_{n ≥ 0} |f_n⁽ⁿ⁾(0)|` is continuous. Each Laurent zero neighborhood contains a nonzero multiple of every monomial. Joint continuity would therefore bound the derivative of order k+1 on a Schwartz zero neighborhood controlling derivatives only through order k. A smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one near zero times `exp(itx)/t^k`, scaled by a fixed nonzero constant into that neighborhood, has unbounded derivative of order k+1 at zero.

Set both radii to one and the width to one half. Use smooth even cutoffs that taper from one to zero on (1/2,1) and a nonzero nonnegative smooth lift supported in (15/16,17/16). The cosine is strictly positive on the sharp integration region, so tapering strictly decreases the mass.

Take outer radius two, transition width one, a smooth even cutoff equal to one on [−1,1], and the Gaussian exp(−x²). The product has value one at zero, so it fails even the zeroth flatness condition.

Over ℚ take S with one finite prime p, the trivial character, the identity class representative, and x = 1. Use the finite indicator of `pℤₚˣ` and an even nonnegative smooth compactly supported function positive at ±1 and supported away from ±p. The norm-one integral is zero since the finite support forces the inverse real component to have absolute value p. The separate factors are both positive.

Over ℚ(i) at its complex stage, take the angular character of degree equal to the torsion order of the integer unit group and a monomial test of the same degree times a radial cutoff. The inverse-argument average at 1 integrates the constant 1. The positive-argument homogeneous average has twice the character weight and vanishes. The proposed map kills a nonzero source class.

Take `F = ℚ`, `S = {∞, 5}`, and let `W` be the image of the real segment `[2,3]` in the norm chart of the trivial character. Tensor an even smooth real bump equal to one at `±1` and supported in `1/2 < |x| < 3/2` with the quadratic character modulo `5` on `ℤ₅ˣ`, extended by zero. At the identity only the S-units `±1` contribute to theta, giving value two. The norm-one idele `(1, 2)` acts by negation on the test and its theta class. Every weight in `W` takes value one on that idele, so each corresponding eigendistribution kills the class.

, first sequence. The coefficient map on tests descends to the indicated quotient, has the printed kernel, and maps onto the printed product. The index set in the display ranges over the selected divisor on the character space.

Under the polar reading, use a real bump equal to one near zero instead. Its simple pole there is allowed by the selected bound and has nonzero residue.

On the character surface a divisor of multiplicity b has b Laurent coordinates in its principal-parts stalk. Sections of that principal-parts sheaf are their product over the discrete support. The Mellin transform of an isotype is supported on its component.

In the a-line notation the local Fourier transform extends at precisely the half weight.

Over ℚ with no finite places in S, the inverse real Fourier transform of two shifted Gaussian peaks gives inputs with uniformly bounded degree-two norms. The logarithmic Sobolev weight makes the norms of their Fourier transforms unbounded at a = 1/2.
As printed, the integral defining the local norm is finite at every positive weight and every compact nonempty interval.
For ℚ with S consisting of the real place, take f(x) = exp(-πx²), a = 1, I = {-1} and s = 0. The two S-units give theta(t) = 2 exp(-πt²), whose square is not integrable near zero against dt/t.

For ℚ, S = {∞}, a = 1, s = 0, and the real Gaussian, the weighted theta is positive throughout [2,3]. Already the intervals [0,b] give unbounded norms as b tends to infinity.
, (10.1.1.15). The product of the S-local homogeneous quotient maps factors isometrically through the Hilbert sum. The factors carry the norm of their weighted homogeneous functions.

Take ℚ(ζ₃), S empty (only the complex place), a = 1, I = {1}, and s = 0. The Gaussian exp(−|g|) in the complex coordinate gives a nonzero theta function that depends only on the norm, so its trivial-character average is vol(J₁) times itself. The Hilbert sum norm is therefore at least vol(J₁) times the norm, and vol(J₁) = π/3 > 1. Only vol(J₁) > 1 is proved: the idelic annulus 1 ≤ |g| ≤ 26/25 has mass at least 2π(T − 1)/T and at most 6 vol(J₁) log T (six units), which forces vol(J₁) > 1. (The printed counterexample over ℚ(i), with factor π/2, works the same way.)

Take ℚ and the archimedean stage. The norm-one quotient is trivial, and projection to the sole factor identifies the product map with the identity on the theta quotient. The range is closed and the induced topology is the intrinsic topology.

The unscaled formula with a specified Laurent exponent.

Take ℚ with the real place and the place above 2, the trivial character and m = 0. Use a test with a simple pole at the trivial archimedean center and a unit-supported finite factor. The support misses the zero of the finite coordinate, but the constant Laurent coefficient is the derivative of the pole numerator, which cannot vanish for both a unit translate and a uniformizer translate.

Over ℚ take the place above 2, χ = 1, tᵥ = m = 0 and t = 1. Use a smooth nonzero nonnegative real bump supported in (exp 1, exp 2) times the indicator of ℤ₂. Its transform is B(s)/(1 − 2⁻ˢ), where B′(0) > B(0) > 0 since log x > 1 on the bump. The residue is B(0)/log 2. The printed coefficient is a₀ = B′(0)/log 2 + B(0)/2, strictly larger.

Over the rationals with no finite places, the correct reflected coordinate for `χ(g) = |g|^(ix)` is the trivial-character coordinate at `s + ix`. The printed shift `s - ix`, applied for every real frequency, would make this coordinate constant on the line `Re s = 1/4`. The weight-one Schwartz–Bergman bound forces the constant to vanish. The rational Gaussian and the functional equation give a nonzero value there, as in the translation refutation above.

Take `F = ℚ`, no finite places, the positive-real norm section, and `ω = 1`. The Gaussian `exp(−x²)` has a nonzero first zeta coordinate at `s = 1/4`, since its radial Mellin integrand is strictly positive. The functional equation then forces the reflected Fourier coordinate to be nonzero there. Translation by a norm-two idele multiplies this coordinate by `2^(1/4)`, while the printed rule multiplies it by `2^(3/4)`, contradicting strict monotonicity of real powers.
The topology generated by the vertical derivative norms in (9.2.2.19), with the order range made explicit on p. 417. The generating open sets are the balls in each of the individual norms.

Take degree zero and base [−1, 1]. Let `c` interleave the lines with abscissas 1 − 1/(n+2) and −1 + 1/(n+2), and let `d` prepend the line at 1 to `c`. For a nonzero smooth bump `h` supported in (0, 1), take the Mellin transforms of the log profiles exp(−n) h(x−n). At each fixed abscissa σ of `c` the order-zero line norm is a constant times exp((σ−1)n). At the prepended line the norm is the fixed positive norm of the transform of x ↦ exp(x) h(x), with the normalization of (9.2.2.19).

Take base [−1, 1], s = 1, z = 1 and k = 0. Interleave the interior abscissas 1 − 1/(n+2) and −1 + 1/(n+2). For a nonnegative nonzero smooth bump `h` supported in (0, 1), the Mellin transforms of the log profiles exp(−n) h(x−n) tend to zero on every sampled line. Their values at 1 are the same positive number ∫ exp(x) h(x) dx, although the printed floor allows k = 0.

Take the trivial rational character, a completed zeta zero ρ with a = Re ρ > 0, and m = 0. For a nonzero nonnegative compactly supported smooth bump b, the profile `h(u) = b(u) exp(-ρu)` has positive ρ-moment. The damped translates `exp(-an/2) h(u - n)` form a bounded set in ordinary Schwartz space, while their ρ-moments have unbounded modulus.

Take ℚ, the pure norm character with exponent i and x₀ = 1. Use the meromorphic normal form of the shifted completed zeta, with a zero ρ obtained by shifting a completed zeta zero by −i. At m = 0 take `φ(s) = (s - ρ) exp(s²)`. The derivative functional is zero, while the convergent shifted moment is `φ(ρ + i) = i exp((ρ + i)²) ≠ 0`.
Use `Φ(s) = exp(2 (s - 1/2)^2 / 9)`, s = 1/2, and k = 0. The left side is 1. Each line norm is `3 √(π e/2)`, so the right side is `√(9 e/(8π)) < 1`.

Given the extension (9.3.2.1), there is a family indexed by the nonnegative integers and all norm-one characters. Each member is in its indexed left isotype and its twisted Fourier transform is supported in the band based on the chosen extension of that same character. The identity lies in the strong closure of their images under the convolution extension (9.3.2.1). Applying that map to B requires B to lie in its stated Schwartz domain, as well as requiring the b-twists to be Schwartz. The band convention in `exists_singletonDecay_isotype_approximation` uses the inverse isotype character. See ERRATA F175.

Take the positive reals times Circle, module the first projection, Haar measure, and b = s = 0. At an element with circle coordinate i, the printed Fourier band forces a kernel with character value i to vanish. Kernels with other character values kill a nonzero L² vector in the i-eigenspace. Their strong closure therefore excludes the identity. The proof also transports the operator-norm closure inferred by the current statement to pointwise closure; neither closure contains the identity.

Use `F = ℚ`, `α = 0`, `s = 2`, `Λ = 2` and `ε = 1/4`. In log norm choose an even smooth cutoff equal to one on `|x| ≤ log(7/4)`, strictly tapering on `log(7/4) < |x| < log 2`, and zero on `|x| ≥ log 2`. The normalized indicators of `0 < ρ < 1/n` are unit vectors perpendicular to the kernel and their images have norm at most `1/n`, contradicting the lower bound for an operator with closed range.

Take the trivial rational character and the meromorphic normal form of the completed Riemann zeta function. There are countably infinitely many distinct zeros and each jet space is nonzero and finite-dimensional. The annihilator consists of finite-support jets and has countable algebraic dimension. The product has uncountable dimension, as seen by embedding complex sequences and using the independent sequences `(a^n)ₙ` for distinct a.

Over ℚ take `ε(Λ) = 1/(2Λ²)` and let `ρ(Λ)` be the indicator of `Λ⁻¹ ≤ |g|_F ≤ Λ`. For `Λ > 2` these are admissible cutoffs. Each jumps at both endpoints along the continuous positive-real section of the idelic norm.

Take the rational field, the trivial base character, a = 1/2 and s = 2. Select only a positive critical-line zeta ordinate t and take a small isolating interval about t. The zeroth jet pairs with the Fourier value at −t, so it vanishes on the band image and its closure. To see that the jet is nonzero, pair it with the indicator of a compact neighborhood times exp(−it log |g|). Every element of the adjoint range of the orthogonal projection that annihilates its image is zero.
With cutoff one, the positive critical-line ordinates below 50 give at least ten jets. A band enclosing them inside (0, 50) has logarithmic bound below four.

Over `ℚ` in the trivial isotype, take a positive critical-line zeta ordinate. Two norm translations of the standard adelic Gaussian cancel its polar values while preserving a nonzero Mellin value at the corresponding frequency on the imaginary axis. The Mellin functional is continuous in the Sobolev norm of degree two. It vanishes on the twisted theta closure by the forward factorization at the critical-line zero.

Over the rationals in the trivial isotype, twist the same polar-free theta used in the descent counterexample by the exponent `-1/2`. Its completed vector is a twisted generator. Its Mellin value at the certified critical-line zero is the nonzero imaginary-axis value of the untwisted test, so it cannot itself be an untwisted theta.
A test of conjugate weight is claimed to act through the indicated isotype by a strongly nuclear operator. The full trace is the sum in (10.3.1.5) with the floor in (10.3.1.4).
The quartic character modulo five and the bump in the range counterexample already contradict the first conjunct.
A test of left-translation weight ω⁻¹ is asserted to give an operator valued in the line quotient isotype ω.

For F = ℚ let the base character θ be induced by a quartic Dirichlet character modulo 5. Take s = 2, a+it a nontrivial zero of its completed L-function and ω = (θ|C¹)⁻¹. Multiply the conjugate of θ(g)|g|^(it) by a nonzero nonnegative smooth bump in log |g|. This test has left-translation weight ω⁻¹. The zeroth jet function has weight ω, and the associated bilinear functional detects the ω⁻¹-isotype. Its transpose eigenvalue is the positive integral of the bump, and it annihilates the ω-isotype. See ERRATA.md F177.

Let F be the splitting field of X³−2 and K = ℚ(ζ₃). The two nontrivial characters of Gal(F/K) have the same Hecke L-function by conjugation. Take a common critical-strip zero β+iγ. It has order at least two for the trivial character of F. Set a = β and s = 3 and choose the trivial representative on the norm-one trivial type. Use the radial autocorrelation of b(x) = exp(−iγx) η(x), where η is a nonzero nonnegative smooth bump in (1, 2). Divide by the norm-one volume to give multiplier B = |b̂|² on that type and zero elsewhere. To bound the actual trace, take the standard adelic Gaussian with finite integer indicators and apply (1−D)(1−cD), where D dilates the argument by an idele of norm c > 1. This kills its value at zero and its additive integral. Its Mellin factor Λ_F(z)(1−c^(−z))(1−c^(1−z)) forces dual support in the trivial-type zero set on the line. Nonzero eigenvalues have generalized eigenspaces supported where B takes that eigenvalue. Only the constant jet at each point has finite dual norm at s = 3. The printed sum counts at least one extra positive term B(γ).

Over ℚ a norm twist of the first certified zeta zero gives a zero at the center of a singleton band. This band is Plancherel-null, so the projection and its adjoint are zero. The zeroth jet still has a nonzero pairing with a compactly supported test in the trivial norm-one isotype.
The printed annulus statement uses all derivative orders below the full zero multiplicity.
One constant gives (10.2.1.12) and the asserted noncontainment for the family with full multiplicities.
For ℚ at a = 2 the zero family is empty and hence lies in the open ball for every C > 0.

In the splitting field of X³−2 use the trivial character and a nontrivial zero of its squared two-dimensional Artin factor. For s = 3 the printed full multiplicity includes k = 1 and the squared norm diverges logarithmically.

Over ℚ take `a = 1/2` and `s = 4`. Use the Dirichlet characters for the basepoints and put the trivial character first. Every primitive Dirichlet row has infinitely many critical-line ordinates (Bauer, Corollary 1), finitely many in each bounded interval, so each admits an absolute-value enumeration. The zeroth jets `(0,j,0)` escape each finite set while their first coordinate is constant. The proof is `Printed.spectralLineJet_cofinite_iff_coordinates_false_of_criticalZeros` applied to the classical theorem `primitiveDirichletL_infinite_criticalZeros`.

The printed claim fails if every primitive Dirichlet character has infinitely many zeros on the critical line (`PrimitiveDirichletLInfiniteCriticalZeros`). Over ℚ take `a = 1/2` and `s = 4`. Use the Dirichlet characters for the basepoints and put the trivial character first. Every row then has infinitely many critical-line ordinates, finitely many in each bounded interval, so each admits an absolute-value enumeration. The zeroth jets `(0,j,0)` escape each finite set while their first coordinate is constant.

Over ℚ take `a = 1/2`, `s = 4` and the enumeration of Dirichlet rows with the trivial character first. The lexicographic initial segment through `(1,0,0)` includes every zeroth jet `(0,j,0)` of the trivial row.
The printed floor cutoff makes each selected jet belong to the negative Sobolev space on the line.

Take the splitting field of X³−2, the trivial character, s = 3, and a+it a nontrivial zero of the two-dimensional Artin factor. That factor occurs squared in the Dedekind zeta function. The cutoff includes k = 1, whose squared norm has a 1/|x| tail in the log norm coordinate x.
As printed, the a-line family fails to be contained in an open ball of some positive radius.

Take F = ℚ, a = 2 and s = 2. All the completed Hecke L-functions are zero-free on this line by the absolutely convergent Euler products and the nonvanishing gamma factors. The resulting empty family is contained in every open ball.
The products of jet norms and biorthogonal vector norms within each zero block have a single bound across all blocks. The family consists of all orders selected by the printed floor cutoff.

For F = ℚ use the trivial base character, a = 1/2 and s = 2. Take pairs of simple critical-line zeta zeros with ordinates t and u tending arbitrarily close. The two cutoffs agree at s = 2. The zeroth jets have the same positive norm and their difference tends to zero by dominated convergence in the reciprocal Sobolev weight. Biorthogonality gives 1 ≤ ‖Λₜ − Λᵤ‖ ‖ψₜ‖, forcing the paired norm products to be unbounded.
The tensor image in the source-first product is claimed to be the unique class whose displayed weighted integral gives the spectral operator, with k evaluated at (x,y).

Over the rationals at Sobolev exponent two, the first certified positive zeta ordinate and a compact Bruhat test give a nonzero spectral convolution. A kernel and its printed weighted transpose cannot represent the same nonzero operator: swapping the variables twice would fix the kernel while multiplying it by two reciprocal weights whose product is strictly less than one almost everywhere.
For the printed index set the jets belong to the negative line space and, in any enumeration, are the functional half of a Markushevich basis of the theta quotient.
The squared Artin factor of the splitting field of X³−2 supplies a double zero. At s = 3 its first derivative is among the printed jets and fails square integrability.
The printed floor-indexed line jets form a normalized basis in the image of the quotient dual.
The splitting-field example at s = 3 includes a positive-order jet of infinite squared integral.
, 444. The asserted basis and its claimed primal normalization together give a bounded regular family biorthogonal to the prescribed jets.

Use the rational trivial component at a = 1/2 and s = 2. For close simple zeta zeros the two evaluation vectors approach one another in the dual norm. A vector pairing to one with the first and zero with the second has norm at least the reciprocal of their distance. The required primal bound fails.

Take F = ℚ, the trivial base character and a = 1/2. Modulate a nonzero smooth radial bump in y = log |g| by exp(icy). Its entire transform has discrete real zeros. Avoid the countably many frequencies c for which a sample is zero. Place infinitely many samples vⱼ at increasing nonadjacent indices nⱼ ≥ 1/|vⱼ|, leaving infinitely many ordinates for the other indices. Then nⱼ|vⱼ| ≥ 1, which violates decay at k = 1.

Use F = ℚ, the trivial base character and a = 1/2. Let K consist of the first and third distinct positive critical-line zeta ordinates. The omitted second ordinate lies inside the closed interval for every ε > 0.

In x = log t take a nonzero smooth bump h supported in (0, 1) and the profiles fⱼ(x) = exp(−j/2) h(x − j). Every printed seminorm tends to zero, since its weight is at most one. The genuine topology includes the zeroth Schwartz seminorm after the exp(x) twist, which grows as exp(j/2).
, second formula. The cutoff spectral function is claimed to represent the geometric truncation. The two reciprocal weights account for (10.4.3.26) and (10.4.3.30).

Over the rationals on the zero-free line a = 2, take s = 2 and the smooth cutoff of radius two and width one quarter. The spectral kernel vanishes. The cutoff's self-convolution gives a nonzero geometric truncation.

For `F = ℚ` choose the trivial extension of the trivial norm-one character and set `a = 2`. The completed zeta function has no zeros on this line, so the enumeration cannot give a value even at index zero.

The printed factorial normalization makes the retained primal biorthogonals bounded, while the full multiplicity factorial grows at most linearly in the absolute zero height. Here the completed divisor indexes the zeros of the character.

Over ℚ take the trivial character, zero twist and only the evaluation at each zero. Bounded rescaled biorthogonals would give a quadratic lower bound on the factorials at unbounded heights; the printed bound is linear.

The printed spectral trace evaluates the test at the unshifted zero z. Its summation variable ρ is z + a, so the printed weight and multiplicity use ρ − a = z. The cited §7.1.4.2 family lives in the unshifted quotient. To type the reference for general a, use its transport by f(s) ↦ f(s+a), which gives evaluation at z−a. At a = 0 the statement and its counterexample require no transport.

At a multiple zeta zero of the splitting field of X³ − 2, take a = 0 and N = 1. The first-derivative functional vanishes on the printed closed span. A radial test with nonzero Mellin derivative sends the retained value vector outside it.

Take F = ℚ with its norm section and induced dual isomorphism. Use the Gaussian exp(−y²/2) in y = log |g|, constant on the norm-one subgroup. With the kernel exp(ixy) its radial transform is √(2π) exp(−x²/2). The printed measure makes its squared norm 2π times the original squared norm, since the fixed norm-one Plancherel measure already accounts for the compact factor. The radial Plancherel measure is dx/(2π).
The printed implication says that the functionals paired with a regular Markushevich family are bounded.

In complex ℓ² take x₂ₙ = e₂ₙ and x₂ₙ₊₁ = e₂ₙ + (n+1)⁻¹ e₂ₙ₊₁. If eⱼ* is coordinate evaluation, the dual pair is e₂ₙ* − (n+1)e₂ₙ₊₁* and (n+1)e₂ₙ₊₁*. Both spans contain the finite-support families, every x has norm at least one, and the dual norms are unbounded.
For a fixed character and shift, a unique family of isotypic exponential-decay tests is biorthogonal to the zero jets. The functional label uses the unshifted zero, as in the displayed formula.

A normalized translate of the test for the highest jet at a certified rational zeta zero has the same biorthogonal pairings. Uniqueness would make the test times its norm character a constant integrable function on the noncompact idele class group, contrary to the nonzero pairing at the highest jet.

In the printed formulation the coefficient functionals must be given by integrable pairings on the ambient Sobolev space. For the rational trivial character, take `a = 1/2`, `α = 1`, and `s = 0`. The `b = 1/2` index from a certified critical-line zero places the order-zero jet on the Sobolev boundary, where the pairing diverges on a weighted L² test.
A test of conjugate weight is claimed to act through the indicated isotype by a strongly nuclear operator. Its full trace is (10.3.2.5), with the printed boundary and interior counts.
At half-width one, the quartic character modulo five gives the same contradiction at an interior zero.
A test of left-translation weight ω⁻¹ is asserted to give an operator valued in the strip quotient isotype ω.

Take F = ℚ, α = 1, s = 2 and the primitive quartic character modulo 5 as in the line counterexample. Choose a+it to be a nontrivial zero of its completed L-function, so the offset b = 0 is interior. The same bump times the conjugate of θ(g)|g|^(it) acts nontrivially on that zeroth jet, which annihilates the printed output isotype.

Use the splitting field of X³−2 and the multiple trivial-type zero β+iγ from the line case. Choose the trivial representative, s = 3, α = 1 and a = β−1. With x the log norm, take the radial test V⁻¹ exp(−iγx) v(x), where V is the norm-one volume and v is a nonzero nonnegative smooth bump supported in (1, 2). Its multiplier reaches its unique maximum modulus R at the upper-edge zero. Applying the printed formula to the convolution powers gives normalized traces tending to 2. For a peripheral generalized eigenvector of the transpose, factoring out exp((1+iγ)x) gives the positive-shift averaging equation with density v(y) exp(y)/R. The equation and dual norm give growth at most polynomial, and the Fourier transform of the averaging density has modulus one only at zero. Only constants then meet the dual norm at s = 3. Thus the peripheral algebraic multiplicity is at most one, contradicting the printed limit of 2.

The annulus uses the reciprocal strip norm and the final open ball uses the negative line norm. The ordinate is required to occur on the a-line as printed in (2). The displacement in the displayed family is constrained by the multiplicity at a+b+it, using the two cases of the definition on the same page.
In ℚ take a = 2, s = 2 and α = 0. The family is empty, so it is contained in every open ball.
The printed floor cutoff on the boundary and the full cutoff in the interior are asserted to produce elements of the reciprocal strip space.

Take F = ℚ, the trivial character, s = 1, α = b = 0 and a+it the first nontrivial Riemann zeta zero with positive ordinate. The printed cutoff includes k = 0. Its squared norm has a 1/|x| tail in log coordinates.
The asserted noncontainment in an open ball is specialized to the allowed singleton interval, where the repeated boundary reference and the stated ambient line norm both apply.
Take F = ℚ, a = 2, s = 2 and I = {0}. On that strip every Hecke L-function is zero-free, so the empty family is contained in every open ball.
The jets indexed by the printed interior and boundary multiplicities belong to the reciprocal strip space and are the functionals of a Markushevich basis in any enumeration.
On the singleton strip with s = 1 a Riemann zeta zero supplies a zeroth jet with divergent squared norm.
The printed index requires an ordinate from the a-line. The conclusion identifies the normalized family in the reciprocal strip space and also locates the annihilator in the negative line space.

For ℚ at a = α = s = 2 the a-line has no zeros. A nontrivial critical-line Riemann zero with ordinate γ supplies a nonzero quotient functional: the jet with b = -3/2 and t = γ is strip-integrable in squared norm and vanishes on polar-free weighted theta tests by the forward zeta integral factorization. An empty family cannot span this dual.

Take F = ℚ, any spectral basepoint choice, a = 1/2, α = 3, s = 2 and N = 2, and test the bound at the interior parameter b = 0 and at order i = 0. The order-zero multiplicity is at least one at the zero of `spectralStripMellinJet_norm_le_false_exists_zero`, and the factor for n = 0 in the falling factorial vanishes, so the right-hand side is zero for every constant C. A test as in `spectralStripMellinJet_norm_le_false_exists_mellin` has nonzero Mellin value there.

Take the rational field, a = 2, α = 1/4 and s = 2. The absolutely convergent Euler product and the nonvanishing archimedean factors give no zeros for any unitary lift in the strip 7/4 ≤ Re z ≤ 9/4. The existential claim already fails at M = 0.

decls.deviation: Interpret the unbound endpoint b using the cited interval [−α, α].
decls.summary: , second formula. The cutoff spectral function is claimed to represent the geometric restriction. The two reciprocal weights account for (10.4.3.47) and (10.4.3.49). The tensor is identified by the operator in (10.4.3.45).

Over the rationals, take a = 3, α = 1 and s = 2. The strip lies to the right of one, so its spectral kernel vanishes. The self-convolution of the smooth cutoff of radius two and width one quarter gives a nonzero geometric restriction.

decls.deviation: Clause (2) omits the offset range. Read it on the domain of (10.4.3.38) in clause (3), the boundary and interior of the strip.

decls.summary: For `F = ℚ` and the trivial basepoint take `a = 2` and `α = 0`. Formula (10.4.3.38) forces the offset at index zero to be zero, so this entry would be a completed zeta zero on the zero-free line of real part 2.
The printed quotient map is a topological linear isomorphism with a translation difference for every selected finite place.

At each reciprocal Euler zero for a place in the primary set S₀ = Sₚ of p. 376, the zeroth reflected Fourier jet defines a continuous linear functional on the full homogeneous theta space. This is the assertion at order zero. Analyticity at the evaluation point expresses ordinary evaluation of the meromorphic continuation there. See `strongCoprimalityFourierJet_mk`, `exists_strongCoprimalityFourierJet_full` and ERRATA F142.

Take F = ℚ, χ = 1, the rational prime 2, and s = 0. Enlarge the primary set S₀ to a finite set S with trivial S-ideal class group. The reciprocal Euler factor vanishes at zero. If the reflected Fourier zeta function of the standard adelic Gaussian were analytic at one, the functional equation would make its original zeta function continuous at zero. Its nonzero residue there contradicts this continuity.
The printed strong dual is a Hausdorff quotient of a closed subspace of a finite locally convex sum of rapidly decreasing sequence spaces.

Over ℚ with trivial character and p = 2, the primary quotient is the smooth periodic space for period log 2. Its Fourier sequence space has strong dual consisting of polynomially growing sequences. This dual is meagre in itself: the closed sets of sequences bounded by m(1 + |n|)^m, for m ≥ 1, cover it and have empty interior. A closed subspace of a finite product of Schwartz sequence spaces, quotiented by a closed subspace, is Fréchet and hence Baire.

Over ℚ take the even quadratic character modulo 5, S = {(5)}, and the uniformizer 5. In the splitting of the idele classes by the positive norm, this character has value one on the uniformizer class. Its nontrivial restriction to the 5-adic units makes the local unit average zero on this isotype. Weil principal value then acts as the identity, giving a zero source quotient. The χ-weighted Haar integral annihilates the printed difference and is nonzero on the product of the inverse compact character with exp(−(log t)²) in the positive norm coordinate t. Thus the target is nonzero.

Take E = ω × φ, where ω = ℂ^ℕ has the product topology and φ = ℂ^(ℕ) has the finest locally convex topology. Both factors are complete and nuclear. Set T(y, b)(x, a) = ∑ₙ aₙ yₙ. The φ-projection of each bounded set is supported on finitely many coordinates, so T is continuous in the strong dual topology. Every zero-neighborhood in ω leaves some coordinate unrestricted, and every zero-neighborhood in φ contains a nonzero multiple of its basis vector. Hence the pairing is unbounded on every product of zero-neighborhoods.

Let E be the Banach space c₀ of complex sequences tending to zero with the supremum norm. It is barrelled. On its dual ℓ¹ the strong topology is the norm topology and the sum of all coordinates is a continuous functional. It is represented by the constant sequence 1, which lies outside c₀. The continuous dual for the Mackey topology of the pairing is c₀, so the topologies differ.

The counterexample follows the Runge construction in ERRATA F22. At stage `L = 2^n`, copy the current entire function from a rectangle of height two with integer center height to rectangles centered at heights `4(L + k) + 2` for `0 ≤ k < L`. Keep the approximation on the old square and prescribe the value four at the new marks on both imaginary tails. Tau Ceti's polynomial Runge theorem supplies the approximations on each finite union of rows. The summable errors give an entire limit, and each source rectangle occurs in arbitrarily late blocks. Every disc inside the strip fits into a source rectangle with room for a fixed interval of shifts. The segment `[-2i, 2i]` has bounded return times at tolerance two, because every sufficiently large translate of the segment meets a mark.

On the multiplicative copy of the real line, use the real exponents `1/(n+1)`. Their limit is omitted, so the set is discrete and lies in the strip with real parts between zero and two. A nonnegative test supported where the modulus exceeds one has every sample bounded below by its strictly positive Haar integral.

Use the additive real line, Lebesgue measure, `U k = (-2⁻ᵏ, 2⁻ᵏ)` and `x = 0`. For `t ≠ 0` put `f(t) = sgn(t) |t|^(-1/2)` and set `f(0) = 0`. Multiply `sgn(t) |t|^(1/4)` by the continuous cutoff `max 0 (min 1 (2 - |t|))` to obtain `φ`. The odd function `f` has zero average for every index. Away from zero on these intervals, `φ(t) * f(t) = |t|^(-1/4)`, so the averages are `(4/3) * 2^(k/4)` and diverge.

Take E to be the finitely supported complex sequences with the ℓ² norm and F to be ℂ. In the completion of E the vector with coordinates 2⁻ⁿ, n ≥ 0, defines a rank-one evaluation on E′, μ-continuous by the singleton compact set. Each tensor with scalar second factor evaluates at a finitely supported vector. The coordinate functionals distinguish that vector from (2⁻ⁿ).

Take one normal and one tangential coordinate and a smooth compactly supported real bump χ equal to one near zero. The test χ(x)χ(y) exp(xy) has x-derivatives at zero equal to the linearly independent functions χ(y)yʲ. For a finite sum of pure products all these derivatives lie in the finite span of the tangential factors.

Take one normal coordinate and no tangential coordinates. The tangential test space is ℂ by evaluation at its single point. For both tensor topologies the product map is the scalar isomorphism f ⊗ a ↦ af.

For F = ℚ(ζ₃), take the archimedean stage and add a finite place dividing the different. Choose a test whose Fourier value at zero is one. Fourier after integer-ring insertion has value at zero equal to the added integer ring's Tamagawa mass, which is less than one; insertion after Fourier has value one. Equal theta classes have equal values at zero, as follows from the global zeta residue at the trivial character. Thus the two classes differ.

For F = ℚ use the odd real test x ↦ x exp(−πx²), at S consisting of the real place and globally tensored with the indicator of the finite integer adeles. Each test is nonzero, and the terms at opposite nonzero rational elements cancel at every global idele. The real-stage sum pairs the terms at the two units ±1. Each theta map sends its test and zero to the same point, so the pullback topology cannot separate them.

Over ℚ at the archimedean stage the norm-one quotient is `{±1}/{±1}`, so the sole summand is the entire theta space with its own topology. Globally over ℚ, the action of the profinite norm-one group factors through a finite group on each finite test level. The finite character projections extend through the inductive limit and the theta quotient to a continuous inverse to the sum map.

For F = ℚ(ζ₃), the norm-one idele classes have Tamagawa mass M = π/(3√3), with 0 < M < 1. Mellin evaluation at the squared norm is nonzero on a normalized Hecke test and is multiplied by M under the global trivial-character average. Idempotence of that average would therefore imply M² = M, a contradiction.
In dimension one the single frequency `1` is rationally independent, and times zero and one have the same image modulo one.

As printed, for every number field F, every test φ vanishing on C_F¹ and every interval I = [−α, α] with α > 0 as in §1.8.4, p. 53, the sum of the local principal values equals M(φ)(|·|^{1/2}) + M(φ)(|·|^{−1/2}) minus the sum of N(c)·M(φ)(c|·|^{−1/2}) over the zeros c in the interior of Ω(C_F)_I, with convergent series. The interior is |σ(c) − 1/2| < α, and a norm section lists each quasi-character once. The complex denominator is the ordinary modulus printed in (12.5.1.1). The local tests vanish at one, so this term is an ordinary integral.

Take F = ℚ(i), α = 1, and φ(g) = h(|g|) − h(|g|⁻¹) for a nonzero nonnegative smooth bump h supported in (9/4, 11/4). All finite local terms vanish because the two norm intervals avoid every prime power and its reciprocal. Inversion interchanges the two pole terms with a minus sign. Only the trivial norm-one character contributes, and the completed Dedekind zeta functional equation pairs s with 1 − s, with equal multiplicity and opposite Mellin values in the centered strip. The restricted functions are invariant under one good subgroup `k'` with `ι k' ≤ a.2`, vanish off the compact set `ι⁻¹ (C ∩ a.1)`, and descend to the elementary quotient of a structural pair `(J, k')` with `J ≤ ι⁻¹ a.1`, where the descent is the stage function composed with an elementary homomorphism. So the restriction factors through one stage of `𝒟(w.Completionˣ)`, and continuity into that Fréchet stage follows from the closed graph theorem, since point evaluations are continuous on both stages.

Principal ideles form a closed discrete subgroup, the class group is locally compact Hausdorff, and the descended norm admits a continuous homomorphic section. Extension along a field embedding commutes with the quotient maps.

The ideles are locally compact Hausdorff and split coordinatewise into the infinite local unit groups and the restricted product of the finite local unit groups. The norm is continuous with closed kernel.

, footnote 27 (finite places). Let `Φ_χ` be the radial profiles of a test `f` (Mellin transforms matching the idelic Mellin integrals, as in `idelicExplicitFormula_mellinMatching`). Summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section, the discriminant–conductor terms minus the prime-power terms of the explicit formula of Theorem B.4.2.2 for `Φ_χ` give minus the sum over the finite places of the scaled Connes–Weil principal values of the restrictions of `f`.

, footnote 27 (conductor terms). Summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section, the conductor part of the discriminant–conductor term (Equation (B.4.2.3)) times `Φ_χ(0)` gives minus the sum over the finite places of `(log q_v / vol O_v^×) ∫_{O_v^×} (f_v(u) - f_v(1)) |u|^{1/2} / |1 - u| d^×u`, a sum with only finitely many nonzero terms.

(Fourier inversion on `C¹` at the identity). The values at `0` of the radial profiles `Φ_χ` of a test `f` (fixed by their Mellin transforms as in `idelicExplicitFormula_finiteMatching`) sum over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section to `f(1)`.

Summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section, the prime-power terms of the explicit formula of Theorem B.4.2.2 for the radial profiles `Φ_χ` of `f` give the sum over the finite places of `(log q_v / vol O_v^×) ∫_{|u| ≠ 1} f_v(u) |u|^{1/2} / |1 - u| d^×u`, a sum with only finitely many nonzero terms.

Summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section, the prime-power terms at a finite place `v` of the explicit formula of Theorem B.4.2.2 for the radial profiles `Φ_χ` of `f` give `(log q_v / vol O_v^×) ∫_{|u| ≠ 1} f_v(u) |u|^{1/2} / |1 - u| d^×u`.

, with Remark B.4.1.6. A family of distributions on the idele class test space whose values are absolutely summable at every test has a continuous pointwise sum, and converges to it in the strong dual: the test space is barrelled and its bounded sets are precompact.

, footnote 27 (one infinite place `w`). Let `Φ_χ` be the radial profiles of a test `f`, as in `idelicExplicitFormula_finiteMatching`. Summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section, the archimedean digamma terms at `w` of the explicit formula of Theorem B.4.2.2 for `Φ_χ` give minus the Connes–Weil principal value at `w` of the restriction of `f`.

, footnote 27 (character sum at a complex place `w`). Let `Φ_χ` be the radial profiles of a test `f`, as in `idelicExplicitFormula_finiteMatching`, and write `g(z) = f(e^z)` for the test in logarithmic coordinates on `F_w^× = ℂ^×` (so `|e^z|_w = e^{2 Re z}`). Summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section, the archimedean digamma terms at `w` are `∫_0^∞ (2 e^{-t} f(1) / t - A(t)) dt - 2 log 2π · f(1)` with the Poisson average `A(t) = (2π)⁻¹ ∫_0^{2π} e^{-t/2} (g(t/2 + iφ) + g(-t/2 + iφ)) / |1 - e^{-t/2 + iφ}|² dφ`.

, footnote 27 (local identity at a complex place `w`). For a test `f` on `F_w^× = ℂ^×`, with `g(z) = f(e^z)` and the Poisson average `A` as in `idelicExplicitFormula_infiniteMatching_complexCharacterSum`, `∫_0^∞ (2 e^{-t} f(1) / t - A(t)) dt - 2 log 2π · f(1)` is minus the Connes–Weil principal value of `f` at `w`.

, footnote 27 (character sum at a real place `w`). Let `Φ_χ` be the radial profiles of a test `f`, as in `idelicExplicitFormula_finiteMatching`, and write `g₊(y) = f(e^y)`, `g₋(y) = f(-e^y)` for the test along the positive and negative half-lines of `F_w = ℝ`. Summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section, the archimedean digamma terms at `w` are `∫_0^∞ ½ (2 e^{-t} f(1) / t - e^{-t/4} (Q(t/2) + Q(-t/2)) / (1 - e^{-t})) dt - log π · f(1)` with `Q(y) = (g₊(y) + g₋(y)) / 2 + e^{-t/2} (g₊(y) - g₋(y)) / 2`.

, footnote 27 (domination at a real place `w`). For the radial profiles `Φ_χ` of a test `f` (as in `idelicExplicitFormula_finiteMatching`), each real digamma kernel `t ↦ K_χ(t)` at `w` (with the radial exponent and sign parity of `χ` at `w`) is integrable on `(0, ∞)`, and `∑_χ ∫_0^∞ |K_χ(t)| dt < ∞`.

, footnote 27 (local identity at a real place `w`). For a test `f` on `F_w^× = ℝ^×`, with `g₊(y) = f(e^y)`, `g₋(y) = f(-e^y)` and `Q` as in `idelicExplicitFormula_infiniteMatching_realCharacterSum`, `∫_0^∞ ½ (2 e^{-t} f(1) / t - e^{-t/4} (Q(t/2) + Q(-t/2)) / (1 - e^{-t})) dt - log π · f(1)` is minus the Connes–Weil principal value of `f` at `w`.
