(Fubini for `C[F] = C¹ × ℝ_{>0}`). For a character `χ` trivial on the image of the norm section `τ`, the idelic Mellin integral of a test `f` against `χ |·|^(s - 1/2)`, divided by the volume of `C¹`, is the Mellin transform at `s - 1/2` of the radial profile `x ↦ c · ∫_{C¹} f(τ(eˣ) u) χ(u) du`, for one constant `c` (fixed by the normalization of the Tamagawa measures) and all `s`.

For a fixed test and a fixed unitary character, the centered idelic Mellin transform of the test decays like the inverse square of the height in the closed critical strip. The test is smooth and compactly supported along the norm, so this is the standard integration by parts in the radial variable.

(Fourier inversion on `C¹`). For a test `f` on the idele classes and a norm-one class `c`, the Fourier series of `f` on the compact group `C¹` converges absolutely to `f(c)`: summed over the characters trivial on the image of the norm section `τ` (these restrict bijectively to the characters of `C¹`), the coefficients `vol(C¹)⁻¹ ∫_{C¹} f(u) χ(u) du` times `χ(c)⁻¹` have sum `f(c)`.

(the counting step, through Lemma B.4.4.8, p. 624). For a good subgroup `k` of the idele classes there are finitely many one-parameter subgroups `b j` of the norm-one classes `C¹` such that the characters trivial on the image of the norm section `τ` (equivalently, the characters of `C¹`) that are trivial on `k ∩ C¹` and have all frequencies `κ_j(χ)` (the derivative of `t ↦ χ(b j t)` at `0`) of size at most `T` number at most `C (T + 1)^d`.

(Fourier inversion on `C¹`, absolute convergence). The Fourier coefficients `∫_{C¹} f(u) χ(u) du` of a test `f` on the idele classes, indexed by the characters trivial on the image of the norm section `τ` (these restrict bijectively to the characters of `C¹`), are absolutely summable.

(the decomposition `C[F] = C¹ × ℝ_{>0}` and the character expansion of the test). For a test `f` on the idele classes, a continuous section `τ` of the class norm and a unitary character `χ`, the radial profile `x ↦ c · ∫_{C¹} f(τ(eˣ) u) χ(u) du` (any constant `c`) is an exponentially decaying Schwartz function of the logarithmic variable `x`: it is smooth because `f` is smooth along the one-parameter subgroup `x ↦ τ(eˣ)`, and compactly supported because the class norm is proper.
, and Lemma B.4.4.9, pp. 624–625. The spectral terms of the idelic explicit formula are absolutely summable at every test.

, summed over characters. Over the unitary characters trivial on the image of the norm section `τ`, the per-character sums of the absolute spectral terms of the idelic explicit formula at a fixed test are summable. This is the uniform half of Lemma B.4.4.9: a test only sees the characters of a Lie quotient of the idele classes, and the zero count of their completed Hecke L-functions must be polynomial jointly in the height and in the archimedean frequency of the character (see the paper-gap note at `summable_ideleClassMellin_completedHeckeZeros`).

On a fixed Bruhat quotient, the total multiplicity of zeros with height and angular frequencies below `T+1` is polynomial in `T+1`. The finite-subsum formulation needs no local finiteness assumption. Compare Iwaniec–Kowalski, Proposition 5.7(1), and, for finite-order characters, Lagarias–Odlyzko, Lemma 5.4.

, for one character. For a fixed unitary character `χ`, the spectral terms of the idelic explicit formula at the zeros of the completed Hecke L-function of `χ`, weighted by their multiplicities, are absolutely summable at every test.

If only finitely many positive-order zeros are omitted by a narrow window, the combined cutoff sums have a holomorphic limit for every approximation family. On the Euler half-plane its value is the polar-corrected logarithmic derivative minus the finite sum of the omitted poles.

If the omitted zeros have summable multiplicity-weighted reciprocal heights, a single matched family gives an actual holomorphic cutoff limit throughout the narrow chart. Across the entire Euler half-plane the discrepancy is the absolutely convergent omitted resolvent.

The completed functional equation reflects the zero-free region for the inverse character to the left of one half for the original character.

Right-hand nonvanishing for the finite continuations in the section-normalized characters implies right-hand nonvanishing for every completed continuation. Imaginary norm twists translate the exponent, and the gamma factors are regular and nonzero in the positive half-plane.

, and §B.4.2, pp. 614–615. Take the logarithmic derivative of the completed Hecke function at `z + 1/2`, add the two polar fractions for the trivial character, and subtract the trivial gamma logarithmic derivative at `5/2`. **Borel–Mittag-Leffler lift.** In a complete locally convex space with a countable basis at zero, consider levels `L k i` of continuous functionals. The velocity is integrable on the parameter interval of a piecewise `C¹` contour.
A continuous scalar function on the trace gives an integrable velocity-weighted function on the parameter interval.
The scalar contour integral of a derivative vanishes when its primitive is defined and differentiable near the trace.
A function continuous on the trace is integrable against the contour measure, and its scalar integral is the parameter integral weighted by the contour velocity.
Bounded convergence for kernels continuous on the contour trace.
The closure of the set on which a null-homologous cycle has nonzero index is a compact subset of its domain.
Integration against the cycle measure sums the ordinary contour integrals with their integer multiplicities.

On a circle in the punctured disc, integrating a scalar evaluation of the Laurent expansion against the local coordinate to the power `-k - 1` gives `2πi` times the scalar evaluation of the coefficient at `k`.
Clearing a pole shifts the Laurent exponent `j - n` to the Taylor exponent `j`.
If the Laurent series has a nonzero negative term, its first nonzero term gives a pole.
At a removable point, each scalar evaluation extends across the center with value equal to the scalar evaluation of the Laurent coefficient at zero.
A vector Laurent series is determined by its scalarizations, each of which is recovered from a circle integral.
All sufficiently small circles recover the residue and lie in the regular domain.
Every point in the domain has a pole-clearing power on a disc whose puncture lies in the original domain of holomorphy.
Filling each removable exceptional point with the constant Laurent coefficient gives a holomorphic representative on the open complement of the exceptional poles.
An isolating circle gives the residue of any representative which agrees with the original function off the exceptional set.
Adding the pole-clearing exponents gives a common power which clears both germs.
Each scalar evaluation of a vector meromorphic germ is meromorphic.
A regular point has a Taylor expansion and hence cannot have negative order.
The index is locally constant off the trace, since it is continuous there and takes only two values.
The scalar Cauchy kernel times a holomorphic function is integrable on the trace. Its integral is given by Cauchy–Goursat and integration by parts.
Uniform convergence in the target is preserved by multiplication with a scalar function bounded on the set.
A continuous linear map sends the derivative of a vector-valued holomorphic function to the derivative of the composite.
The Taylor errors on a closed subdisc remain bounded even after multiplication by the truncation index: this can be tested on each functional separately.
Lift a first scalar derivative by restricting to a smooth real curve inside the domain.
Iteration gives vector representatives for all scalar derivatives on the open set.

On a circle in the punctured disc of convergence, integrating a scalar evaluation of the function against the local coordinate to the power `-k - 1` gives `2πi` times the scalar evaluation of the Laurent coefficient at `k`.
Integer powers of the local coordinate are continuous away from the center.
A scalar derivative on a dense subset extends to an ordinary derivative at each of its points if the missing values are the limits from that subset.
Vanishing scalar integrals on simple contours imply complex differentiability by the rectangular form of Morera's theorem.
Scalar holomorphy makes the vector difference quotients Cauchy in the target topology. Quasi-completeness gives their limit in the original space.
Fill a single isolated puncture by lifting the bounded scalar extensions to the quasi-complete target.
A holomorphic Taylor expansion, divided by a power of the local coordinate, is a Laurent expansion of the cleared function.
Integrating on an affine reparametrization of a straight side is a real change of variable. Only the open parameter interval contributes.
The denominator in the Taylor kernel accounts for the power used to clear the pole.
The four affine sides of the counterclockwise unit square, each traversed in one quarter of the parameter interval.
Stretch the unit square to a rectangle with the specified lower left and upper right corners.
Dixon's argument for a finite weighted family. Glue the integral of the divided difference to the exterior Cauchy transform wherever the total index vanishes.
Cauchy–Goursat for a null-homologous weighted family, obtained by applying the divided-difference formula to the function `w ↦ (w - z) * g w`.
The Taylor series of a Banach-valued holomorphic function converges uniformly on every smaller open disc.
Uniform convergence in a polynormable space is seminorm-smallness of the difference.
A holomorphic function is weakly holomorphic.
A point on the cover together with its discrete fibre.
Null sets upstairs are null on almost every fibre. Outer regularity lets us apply the compact level estimate to open supersets of arbitrarily small measure.
A group automorphism lifts on each discrete fibre to an affine map with the same real-linear part on every fibre.
A seminorm-bounded closed disk carries the pointwise topology by compactness.

The chain rule on a lifted fibre expresses each mixed partial after an affine change of variables as a finite linear combination of mixed partials before the change. Its coefficients depend only on the linear part and the derivative orders.
The next-order seminorms give a common Lipschitz constant for each mixed partial.
On the pure lattice group `ℤ^r` (no real, torus or finite part), each weighted derivative bound is the supremum over the lattice of the monomial times the function.
Each weighted bound of the pullback is controlled by a continuous seminorm of the original Schwartz function.
A bound on all weighted derivative evaluations bounds the defining seminorm.
On each coordinate box the partials of a bounded sequence have a uniformly Cauchy subsequence. A countable product gives the same subsequence for all boxes and orders.
The elementary Schwartz space is complete.
Separating the finite coordinate identifies its elementary Schwartz space with a finite product of elementary Schwartz spaces.
The smoothness and decay conditions only use the finite factor as an index. Realize a nonempty finite index as a cyclic group to apply the Fréchet theorem.

A weighted coordinate monomial composed with an elementary group automorphism is a finite linear combination of coordinate monomials on the same group. The projection onto the real and lattice factors kills the compact torus and finite factors, and additivity gives linear coordinate forms on the remaining two factors.
A bounded sequence has a subsequence Cauchy in every defining seminorm.
For a polynomial weight and a constant-coefficient polynomial differential operator, the supremum of the weighted operator is a continuous seminorm on the elementary Schwartz space.
Reading a Euclidean Schwartz function in the real coordinate gives a continuous linear equivalence with the corresponding elementary Schwartz space.
One additional coordinate weight gives uniform decay of a bounded family's weighted partials outside a sufficiently large real and lattice box.
The weighted derivative defining each elementary Schwartz seminorm.
Multiplication by a discrete slice scales every real and torus derivative by that slice's value.
If derivatives and weights separate into two factors, pointwise multiplication induces an embedding from the injective tensor of the factor spaces.
Multiplying a Euclidean slice and a torus slice multiplies their independent derivatives and the real weight.
Each seminorm of an elementary Schwartz space satisfies the absolute summability estimate on a suitable neighborhood of signed sums.
On each real cube and lattice fibre a fixed extra polynomial weight controls the sum of mixed partials even at independently chosen points.
Each polynomially weighted directional derivative admits a neighborhood bound for the sum of absolute evaluations at a common point.
Each elementary seminorm can be estimated at one lifted point up to a factor of two. The zero seminorm value permits any point.
The single-fibre torus orbit is generated, in closed linear span, by pure tensors. Its torus Fourier coefficients are Euclidean Schwartz functions times characters.
Each weighted derivative evaluation is a continuous linear functional.
Cutting off discrete fibres and translating the torus preserves all the seminorm bounds.
The standard torus characters belong to its elementary Schwartz space.

A nonnegative compactly supported bump fixes the normalization of Haar measure on the dual. Its spectral measure gives positive mass to a compact set, so the averaging identity on that set ensures its squared Fourier integral is finite.
Restricting to one lattice and finite fibre and the identity of the torus gives an ordinary Euclidean Schwartz function.
A Fourier density under a finite regular spectral measure corresponds to convolution with the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of that measure.
A Fourier norm identity for compactly supported continuous functions extends to integrable square-integrable functions by approximation in both norms.
The Fourier norm of a single nonzero compactly supported test function fixes the scalar between two regular Haar measures satisfying Plancherel.
The supremum of a monomial times a sequence is at most the weighted absolute sum whose order is the total degree of the monomial.
The product weight `∏ 1 / (a_k + 1/2)^2` has finite sum over `ℤ^r`.
Evaluating the Fourier–Stieltjes representation at the identity identifies the total mass with the integral of the squared source norm.
The translate of one spectral measure and the other spectral measure agree after weighting each by the squared Fourier magnitude of the other function.

A product-measurable representative for the convolution kernel, carried on a rectangle with σ-finite sides. The two sectionwise identities avoid any measurability assumption on multiplication for the product σ-algebra.
The autocorrelation has compact support, and its Fourier integral is the squared modulus of the Fourier integral of the original function.

The range of an L² Fourier isometry has trivial orthogonal complement. Orthogonality to translates of each integrable test function forces the product of its conjugated transform with the orthogonal vector to vanish almost everywhere.
Multiplying an L² function by a character translates its Plancherel transform.
A finite regular measure on the dual is determined by its integrals against the evaluation characters.
Each weighted derivative evaluation is bounded by its defining seminorm.
A small L¹ translation difference bounds the transform times the displacement of the character at the translating element.
It suffices to check the signed-sum criterion on a generating family of seminorms: the bounds are stable under sums, nonnegative multiples and domination.
A nonzero L² function with orthogonal modulations gives a normalized measure whose Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients vanish at those modulations.
Each weighted absolute sum of a lattice sequence is bounded by a constant times finitely many suprema of monomials times the sequence.
The identification of rapidly decreasing sequences with Schwartz functions on `ℤ^r`, stated with an explicit universe for the trivial finite factor.
Multiplication by the `j`th weight is a continuous linear map from the rapidly decreasing sequences to `ℓ¹` whose norm is the `j`th defining seminorm.
Increasing a coordinate multiplicity inserts one copy of that direction.
Assemble the real and torus coordinates of one unit cube.
A single positive polynomial controls the lattice weight throughout the unit cube.
Multiplying by a coordinate monomial spends only the polynomial part of the weight, leaving a summable factor on the cube labels.
Regroup a finite sum by labels and dominate it by a summable majorant.
Choosing the opposite phase at each value of a functional realizes the sum of their norms as the norm of one signed sum.
The sum over `ℤ^r` of a product of one-variable weights is the `r`-th power of the one-variable sum.
A mixed partial multiplied by its real and lattice monomials.
Every point has a unique right `H`-translate in the Borel section `Δ`.
A Borel set meeting every coset exactly once is a strict fundamental domain for the right action of `H`.
Right multiplication by `H` does not change the coset.
The fibre integral of the norm of a compact test satisfies Weil in lower-integral form.
On a compact subset of a strict fibre level set, finitely many test bumps give a single minorant for the open set upstairs.
The top subgroup of `Multiplicative (ULift ℤ)` is not compact.
Compact lifting controls all the continuous direct sum seminorms by seminorms of the difference coordinates. This suffices for acyclicity of a Fréchet system.
A pointwise family lifting a compact set has bounded range.
If projections along an ascending chain eventually agree on each fixed stage, their successive differences rule out a bounded set escaping every stage.
Any two structural pairs have a common upper bound.
Integrate against Haar measure normalized to mass one on a compact group.
A surjective continuous homomorphism pushes normalized Haar measure to normalized Haar measure.
Compute a kernel average on the image group in the structural quotient.
Equality of annihilator intersections gives equality of the images of the compact averaging groups modulo the source kernel.
The intersection of an open ascending union with a compactly generated subgroup is already contained in one member of the union.
An elementary presentation gives a compact generating neighborhood.
The Pontryagin dual of the additive reals is connected.
Smoothness on the covering vector spaces gives continuity on the elementary group.
Continuous evaluation of a linear map to a normed space follows from a single continuous seminorm bound.
The stage-valued averaging map is continuous by barrelledness and the uniform bound for each of its evaluations.
Restrict a bounded seminorm along a continuous linear map from a first-countable stage.
A uniform bound on all evaluations gives a continuous map into an elementary Schwartz space from a barrelled space.
Evaluation on a countable family of uniformly dense tests separates points and supplies at least one nonzero value at every point of the group.
In a real–torus–discrete decomposition of a compactly generated group, the discrete factor is finitely generated and splits as a free abelian group times a finite group.
The target of an open continuous map from a real vector group has an elementary presentation if it is compactly generated.
A Schwartz function on an elementary group which descends from an open subgroup through an open quotient is Schwartz on the quotient.
Only the torus and finite coordinates of an elementary group can receive a nonzero continuous homomorphism from a compact group.
Independent closed seminorm bounds cut out a compact convex disk in an elementary Schwartz space.
Translating the compact coordinates and cutting out whole discrete fibers does not increase any elementary Schwartz seminorm.
An affine lift on every discrete fibre uses the same linear part.
Elementary Schwartz functions separate points and have no common zero. A pure tensor tests the Euclidean, torus, lattice and finite coordinates.
A continuous homomorphism from a torus to a real vector group vanishes, since the multiples of a nonzero vector cannot all lie in a compact range.
The subgroup of a finite torus killed by doubling has cardinality two to the power of the number of circle coordinates.
A first countable vector topology admits a nonzero rescaling of any sequence whose terms then form a bounded set.
For a real structural pair with trivial good subgroup, the quotient identifies with the real line by sending the class of each element to that element.
Some compact subgroup has a σ-compact annihilator. The subgroup is the intersection of a decreasing sequence of compact identity neighborhoods.
Descend the realized function, including its extension by zero, to the quotient of the entire group by the stage kernel.
A compact subset of a quotient of a locally compact group lies in the image of a compact set.
The uniform norm on functions is continuous in the final topology, since the zero-order seminorm of each stage dominates it.
A Euclidean Schwartz bump can take value one at one point and vanish at a second.

A sequence of linear functionals that eventually vanish on each stage cannot be nonzero on a corresponding sequence in a bounded set. The functionals can be rescaled and combined into one seminorm continuous on every stage.
A real-valued additive character on an open subgroup extends across the discrete quotient, preserving continuity.
A Fréchet source factors through a stage of any exhaustive injective Fréchet system.
A number field has a finite place since its ring of integers is not a field.
The trivial subgroup is the only good subgroup of the additive reals.
A good subgroup of the real line is trivial, since a compact subgroup cannot contain all integer multiples of a nonzero real number.
If the dual is locally Euclidean, the subgroup generated by a suitable compact neighborhood has no nontrivial characters on its quotient, so it equals the whole group.
A cofinal sequence with embedding transitions induces the same final locally convex topology as the full system. Each stage embeds by factoring through a stage of that sequence.
Restriction to a closed subgroup is an open map on the dual groups.
The open subgroup of a structural pair for the additive completion is compact.
The compact sets of the additive completion are contained in compact open subgroups.
Every elementary stage of an ultrametric local field is finite-dimensional. A sufficiently small open subgroup maps trivially to its elementary quotient.
Membership in a double supremum of submodules whose sigma-indexed family is nonempty and directed is membership in one of the submodules.
In an additive ultrametric field, powers of a small nonzero scalar generate cyclic additive subgroups eventually contained in each zero-neighborhood.
Principal units approaching one give small cyclic groups under any continuous homomorphism with trivial kernel.
The compact-open neighborhoods of the trivial character test values on compact sets.
A countable union of images of finite-dimensional stages has countable rank.
A compact identity neighborhood generates a connected locally compact group.
In any elementary presentation of a real structural quotient, the torus and discrete factors are trivial and the real coordinate is a linear equivalence.
A real structural pair has full open subgroup and trivial kernel, so its quotient map identifies it with the real group.
Along any elementary chart of a real structural quotient, the descended function is the original function precomposed with a linear projection.
The full real group with trivial kernel has a one-dimensional elementary presentation.
The ranges of the stage realizations, indexed by a pair and a presentation of its quotient, form a directed family of submodules.
The range of a stage realization grows along the order on structural pairs, for any choice of elementary presentations of the two quotients.
Normalized averaging is linear on continuous functions, is invariant under kernel translations, and fixes a function already realized in this stage.
Averaging along an ascending chain eventually gives the same result on every element of a fixed stage.
Some structural pair with an elementary presentation exists.
The intersections of a fixed stage's open subgroups in the group and its dual with the corresponding subgroups in an ascending chain both stabilize.
Every stage average has a representative in the averaged stage. First realize it in a common larger stage, then descend using kernel invariance.
Linearity and uniqueness of the representative lift averaging to a linear map into the elementary stage.
A bounded set in the full Schwartz–Bruhat space is the image of a bounded set in one stage, obtained by applying that stage's continuous retraction.
Successive differences of the cutoff and averaging projections force a bounded set to lie in one stage.
The indicator of a compact open subgroup is realized on its one-point quotient.
An element can be realized in a stage above any given structural pair, with any chosen presentation of the larger quotient.
A cofinal sequence of structural pairs with compatible transitions presents the Schwartz–Bruhat space as a locally convex inductive limit.
A stage bound also bounds a realized function on the whole group.
A sequence of nonidentity points generating arbitrarily small cyclic groups obstructs metrizability, since bounded tests must share a single stage kernel.
On a cofinal cone the projections of a fixed test form a bounded set.
On each test, consecutive projections in an increasing chain eventually agree because the two intersection subgroups stabilize on its stage.
The stage maps for all pairs and presentations cover the Schwartz–Bruhat space.
If the Schwartz–Bruhat limit is metrizable, a single structural stage covers it. The strict Fréchet presentation is then complete, so its identity factors through a stage.
A countable separating family induces a second-countable topology on each compact set. The interiors of a compact exhaustion then cover the group.
Finite products of a compact generating set and its inverse give a countable compact covering of a compactly generated group.
Countably many tests that have no common zero cover the group by countably many compactly generated support subgroups.
A compact convex set of pointwise functions containing every cutoff translate of a test also contains its normalized stage average.
The uniform seminorm of the input bounds the values of its averaged representative.
For a fixed elementary test a compact disk in its own stage represents all averages whose cutoff contains its kernel and whose kernel lies in its support subgroup.
Inside the larger stage, support and invariance are closed pointwise equations. Descent identifies their common solution space with the range of the transition.
Inside a common stage, every cutoff and compact translate is represented by an elementary test satisfying the original seminorm bounds.
An injective continuous linear map between Fréchet spaces with closed range is a closed embedding: apply open mapping to its corestriction onto that complete subspace.
On a discrete fibre an open-subgroup cutoff either vanishes identically or its quotient coordinate lifts to an affine map with fibre-independent linear part.
Two open coordinate maps from a common group produce the elementary representative, with zero extension off the range of the larger-stage coordinate map.
A Schwartz function pulled back by a quotient with compact kernel and extended by zero from an open subgroup is still Schwartz.
The ambient noncompact coordinates descend through an open surjection with compact kernel. Consequently their monomials are polynomial weights in the quotient coordinates.
Every value in the elementary chart is attained at a point of the open subgroup.
On a torus a character is Schwartz. Translation multiplies every derivative on its vector cover by a scalar of norm one.
The product of two groups of order two is not cyclic, since its exponent is two.
Left translation preserves each finite order of Bruhat differentiability with the same good subgroup.
On each structural quotient, differentiation along a one-parameter subgroup lowers the order of Bruhat differentiability by one and preserves the good subgroup.
All rows of a fixed test, multiplied by any fixed weight in the column variables, lie in a bounded subset of the row Schwartz space.
A scalar directional derivative must vanish on constants and hence on all characters. Character separation then forces its one-parameter subgroup to be trivial.
The algebra generated by the one-parameter derivatives preserves the Schwartz submodule.
The images of the open and compact subgroups form a structural pair on the quotient.
The finite word presentation identifies a symbol with a polynomial in the noncompact coordinates.
The polynomial seminorms bound the symbol times a Schwartz function on an elementary group.
Products of real-valued homomorphisms are symbols of suitably normalized words on the dual.
An annihilator is the intersection of the closed kernels of point evaluations.
A continuous functional on a completed inductive tensor is determined by pure tensors.
Two continuous linear maps on a completed inductive tensor agree if they agree on the images of all pure tensors.
On an elementary presentation of a structural quotient, a translated one-parameter subgroup lifts to an affine line in the real and torus cover of a single discrete fiber.
An affine map from a real normed space to an elementary group pulls back functions that are smooth on each covered discrete fiber to smooth functions.
On an elementary group, differentiability of class C¹ on each lifted discrete fiber gives continuity of the orbit derivative.
The quotient action gives translation by elements of the stage's own open subgroup.
Translation is jointly continuous when the function varies in a fixed structural stage. Locally the translating element and the function are handled in one larger stage.
The coset integral factors continuously through a single elementary quotient stage.
Integration sends a stage into the fixed space of its image stage projector.
Glue stage maps on an exhaustive directed family of linear images by taking the union of their graphs. Injectivity in each stage makes the union a graph.
The product measurable structure on an elementary group agrees with its Borel structure.
A continuous real-valued homomorphism kills the compact factors and is linear in the real and lattice coordinates.
On bounded sets of translating parameters, each translated seminorm is dominated by a single continuous seminorm of the original function.
Multiplication by a compactly supported elementary test is continuous by point evaluation.
The zero-order seminorm controls evaluation uniformly on the elementary group.
Smoothness on the covering space descends to continuity on each discrete fiber.

A weighted mixed partial of a fixed-direction derivative on the elementary cover is controlled by finitely many seminorms of the original function. The weights are unchanged and one derivative index is raised by one.
On an elementary group the largest structural stage has zero kernel and realizes the whole space.
Embed the real and torus factors in a vector space and localize a bump on one discrete fiber.
Rapid decay in the real and lattice directions makes an elementary Schwartz function integrable for any Haar measure on its elementary group.
A compactly supported function smooth on every fiber has finite weighted partials.
Bounded symbol-weighted derivatives bound each defining seminorm on the full elementary stage.
On every elementary stage an orbit derivative is a continuous linear operator, and every orbit curve of a stage function is differentiable at zero.
Split off the real and lattice factors, then normalize a positive test over the compact remainder.
Polynomial decay of the transforms of all tests on a stage bounds the mixed partials of their transforms on the dual stage.
Multiplication by a continuous real additive functional preserves elementary tests.
Products of two pullbacks are Schwartz when their noncompact coordinates control the source coordinates.
A product chart identifies the elementary product test space with the completed inductive tensor of its factors. Point evaluation identifies its action on pure tensors.
The weighted rows of a product test let a distribution on the first factor act on its slices, producing a Schwartz test on the second factor.
Lift the vector and free lattice factors through an open quotient. The remaining coordinates lie in the compact torus and finite factors.
A stage can be enlarged to contain any prescribed translating element.
Every point belongs to the open subgroup of a structural pair with the given good subgroup.
Products of the directional generators realize all ordered iterated derivatives on the cover.
A vector of the real and torus cover defines a one-parameter subgroup realizing its directional derivative.
Translation by an elementary one-parameter subgroup lifts on each discrete fiber to translation by a real multiple of a fixed vector.
Every real and lattice coordinate monomial is the pullback of a symbol along the given biduality map.

The inverse Fourier integral `g ↦ (x ↦ ∫ g χ · χ x dν)` maps Schwartz–Bruhat functions on the dual continuously to Schwartz–Bruhat functions on `G`: it is the Fourier transform on the dual followed by transport along `x ↦ (evaluation at x⁻¹)` to the double dual.
Choose a structural quotient with a neighborhood whose entire lifted fiber lies in the given open set.
A good subgroup is contained, together with any prescribed point, in an open compactly generated subgroup.
On each affine lift, mixed partials of the integral are integrals of Schwartz derivatives. The derivative test depends only on the original test and the list of directions.
Translating a compact set gives a uniform bound on the Haar mass of its intersection with a closed subgroup. Translate a point in the intersection to the identity.
The reciprocal quadratic product weight has uniformly bounded integrals on all cosets. Partition the real and lattice coordinates into unit boxes indexed by an integer lattice.
A rectangle around four support points contains a product of tests with nonzero pairing.
Localizing each factor by a cutoff transfers vanishing from pure products to all nearby tests.
A topological group isomorphism restricts to a subgroup and its image.
Transport of structural pairs preserves their open subgroups and good kernels.
The transported presentation uses the same elementary coordinates.
Transport of pairs induces the corresponding isomorphism on their quotients.
Pushing a realized stage through a group isomorphism just changes its quotient presentation, leaving its elementary Schwartz space unchanged.
In an affine family of characters every dual derivative is a Fourier integral of another test on the same source stage. The new test is independent of the base character.
An embedded Fréchet stage gives its range the same additive uniformity.
Use the whole compactly generated group as the open subgroup of the structural pair.
A compatible family of rectangular kernel inverses defines a continuous inverse on the directed union of product stages.
Translation invariance makes the average of evaluations the indicator of the double annihilator.
Normalized Haar integration is independent of the chosen Borel measurable-space instance.
In a finite-dimensional parameter, differentiate a family of integrals whose directional derivatives again belong to the family, with local integrable majorants.
Integrate along a unit time interval, then use translation invariance on the σ-compact support.
Pullback embeds the annihilator of the image as a closed subgroup of the original annihilator.
The compact annihilator of the open dual subgroup recovers the original good subgroup.
Using the embedded ranges puts the Fréchet stages in the universe of the limit.
Appending a direction differentiates the original function before evaluating the preceding mixed partial.
Exhaust the group and its dual simultaneously. Taking annihilators reverses the latter chain, and shifting the former puts even the first compact kernel in every open subgroup.
A strict inductive presentation by a countable cofinal family of stages, with exhaustive union and the prescribed seminorm topology.
Cofinality gives precisely the generating topology and the exhaustive union.
Compatible lifts along an exhaustive directed union produce a continuous inverse. The continuity criterion and the determining family for the inverse are supplied separately.
Analytic properties of the countable strict elementary presentation.
A strict cofinal presentation by elementary Schwartz stages gives completeness and nuclearity on both sides of strong duality.
Apply the Weil formula to a compact average at trivial characters and translation invariance elsewhere.
Pair the twisted function with probability Haar on the annihilator to compute the transform of a cutoff.
The integrated orbit derivative of a function times a conjugate character vanishes.

The inverse Fourier integral and the forward transform are adjoint on integrable test functions. Compactly supported approximations provide a product-measurable kernel even when the product topology and product σ-algebra have different Borel sets.
Invert an integrable Plancherel transform by pairing against indicators of finite-measure sets.
Use the universal mapping property of the completed tensor to apply a gluing criterion for a kernel. The stage inclusions may come from any two test spaces.
The two projective tensor completions obtained by a change of first factor are canonically equivalent.
Apply the LF open mapping theorem to a map represented by a continuous linear surjection.
Transport the elementary kernel equivalence through a rectangular quotient and extension by zero.
Compute the structural stage projection using any normalized Haar measure on its kernel.
Pull back a Schwartz function on the structural quotient and extend it by zero.
Compose the inverse elementary identification with the canonical stage inclusion.
The closed subgroup contains the support of the lift over the closed support downstairs.
A Schwartz–Bruhat stage is integrable after pullback along the quotient by its compact kernel and extension by zero from its open subgroup.
Differentiation on a structural stage agrees with differentiation on its elementary quotient, including the zero extension off the open subgroup.
Every stage realization extends to a bounded continuous function on the group.
Compactly supported Schwartz functions act continuously by multiplication on all stages.
A common structural stage realizes the product with a fixed compactly supported test.
Lift an elementary test supported in a small quotient neighborhood and extend it by zero.
Iterating the binary kernel isomorphism gives products determining every continuous functional.
Pushing a function through a group isomorphism is continuous for the Schwartz–Bruhat topology because it carries each stage into a stage.
Once Fourier transforms of Schwartz–Bruhat functions are known to be Schwartz–Bruhat, they are integrable, so Plancherel inversion holds pointwise.
The Fourier integral is linear on the space of Schwartz tests.
Both Schwartz functions and their transforms are integrable, so Plancherel inversion holds pointwise.
A cofinal sequence of structural stages presents the Schwartz–Bruhat space as LF.
A linear map of functions that has continuous Schwartz lifts on every source stage has a continuous lift to the full Schwartz–Bruhat spaces.
A Schwartz function is supported on a σ-compact open subgroup.
Powers of a symmetric compact generating set cover the group.
The Haar measure restricted to a σ-compact support is σ-finite.
Differentiating a slice in a fixed list of directions differentiates the same ambient test for every translate.
Bruhat smoothness descends to ordinary smoothness on every fiber of the full elementary stage.
Normalized averaging fixes a supported, kernel-invariant function.
Recover an open subgroup of the dual by separating in its quotient and writing every separating bidual character as evaluation.
Compact exhaustion followed by taking successive upper bounds gives a cofinal sequence of compactly generated open subgroups.
Compact support descends from a realization to its elementary test.
A Fourier multiplier identity on generators extends to the algebra they generate.

Pull the elementary seminorms back along the quotient and split their multi-index into its radial and norm-one orders.

Lebesgue measure on the real factor, normalized volume on the torus, and counting measure on the discrete factors.

The fundamental theorem of calculus, averaged over a unit interval.

Zero extension intertwines every compact-direction derivative and every radial derivative in the product coordinates.
