Matching quotient coordinates transfer a fixed stage by zero extension. The two averaging retractions give its induced topology.
Identify functions fixed by the compact subgroup with functions on the elementary quotient, using the averaging retractions for the two full stages.
Differentiating a Fourier transform is the Fourier transform of multiplication by `-(2 * Real.pi * I) * x`.
The Fourier transform of the `j`-fold monomial multiplication is the `j`-fold differentiation of the Fourier transform, up to the constant `(-(2 * Real.pi * I))⁻¹`.
One step of the commutation, in the useful direction.
Changing generators of the complex span of linear transforms preserves their generating Lᵖ seminorms.
An inducing linear map pulls a generating family back when the transforms extend by zero across a measure-preserving embedding onto the range.
Comparison with an integrable majorant and a finite sum of norms in the linear span.
Polynomial weights and powers span the same family. Taking the absolute value of a polynomial preserves its Lᵖ norm after multiplication.
The degree-zero weight recovers the constant term in each shifted power.
Pointwise suprema are the L∞ norms for counting measure on the full power-set σ-algebra, so they obey the same finite-span comparison.
For a compact subgroup, goodness is equivalent to the quotient being locally Euclidean.
The derivative of a symbol along a one-parameter subgroup is another symbol.
Change the seminorms on each admissible stage using the same cofinal bound.
An idele direction is determined by its archimedean velocity. Its finite component is constant along the connected parameter line.
The reciprocal product weight is integrable by separation of the real and lattice coordinates.
Rewrites `(1 + |k|)⁻²` in extended nonnegative reals as a real number.
Iterating the first-order operator along a one-parameter subgroup differentiates its translated orbit in the real parameter.
The radial direction and the norm-one directions inject as a direct sum into the full space of directions.
The monomial weighting is additive in the sequence.
Unfolds the monomial-weighted sequence at a lattice point.
A coordinate monomial is bounded by the matching power of `1 + ‖a‖`.
The monomial weighting commutes with scalars.
Each weighted sup norm is at most the weighted absolute sum whose order is the total degree of the monomial.
The weighted sup norms of a rapidly decreasing sequence are finite.
For counting measure, bound the monomial Lᵖ norm by its absolute sum and then by the rapid-decay bound of the same total degree.
The series `∑ₖ (1 + |k|)⁻²` over the integers is finite.
The product weight `∏ (1 + |aᵢ|)⁻²` sums over the lattice to the `n`-th power of the one-dimensional sum.
The product weight `∏ (1 + |aᵢ|)⁻²` has finite sum over the lattice.
`∂_{1}` on one real variable is the ordinary derivative.
The Fourier transform is an isometry for the `L²` norm on Schwartz functions (in `lpNorm` form).
Pointwise domination translates into a bound of `lpNorm` by the `√2`-multiple of a combination of two `lpNorm`s.
Scalar multiplication scales the `L²` norm of a Schwartz function.
A linear combination of transforms has Lᵖ norm bounded by the corresponding finite maximum of seminorms times the sum of the coefficient norms.
The ideal classes of ideles that are units outside S are precisely the classes that become trivial over the S-integers.
The product rule for one coordinate of a monomial-weighted mixed partial.
Multiply a linear family of functions by a weight, linearly in each argument.
The shifted and unshifted powers span the same transforms. At order zero the shifted weight is two, so one can subtract half of it to recover any pure power.
Rewrites a product of powers of coordinate absolute values times a norm as the norm of the monomial times the value.
Duality identifies a direction on the quotient with a real homomorphism on the open annihilator, which extends to the whole dual group.
A based lift of a real one-parameter subgroup is multiplicative by uniqueness of lifts on the real plane.
One plus the Euclidean length of a lattice point is at most the product of one plus the absolute values of its coordinates.
The comparison `1 + ‖a‖ ≤ ∏ (1 + |aᵢ|)` in extended nonnegative reals.
Binomial expansion of `(1 + n) ^ M`.
Splits off a factor `(1 + n)⁻²` from a power of `1 + n`.
For nonnegative reals, `1 + ∑ fᵢ ≤ ∏ (1 + fᵢ)`.
A fixed stage inherits the global Lᵖ topology by zero extension and uniqueness of Haar measure on the compact norm-one subgroup.
A real-valued homomorphism extends algebraically by divisibility. Continuity on the open subgroup gives continuity at the identity of the whole group.
The exponential coordinate used by the norm section as a one-parameter subgroup.
Expands `∏ (1 + |aᵢ|) ^ M * ‖z‖` as a sum over the monomials of degree at most `M` in each coordinate.
Bounds `∏ (1 + |aᵢ|) ^ M * ‖z‖` by `2 ^ (M * r)` times the largest monomial in the box of degrees at most `M`.
Splits off the factor `∏ (1 + |aᵢ|)⁻²` from a product of powers.
Pointwise bound of a term of the `j`-th weighted absolute sum by the product weight times finitely many weighted sup norms.
The `j`-th weighted absolute sum is bounded by a constant times the largest of finitely many weighted sup norms.
Sequences in the rapidly decreasing space add pointwise.
Each weighted absolute-sum seminorm is dominated by a multiple of the supremum of finitely many weighted sup seminorms.
Scalars act pointwise on rapidly decreasing sequences.
Differentiating the Fourier transform corresponds to taking the Fourier transform after multiplication by a power of the coordinate.
The weighted derivative's L² norm is controlled by the corresponding Fourier seminorm via Plancherel.
Bounds on Fourier L² seminorms give uniform bounds on the weighted L¹ norms of the original derivatives by Cauchy–Schwarz.
A Schwartz function on the line is pointwise bounded by the L² norms of itself and its derivative.
The real Schwartz seminorm `(k, n)` is bounded by the three Fourier `L²` seminorms with indices `(k, n), (k - 1, n), (k, n + 1)`.
Iterating the multiplication-by-`x` operator gives multiplication by `x ^ j`.
The splitting product maps properly onto the elementary quotient. Its logarithmic coordinate recovers the first projection, whose fibers are compact.
Pull the logarithmically weighted Lᵖ family on the elementary quotient back to the fixed subspace in the norm splitting.
On a compact-by-real elementary group, the weighted operator span is generated by powers of the real coordinate times monomials in any spanning set of directions.
On a split extension of the line by a compact kernel, each first-order symbol is a scalar multiple of the real coordinate. Its powers generate all polynomial symbols.
The multi-index with a derivative in each coordinate of `s` and order zero elsewhere.
Inserting a new coordinate increments precisely that component of the multi-index.
The series `∑ₖ (|k| + 1)⁻²` over the integers converges.
Evaluating a torus partial on a real lift agrees with evaluating it on the quotient.
Varying a single circle coordinate in the real cover adds one derivative in that coordinate to the mixed partial.
Averaging the one-coordinate estimate over each coordinate bounds the value of a torus partial by the L¹ norms of its square-free further partials.
The fundamental theorem of calculus bounds the norm at one point of a circle slice by the integrals of the slice and its first derivative.
On the pure torus stage, the canonical Schwartz seminorm is the supremum of the corresponding mixed partial on the quotient.
The closed unit cube with lower corner `x`, in Euclidean coordinates.
Integrating the norm of a Schwartz function over a unit cube is bounded by its global Lᵖ norm, by Hölder on a set of measure one.
Translation gives the derivative at every time from the derivative at zero. Zero velocity therefore makes the whole curve constant.
The product rule preserves the linear span of symbol-weighted differential operators.
A section of a surjective module identifies the product of the norm-one subgroup and the positive reals with the group.
The pushforward of a Haar measure on the kernel times `dt/t` along the product decomposition of a section is a Haar measure.
A Haar measure normalized on a half-open logarithmic band has the required growth on symmetric modulation intervals.
For a module with image generated by `a > 1`, the Haar measure giving the norm-one subgroup mass `log a` has mass `2 log Λ + O(1)` on the inverse image of the closed interval from `Λ⁻¹` to `Λ`.
For a surjective module, the Haar measure whose image under the module is `dt/t` has mass exactly `2 log Λ` on the inverse image of the closed interval from `Λ⁻¹` to `Λ`.

A surjective proper modulation admits a continuous homomorphic right inverse. Extend the real frequency on characters pulled back along the modulation to all characters of the group, then use character separation to lift the resulting one-parameter subgroup.
Two Haar measures with mass `2 log Λ + O(1)` on the inverse images of the closed intervals from `Λ⁻¹` to `Λ` are equal: they differ by a scalar, and the logarithm is unbounded.
For cyclic module image, rescaling Haar measure so that the kernel has mass equal to the logarithm of the positive generator gives the canonical logarithmic growth.
The pushforward of probability Haar measure on the kernel times `dt/t` gives mass exactly `2 log Λ` to the inverse image of the closed interval from `Λ⁻¹` to `Λ`.
The measure `dt/t` is a Haar measure on the positive reals: it is the image of Lebesgue measure under the exponential isomorphism.
The symmetric interval from `Λ⁻¹` to `Λ` has mass exactly `2 log Λ` for `dt/t`.
An injective equivariant map pulls back each target isotype to the source isotype.
To intertwine an operator on a completed inductive tensor product with a continuous linear map, it suffices to check their actions on pure tensors.
A topological group isomorphism restricts to a subgroup and its image.
Schwartz–Bruhat functions are continuous because every elementary stage realization is continuous.
Point evaluation on the Schwartz–Bruhat space is continuous because its absolute value pulls back to a continuous seminorm on every elementary stage.

Equivariant injections with dense range remain dense on the isotypes when the compact-group averages exist. For infinite Haar measure, weak integrability of the twisted target orbits forces the target isotype to vanish.
Operators that intertwine the projectors descend uniquely to their kernel quotients. The descended maps agree on the image of the map relating the two operators.
The normalized Pettis average on the Schwartz–Bruhat space satisfies the scalar integral formula at each point.
On a compact kernel the character-twisted orbits admit a continuous Schwartz–Bruhat Pettis average.
The normalized twisted coset integral is a quotient map onto the Schwartz–Bruhat profiles, and evaluates the isotypic projector along the section.
Pullback by a topological group isomorphism is continuous on Schwartz–Bruhat spaces. Each structural quotient uses the same elementary coordinates after pullback.
Transport a structural pair and its presentation by a topological group isomorphism, preserving the elementary Schwartz functions in the stage.
Isotypic averages commute with a continuous equivariant linear map.
Profiles that parametrize the projection of a dense subspace give a dense embedding into the complete kernel quotient.
A continuous linear functional evaluates a Pettis integral over the whole space as a scalar integral.
Point evaluation as a continuous linear functional on Schwartz–Bruhat functions.
An equivariant continuous linear map from the Schwartz–Bruhat space intertwines the normalized Pettis averages.
A topological group isomorphism transports Schwartz–Bruhat functions by precomposition with its inverse.
The tensor isomorphism gives pullback of profiles and restriction to the section.
The source projector has the normalized Pettis formula and takes values in the isotype.
The weighted profile functions are precisely the isotypic Schwartz–Bruhat functions.
If a tensor isomorphism multiplies evaluations in product coordinates, it intertwines left translation on the completion.
Pushing a function through a group isomorphism is continuous for the Schwartz–Bruhat topology because it carries each stage into a stage.
Transport of structural pairs preserves their open subgroups and good kernels.
The transported presentation uses the same elementary coordinates.
Transport of pairs induces the corresponding isomorphism on their quotients.
Pushing a realized stage through a group isomorphism just changes its quotient presentation, leaving its elementary Schwartz space unchanged.
Moving the inverse contour between two lines preserves its value at every positive argument.
Restriction to a vertical line as a real Schwartz function.
The weighted Lᵖ norm of the trace on a single line.
Weighted values inside the strip are bounded by the two boundary trace norms.
Both neighboring trace norms control each Schwartz seminorm on the intermediate line.
Pulling back a structural pair across a compact quotient preserves its elementary quotient.
The modulation is trivial on each compact subgroup.
Pullback from a compact quotient is continuous because it lifts each structural stage with the same elementary coordinates.
Evaluation on Schwartz–Bruhat functions is continuous by the stage seminorms.
Differentiate the profile before applying the exponential twist.
On a compact set of profiles, interpolating its observed jets gives finite-rank operators of cubic rank whose errors, multiplied by the sixth power of the stage, still range over a bounded set.
Integrating on the ray away from zero bounds a weighted derivative by the weighted L² norm of the next derivative, with one unit of spare exponential decay.
Changing exponential weight preserves the vanishing of a jet.
Transposing finite interpolation on a test set approximates the local Banach comparison of the strong dual in operator norm.
Evaluation on an elementary stage is bounded by the zeroth Schwartz seminorm.
The elementary Schwartz space with one real factor and trivial remaining factors is the usual Schwartz space on that real factor.
Multiplying an elementary Schwartz function by `φ ∘ Λ` keeps it Schwartz, when `Λ` is affine on each fibre of the cover and `φ` has bounded derivatives of all orders.
Each jet observation is a continuous linear functional of the profile.
Two countable sequences of exponents bracket every exponent of the interval and suffice to generate the topology.
A finite sum of Schwartz seminorms controlling the derivatives of an exponential twist on the half-line where that exponential is at most one.
On each half-line the corresponding endpoint controls the Schwartz seminorm of every intermediate twist.
A finite-rank map into a space of dimension d costs at most d times its operator norm in the injective-tensor bound for its evaluation form.
The Fourier argument corresponding to a unit of imaginary Mellin height.
Differentiating a holomorphic function along a vertical trace introduces a factor of i.
The real exponential weight is precisely the power weight in positive-real coordinates.
Norm-convergent finite-rank approximations with summable rank-weighted increments give an integral evaluation form.
Cubic rank growth and sixth-order error decay suffice for summability of the rank-weighted increments.
The inverse image of a good subgroup of a compact quotient is good.
The image in the product is closed because the compatibility equations between weighted profiles are closed pointwise conditions.
A good subgroup is compact, being closed in its double annihilator.
A closed linear embedding into a countable product of complete metrizable additive uniform spaces gives a Fréchet space.
A topologically embedded linear subspace inherits nuclearity through the continuous linear equivalence with its range.
Real derivatives of the restriction to the real line of a function holomorphic near it.
An iterated derivative may be evaluated after transporting its order along an equality.
Differentiating along a list ending in `v` is differentiating `∂ᵥP` along the rest.
Pullback by a real coordinate carries the Schwartz condition for each logarithmic twist to the corresponding modulation twist, in both directions.
A smooth multiplier of `log m` with bounded derivatives acts continuously on Schwartz–Bruhat functions, by applying it on each elementary stage.
The power weight in a positive-real coordinate agrees with the exponential weight in its logarithmic coordinate.
Reflection, Fourier transform, and rescaling turn an exponential twist into its vertical Mellin trace.
The polynomially weighted exponential envelope belongs to L² on both half-lines.
A countable bracketing family of exponents embeds a decay stage as the closed space of compatible Schwartz–Bruhat twists.
The quotient underlying a decay stage is second countable. Properness gives σ-compactness, and compact generation of the dual gives Euclidean charts.
The Schwartz–Bruhat space of an elementary compact quotient is metrizable via the Schwartz space of its largest structural pair.
A decay stage is separable once the quotient is second countable, its Schwartz–Bruhat space is metrizable, and the stage embeds in a countable power of it.
The topology of a decay stage is induced by the joint map to the product of its Schwartz–Bruhat twists.
Translating the exponent set by the negative of a weight exponent makes multiplication by that weight a continuous linear equivalence.
The singleton twist is a linear bijection, with inverse weighting at the opposite exponent.
A weight by `c` acts continuously between decay spaces whenever each target exponent plus `c` belongs to the source. The map uses the same compact quotient at each stage.
An intermediate twist is the sum of the endpoint twists times a function of `log m`.
Derivatives of a function of an affine real functional.
Pullback by the logarithmic coordinate identifies the decay submodules and intertwines their twists.
Exponential decay in a positive-real coordinate is the projective condition on the real logarithmic profile.
Intertwining the coordinate maps of two projective topologies lifts a linear equivalence to a continuous linear equivalence.
A real coordinate gives a maximal structural pair with a one-dimensional elementary presentation.
A structural stage descends continuously to the quotient by its compact subgroup, where normalized Haar averaging recovers the descended function.
Pullback by the quotient map of a compact subgroup preserves Schwartz–Bruhat membership.
A largest Bruhat structural pair realizes every Schwartz–Bruhat function.
A Schwartz function on the line is pointwise bounded by the L² norms of itself and its derivative.

A first-countable Schwartz space is separable. For each continuous seminorm a totally bounded zero-neighborhood spans the space, so the space is separable for that seminorm, and countably many seminorm balls form a basis at zero.
A bijective inclusion from the sole stage of a locally convex limit is a continuous linear equivalence for the final topology.
Multiplying a stage realization by a function of `log m` with bounded derivatives is again the realization of a stage function on the same structural pair.
The Mellin transform of a logarithmic profile, extended by zero outside the strip.
A sublist of a concatenation of constant blocks is again such a concatenation.
The two-sided exponential weight has bounded derivatives for positive exponents.
The weight `(e^{-αt} + e^{βt})⁻¹` is smooth with bounded derivatives of all orders, by Cauchy estimates on a horizontal strip.
Multiply a Schwartz function by the vertical polynomial weight and include it in Lᵖ.
Leibniz's formula bounds the weighted derivative wherever the exponential is at most one.
If every coordinate is recovered continuously from two test coordinates, those test coordinates detect boundedness of the whole family.
Applying a continuous linear map to two bounded families gives a bounded family.
One bounded Schwartz–Bruhat coordinate supplies a common compact subgroup of invariance. Normalized averaging then bounds the other coordinates on that quotient.
A surjective inducing continuous linear map out of a separated space can be bundled as a continuous linear equivalence with the same evaluations.
Closed subspaces containing the split products on a single quotient contain that whole stage.
On a compact kernel with non-compactly-generated dual, evaluation differences detect nontrivial points while vanishing eventually on every bounded Schwartz family.
A compactly supported scalar Schwartz function is the sum of the two given twists of a single compactly supported smooth decay profile.
Separate continuity can be tested on the defining coordinates of the target. When the target is complete, the resulting tensor map extends to the completion.
Flipping the two factors preserves the separately continuous seminorms that generate the inductive tensor topology. The two flips remain inverse on completion.
A closed subspace containing all split products contains every quotient stage.
A map from a bornological space into a decay space is continuous if all its weighted profiles are continuous.
A weighted coordinate is continuous on the final decay topology, since on each stage it is the quotient twist followed by Schwartz–Bruhat pullback.
A seminorm bounded on bounded sets of a first-countable space is continuous. Apply the bounded linear map criterion to the identity into its seminormed copy.
Bounded stage inclusions carry bounded families back to the full decay space.
An intermediate twist factors continuously through the sum of the endpoint twists.
Reconstruct a function from the sum of its endpoint profiles. Each intermediate twist of the reconstruction is a bounded smooth function of the log modulation times the unweighted input.
For the induced topology, boundedness is precisely coordinatewise boundedness.
Lift the ordinary products of all scalar twists to one bilinear map into the decay space.
Translates of a bump with disjoint supports give an infinite independent family of scalar decay profiles. Montel compactness therefore rules out a bounded neighborhood.
The kernel leaves the weight constant on each orbit, so it factors out of the normalized projector integral.
The kernel of the quotient modulation is the quotient of the original kernel.
The cofinal quotient stages have increasing ranges in the decay space.
On split coordinates, the sum of two twists of a pure function is the ordinary product with the sum of the two weighted scalar profiles.
A function is invariant under the compact subgroup exactly when every kernel slice is fixed by the projection obtained by averaging and pulling back.
Every weight is strictly positive, so a single weighted profile determines the function.
The kernel preserves the modulation, so twisting commutes with translation by a kernel element and detects the same character subspace.
Translating a weighted profile introduces just the constant weight at the translating element.
On a quotient stage, approximate finitely many twists simultaneously using compactly supported scalar factors and the sum of the two extreme weights.
To test density in an induced product topology, finitely many coordinates can be reconstructed from a single dense image.
A closed subspace containing the images of pure tensors from a dense subset of the right factor contains the full image of a completed tensor equivalence.
The closure of a linear image is the whole space if the image contains the pure products and these generate every quotient stage densely.
Split products have dense span in the full decay topology.
On a disk about zero the first derivative of an exponential integral is dominated by its two real weights a little outside the disk.
The compact components of a cofinal sequence of Bruhat structural pairs are cofinal among compact subgroups with compactly generated annihilator.
Translation in logarithmic coordinates acts on each weighted Schwartz profile by Schwartz translation followed by multiplication by a constant.
Identifying embedded stages with their ranges preserves the final seminorm tests.
Complete the separately continuous product after testing its slices by all twists.
An embedded Fréchet stage is linearly homeomorphic to its image and gives that image the same complete metrizable locally convex structure.
Every compact-subgroup stage admits a refinement on whose quotient a given unitary character descends.
A bounded inverse on a comparison space gives a continuous inverse on a bornological function space when the comparison embeds by weighted coordinates.
Equality of two point evaluations after a tensor map can be checked on pure tensors.
A linear surjection with a continuous linear section is open by translating the section.
An injective continuous homomorphism pulls back a neighborhood containing no nontrivial cyclic subgroup, which supplies Euclidean local coordinates on a locally compact group.
The split kernel coordinate and the modulation together detect small cyclic subgroups.
The topology of a decay stage is induced by the joint map to the product of its Schwartz–Bruhat twists.
The joint twist map has closed range because its coordinates obey pointwise compatibility equations with any one fixed twist.
The pointwise multiplier on the decay submodule is well-defined because it commutes with each real twist and preserves Schwartz–Bruhat functions.
Multiplication in split coordinates extends to a continuous linear map from the completed inductive tensor product to the decay space.
Pulling back the decay-space topology by multiplication gives the topology of the completed inductive tensor product.
Multiplication from the completed tensor product reaches every decay function. The quotient-stage isomorphisms give preimages for functions in the individual compact-subgroup stages.
Unitary character multiplication commutes with the real twists and is continuous on the inductive limit by refining each source stage to a quotient carrying the character.
The quasi-character multiplier is the composition of its unitary multiplier and the real shift given by its abscissa.
Equivariance on the image of the algebraic tensor product, where it follows from the split-coordinate formula on pure tensors and linearity.
The polar of a closed dual seminorm ball is bounded, and bidual surjectivity identifies its bipolar with the ball. Thus these balls are strong neighborhoods.
Nuclearity passes from embedded nuclear Fréchet stages to their locally convex limit.
If a nuclear factor embeds into a product, its coordinate tensor maps into the completed injective tensors embed the full projective completion.
A Schwartz test function on the quotient kernel pulls back to the original kernel.
All scalar twists together embed the scalar decay profiles in a product of ordinary Schwartz spaces on the multiplicative positive reals.
Normalized averaging over a compact subgroup descends every invariant function.
An elementary group has a largest Bruhat stage, whose realization is a homeomorphism.
A split evaluation determines the original function.
The ordinary Schwartz representative of a weighted pure product is determined by its values in split coordinates.
Identify multiplication as an inducing map by embedding its projective comparison in the product of its ordinary weighted kernel coordinates.
Quotient pure products pull back into any subspace containing the global split products.
Each split pure product defines a decay function on the entire interval.
The Schwartz kernel theorem transported to the coordinates of a splitting.
A decreasing cofinal sequence of indices for a family of embedded stages has the same union and final locally convex topology, and its maps into the union are embeddings.
Pulling back a pure product in split coordinates puts its stage realization in any subspace containing all global pure products.
Boundedness of a seminorm gives continuity on each metrizable stage and hence on their locally convex final topology.
Restriction embeds the strong dual of a strict LF-space as the closed space of compatible functionals on its defining Fréchet subspaces.
The closed compatible families form a complete subspace of the product of stage duals.
Restriction to the stages realizes the strong dual inside a product of nuclear duals.
Embedded Fréchet stages give a strict LF presentation by their ranges.
An inducing linear map with dense range from a complete space onto a Hausdorff target is surjective.
The ranges of the cofinal Bruhat stages exhibit the Schwartz space as a strict LF-space.
Joint continuity on pure tensors would bound a functional that was chosen to be unbounded on a member of the neighborhood basis of the first factor.
A family of functionals that vanishes eventually on every bounded set of the second factor gives a continuous inductive tensor seminorm by taking the supremum of the norms of the paired functionals.
An embedded stage and a split tensor inclusion are equivalent if the image of the stage is the fixed space of the tensor projection in ambient coordinates.
Continuous linear maps out of the completed inductive tensor are determined on pure tensors.
Tensor a retraction with the identity. Its projection on the completion commutes with every contraction against a functional of the second factor.
A bounded bijection in both directions from a bornological space identifies its topology with the one generated by bounded seminorms on the target.
Continuous linear maps induce a uniformly continuous map on the inductive tensor product.
The test exponents `1/(k+2)` tend to the lower endpoint 0, and `1 - 1/(k+2)` to the upper endpoint 1, in the extended reals, without reaching them.
Translates of a fixed Schwartz function by `n`, damped by `exp (-c n)` with `c > 0`, form a bounded set: the polynomial growth of the seminorms in `n` loses to the damping.
The bump profiles `exp (-n) ψ (x - n)`, twisted by an exponent `a < 1`, are damped translates of their `n = 0` member, so they form a bounded set of Schwartz functions.
The same profiles twisted by the endpoint exponent 1 take the value 1 at `x = n`, so the family itself is unbounded in the logarithmic model.
A family of Schwartz functions with `G n n = 1` is unbounded: the seminorm `sup |x| |G x|` of `G n` is at least `n`.
In the identity-modulation model on the positive reals, an interior twist of the family is the Schwartz–Bruhat function with the corresponding logarithmic profile.
A differential operator involves finitely many words, even when the space of one-parameter subgroups has no finite basis.
Inside the strip the absolute integral is dominated by the sum of the two endpoint integrals, splitting according to whether the modulation is below or above one.
Each twisted image of a differentiated bounded family is still Schwartz–Bruhat bounded.
Every smooth compactly supported function is the realization of an elementary Schwartz stage.

decls.deviation: If the modulation along the subgroup is exp(rt), the derivative of the weight at exponent a has coefficient a * r.
decls.summary: First-order differentiation preserves each exponential decay condition by the product rule for the modulation weight.
On any structural quotient to which a smooth function descends, its descent is smooth at every order, even when the original finite-order witnesses use different kernels.
Support of a test function supplies the compact set for its Schwartz stage.
A transition between elementary stages restricts to any enlargement of the compact support.
In each discrete fibre, the lift of a continuous real-valued additive character is an affine, smooth function of the real and torus cover coordinates.
Smoothness on the cover descends through an open surjective elementary homomorphism.
The test topology makes the identity map to the Schwartz–Bruhat space continuous.
Each fixed-support stage descends to a single compact-subgroup decay stage. Its twists are continuous Schwartz multipliers on the quotient.
It suffices to hit pure tensors whose second factor belongs to a dense set.
Rescaling one smooth cutoff approximates a log profile in every Schwartz twist.
On a neighborhood of the origin the elementary cover is injective.
Openness of the homomorphism makes its linear lift between universal covers surjective.
Compact support bounds every polynomially weighted partial on an elementary group. The lift in the torus coordinates need not be compactly supported.
On a prescribed compact set, a weight acts by a continuous Schwartz multiplier.
Truncate an exponential outside a compact set without changing its values there.
Passing to the ranges of a cofinal sequence of embedded stages preserves the final locally convex topology.
The fixed-support smooth topology is induced from the Schwartz topology.
A closed linear embedding in a Fréchet space gives completeness and metrizability for the induced uniform structure.
Properness of the modulation pulls compact support in the log coordinate back to the group.
Integration by parts against a quasi-character follows by integrating the derivative of the product, whose Fourier transform vanishes at the trivial character.
Untwisting by a real power of the modulation preserves every finite order of Bruhat differentiability. The same good subgroup fixes both functions.
Each twist is continuous on every compact-quotient stage, hence on the final decay space.
A continuous real-valued additive character vanishes on a subgroup with open annihilator.
A decay function with a compactly supported profile in split coordinates is a test.
Twisting a first derivative gives the derivative of the twist minus a scalar multiple of the twist itself. The scalar is independent of the function.
The unitary character obtained by dividing a quasi-character by its norm.
On each Fréchet stage, Fatou's lemma gives lower semicontinuity of the L¹ seminorm. Barrelledness then makes it continuous, so it is bounded on bounded Schwartz–Bruhat sets.
A bump around one with outer radius at most one isolates the integer one.
For a radial character of phase `t`, the printed shift cancels the character at every Fourier coefficient.
At the identity the two sides of the printed formula give incompatible dependence on the phase, at every type level.
On a subsingleton topological group, the Dirac measure at the identity is a Haar measure.
Continuity of the `ULift`ed Sierpiński indicator of a set is openness of the set.
If every set containing `x` is closed, the open subsets of the connected component of `x` are those that miss `x`, and the whole component.
If every set containing `x` is closed, the closure of the complement of the component of `x` is Hausdorff.
If every set containing `x` is closed, two distinct points of the closure of the complement of the component of `x` have disjoint open neighbourhoods in `X`.
Some compact Hausdorff space has a subset that is not closed.
The affine transition has derivative bounds with precisely one or two powers of its scale. The constants are global for all the affine translates.
Split at the same character's value at two. The difference in the parameter and the difference in the character are separately absolutely integrable.
The local character transfers to a measurable unitary multiplier in the archimedean coordinate. The chart preserves integrability and evaluates the local functional.
With the radial cutoff fixed, Fubini combines the local integral and the mollification into a single weighted Mellin integral.
In additive coordinates the real part of the local integral is the real phase times a nonnegative radial density. Divergence transfers from the trivial character.

A unitary multiplier equals one at the singularity. Its real part is at least one half nearby. Away from that neighborhood the absolute density is bounded by an integrable multiple of the inverse square of the normalized local norm.
Transfer the weighted difference back to the two separately integrated local terms at each fixed cutoff. The limiting local integral is absolutely integrable.
A locally integrable majorant for an entire family bounds its derivatives by the Cauchy estimate on a smaller disk. Difference quotients give derivative measurability.
On the real chart the vanishing factor cancels the denominator. On the complex chart it leaves an integrable inverse-distance singularity at one.
The same matched family gives convergence of the finite sum over all infinite places.
On a matched translate x, factor a power of x to shift both parameters one unit right. The endpoint cancellation bound then holds even for negative real parts.
A nonnegative, mass-one mollifier preserves the cancellation estimate under its integral, uniformly for parameters in a bounded part of the half-plane.
Local domination yields both integrability of the limiting difference and joint convergence as the parameter varies and the cutoffs are removed.
A coordinate formula that also transfers integrability gives the result for the actual two local archimedean terms, separately integrated at each cutoff.
For the corrected squared complex denominator, one power of the distance to one cancels on the inner annulus. Outside radius two the radial density decays as `‖u‖ ^ (-2*a-3)`.
Each fixed cutoff is supported away from norm one, so its individual complex place density is continuous and compactly supported.
The inverse distance to one is locally integrable in the complex plane.
The radial tail in the complex plane is integrable for exponents below minus two.
The local coordinate formula, with its trivial-character specialization.
The local multiplicative measure in either infinite-place coordinate has density the reciprocal normalized norm against its additive Tamagawa measure.
The real and complex coordinate bounds apply to each actual matched family, with an integrable limiting density on the original group of local units.
A single matched family realizes the full finite archimedean sum.
A common integrable bound for the matched smoothed kernels also bounds their pointwise limits. Dominated convergence applies while the complex parameter varies.
All real places give the same trivial-character integral as the rational real place.
Away from the lower transition the dilated cutoff agrees locally with the upper transition. The two transitions are disjoint for `R ≥ 4`.
The dilated cutoff is supported between the lower mesh and twice the radius.
The positive part of the digamma integrand dominates a reciprocal near zero. Its negative part has a uniform integrable bound.
On the closed right half-plane, averaging a cutoff power against a probability mollifier preserves its unit bound.
Near the identity all powers sampled by a sufficiently small mollifier have nonnegative real part after the archimedean phase is applied. The cutoff and the mollifier can shrink independently.
For these cutoffs the lower transition occupies one mesh interval and the upper transition has width comparable to its radius.
A mollifier supported between `-ε` and `-ε/2` leaves a contribution of order `ε log (1/d)` when the cutoff already equals one on `[1+d,2]`.
At real parameters two and four the power difference is a nonnegative real function.
One matched cutoff family supplies the reference differences and a uniform reciprocal-height bound for individual Mellin moments.
The explicit spectral family has matched supports at the lower cutoff. This same family can therefore be used in the archimedean limit.
The normalized signed explicit formula specializes to every one-sided full-window cutoff.
Exchange Mellin integration with the mollifier for a single cutoff power.
Write a difference of smoothed Mellin moments as the mollifier average of the moments of the translated, cut-off difference.
The Mellin integral of a cutoff is the integral of its translated powers against the mollifier.
A positive horizontal separation between the Mellin variable and the cutoff parameter bounds all Mellin moments uniformly in both imaginary parts.
The derivative of the inverse power on `[1,x]` is bounded by the norm of its exponent.
Distinct pairs of a finite place and an exponent give distinct positive prime powers.
At the real place of ℚ, a lower integral against the local multiplicative Tamagawa measure is the Lebesgue integral with density `|t|⁻¹` in the real coordinate.
On a full rational window the exterior sum vanishes by the critical strip, so the combined real-place and spectral term has a finite limit for every family.
A limit for the rational real-place difference fixes the full spectral limit on the trace overlap by the explicit formula.
With a nonnegative real radial profile the real part of each trivial-character prime-power contribution is nonnegative.
At parameter two the radial approximant is real and nonnegative.
A matched convolution inherits the vanishing factor of the shift-two difference, uniformly on right half-planes.
The vanishing factor cancels the positive-branch singularity. The remaining density is integrable at infinity when the lower real bound exceeds minus one half.
A continuous compact radial test supported strictly above one has integrable density on the rational real chart.
Each cutoff is supported a positive distance above one. A cofinal choice of mollifier indices makes its support radius smaller than this distance.
For matched supports, the smoothed rational archimedean differences converge locally uniformly. Domination is applied on both real sign branches at once.
The shift by two introduces the factor `1-x⁻²`. On a matched mollifier support this is bounded by a constant times `(t-1)/t`, even as `t` tends to one.
The fixed-cutoff profiles are continuous and compactly supported.

For the translated inner kernel of an actual matched additive convolution the second derivative costs one inverse mesh unit in the lower boundary layer, and decays like `t^(-m-2)` throughout the remaining support.

The translated profile multiplied by the chosen smooth cutoff has uniformly bounded weighted zeroth and second radial derivatives. The lower-layer cost `R` is integrated over an interval of length `1/R`.
The derivative costs one inverse mesh unit near the lower cutoff and decays with the translated power elsewhere.
The cutoff keeps a translated power away from its jump at one.
After integration, the lower cutoff layer and the tail give a bound independent of the mesh.
For a matched cutoff family the individual moments obey the reciprocal-height bound, while subtracting the value at two gives a holomorphic limit throughout each narrow chart.
Absolute convergence of the reciprocal-height majorant lets the smoothed Mellin sum pass to its limiting resolvent, locally uniformly in the Euler chart.
In a full window, bounded prime terms and convergent polar moments transfer divergence of the signed sum to the spectral sum.
Local digamma divergence at each infinite place passes to the signed one-character explicit formula.

The kernels `t ↦ h(t) ρ(t - v)` of the mollified cutoff are `C²`, vanish to first order at the ends of a fixed interval `[a, b] ⊂ (0, ∞)` containing the cutoff's support, and have value and second derivative bounded uniformly in `v`.

At a fixed cutoff the Mellin transforms of the approximants decay like `(1 + |Im s|)⁻²` on vertical strips, uniformly for `z` in a compact set. The approximant is the cutoff times the mollified power, a smooth function supported in a fixed compact subset of `(1, ∞)` whose radial derivatives are bounded locally uniformly in `z`. Two integrations by parts in the logarithmic coordinate give the bound.

At a fixed cutoff and a fixed Mellin variable `s`, the Mellin transform of the approximant is entire in the parameter `z`. The approximant is supported in a fixed compact subset of `(1, ∞)` and is entire in `z` at each radius (`introTraceApprox_differentiable`), with bounds locally uniform in `z`.
A Mellin transform of a function vanishing outside `(a, b)`, with `0 < a`, is the interval integral over `[a, b]`.
Two integrations by parts bound an interval Mellin integral of a `C²` function vanishing to first order at both ends by `C / (1 + |Im s|)²` on a vertical strip.
The radial power is bounded on `(-∞, L]` uniformly for `|Re z| ≤ r`.
On `[p, q] ⊂ (0, ∞)`, a real power is bounded by the sum of its values at the ends.

, for the proof that the zero sum is entire. Weighted zero count: for every unitary character `χ` and every half-width `a`, the zeros of the completed Hecke L-function in the open window `|Re s - 1/2| < a`, counted with their orders, satisfy `∑ ord(ρ) / (1 + |Im ρ|)² < ∞`. This is the classical consequence of the zero count `N(T + 1) - N(T) = O(log T)` for Hecke L-functions.
The completed divisors of imaginary twists agree after translation in the critical strip.
Imaginary norm twists translate the finite L-function. The gamma factor is regular and nonvanishing throughout the positive half-plane.
Dividing by the restriction to the norm section gives a normalized character and a purely imaginary translation of its exponent.
The gamma factor of a twist by `|·|^{iy}` is the shifted gamma factor.
The zero divisor of a twist by `|·|^{iy}` is the divisor shifted by `iy`.
Twisting a unitary character by `|·|^{iy}` shifts its norm twists by `iy`.
For the parameter-two approximants, the sum of infinite-place digamma integrals in the one-sided explicit formula has real part tending to minus infinity.

For one-sided profiles converging to the parameter-two power, the real part of the digamma integral tends to minus infinity. The positive part of the opposite integrand dominates a reciprocal near zero, and its negative part has a uniform exponential majorant.
Each positive-coordinate radial approximant at parameter two satisfies the one-sided digamma estimate.
A compact positive-coordinate profile vanishes near the gamma kernel’s singularity.
At parameter two, convolution against a probability mollifier preserves the unit bound.
The logarithmic test is supported on positive coordinates.

The negative orders of the completed function form a finite set in the left closed half-plane Re s ≤ 1.
A nonnegative part diverges if it eventually dominates a multiple of the reciprocal coordinate on a right neighborhood of zero.
Split the signed divisor sum into its full zero window and the finitely many poles.
Imaginary translation bijects the two zero windows, preserves the orders, and transfers the Mellin weight to the radial test.
The norm twist of a character cancels the inverse phase on its radial profile.

The full-window trace identity for an arbitrary character follows by normalizing on the norm section. The underlying adelic test and its local geometric terms are unchanged. In the normalized trivial isotype the two polar moments are translated.
Translation differentiates the cutoff-free complex power through order two on the interior of the support.
A difference of translated powers vanishes to first order at the lower endpoint. Its first two radial derivatives have uniform power decay for bounded parameters.
On the lower transition both powers agree at one before translation. For `t ≥ 2`, the triangle inequality and the ordinary inverse-power estimate suffice.

Pair the two translates 1+x and 1−x in the complex plane. Away from x=0 the parallelogram identity puts one outside the unit disk. The limiting lower bound is a positive multiple of the nonintegrable density ‖x‖⁻².
The complex Tamagawa measure has twice the Euclidean density, so the divergent real integral has coefficient 1/π.
Fatou’s lemma makes nonnegative cutoff integrals diverge when they eventually dominate a nonintegrable density pointwise on a measurable set.
A strictly increasing reindexing of both cutoff sequences preserves admissibility.
Restriction of an integrable local term to radii above one preserves integrability.
, and Theorem B.4.2.2, p. 616. For a radial test supported above norm one the complex local trace term equals the negative digamma integral.
At a complex place, angular integration leaves the absolute value of the character's integer frequency.
The normalized Haar integral commutes with conjugation and inversion of the radial profile.
The additive coordinate retains the value of the local character on every unit.
Inversion and conjugation preserve absolute integrability of a local term.
Inverting a local unit exchanges a profile with its conjugate at the reciprocal radius.
Inversion preserves the square-root weight divided by the normalized distance from one.
The two samples of the digamma kernel correspond to the two half-lines of the logarithmic profile.
Angular integration of an exterior Fourier mode, with Euclidean area measure.
Above one the step-two difference cancels the real-place denominator on both sign branches. Their densities are the sum and difference of two integrable powers.
In the rational real chart the multiplicative measure is `dt/|t|` and the two signs of the unit give the denominator `|1-t|`.
The parity sign average cancels one factor of the real digamma denominator.
The even and odd real characters give the two sign averages in the real gamma factor.
The zero of a differentiable compact profile cancels the denominator at the origin.
When the profile vanishes at one, splitting the local integral produces two one-sided profiles.
One weighted radial derivative gives inverse first-power decay in the Mellin height.
Two weighted radial integrals control the Mellin transform throughout a half-plane, with a constant independent of the upper end of the support.
At every archimedean place a unitary character differs from one by at most a constant times the distance from the identity.
After first-order cancellation in dimension d, the singularity at the identity is bounded by the locally integrable power ‖t − 1‖^(1−d). At infinity the additive Haar density is bounded by ‖t‖^(−2d).
Transport the additive majorant to local units. The norm-one sphere has measure zero, so the limiting half value of the radial test at one does not affect the integral.
The common cutoff multiplies the difference of the two geometric integrands. Their known integrability therefore gives convergence by dominated convergence.
For a one-sided cut power, only the positive sample in the local digamma kernel survives.
At each infinite place, the local trace of a cut power is a single weighted exponential integral.
Multiplying the limiting power by a fixed cutoff produces a continuous compact test.
Multiplication by the same bounded cutoff preserves the Gauss difference limit.
Subtract the two convergent Gauss integrals before integration at zero.
Each individual gamma integral converges with its compact logarithmic cutoff.
A continuous compact radial profile supported above one has an integrable local trace at every infinite place.
The geometric subtraction equals a difference of digamma values, with factor one half at a real place and factor one at a complex place.
The limiting subtracted archimedean integrals, with the corrected local Tamagawa kernels, are analytic throughout their open half-plane of integrability.
A genus-one factor with multiplicity differs from one by at most twice its multiplicity times the squared displacement near the origin.
Changing the reference of one genus-one factor multiplies its normalized value by an exponential of a linear function.
The logarithmic derivative of a normalized genus-one factor is the difference of its resolvents at the variable and reference points.
Square summability of the reciprocals, weighted by the given positive multiplicities, gives an entire genus-one product and its precise zero set.
Separating a single factor from the entire product identifies its vanishing order, since the complementary product is nonzero there.
At any point off the shifted zero set, the squared reciprocals of the distances to the zeros are summable with their actual multiplicities.
Subtraction at the reference point gives an absolutely summable resolvent difference at every point away from the selected zeros.
Restriction of the Bruhat test to local units gives the ordinary integrability at each infinite place.
At a complex place, vanishing at zero removes the finite-part cutoff.
Multiplicative Haar integration at a complex place uses the inverse squared radius.
In the complex coordinate of an infinite place the additive test is a classical Schwartz function.
A test vanishing at one gives the ordinary integrable complex-place kernel, normalized by 1/(2π).
A Euclidean presentation transports an additive Bruhat test to an ordinary Schwartz function.
Orthogonality restricts the exterior-zero cancellation for this test to its own isotype.

Decompose the finite local Connes–Weil integral into positive and negative valuation shells. The integral over units vanishes because the radial profile vanishes at one. At a ramified place, translation by a unit with nontrivial character annihilates the whole integral.
The integer-unit translate of an integrand with a nontrivial character has integral zero under multiplicative Haar measure.
Restrict the global zero sum to the chosen isotype. Orthogonality makes every term off the embedded single-character window zero, and the same norm-one volume multiplies all remaining moments.
A radial Bruhat test in a normalized character recovers its compact smooth logarithmic profile.

A norm-one translation annihilates the Mellin integral of the radial test against every other character trivial on the chosen norm section. In its own character the integral is the radial Mellin moment times the norm-one volume.
The fixed-cutoff character trace uses the cancellation of the exterior zeros only for the given test. Full windows supply this from the classical critical strip.
In a sum over the valuation lattice, group the shells of valuations `k + 1` and `-(k + 1)` when the central shell contributes zero.
Only finitely many prime powers can meet the bounded radial support of the adelic test.
Compact support along the norm section bounds both the radial variable and its inverse.
A Schwartz test vanishing at zero is integrable against the reciprocal squared radius in the plane.
The two noncentral valuations give reciprocal square-root weights, both with denominator q to the half power.
The noncentral ultrametric denominator depends only on the norm.
The norm-one Tamagawa volume is finite and nonzero.
Convergence of the prime and polar terms gives the entire shifted Euler half-plane.

For any approximating family the combined archimedean and spectral terms converge locally uniformly on `Re z > max a 1` to the regularized shifted logarithmic derivative: the fixed-cutoff trace identity writes the combined sum as the polar moments minus the prime-power sum, and both of those converge there.
The overlap limit follows from the prime and polar limits whenever the exterior-zero terms cancel in the fixed-cutoff trace identity.
A fixed-cutoff identity gives the overlap limit by convergence of its prime and polar terms.
Chapter 12's cancellation for every test makes the exterior zero set empty. The one-character full-window formula then gives the cutoff limit for every family.
Outside a window of radius eight, half the Poisson kernel at real part eight majorizes the kernel at real part two. Inside the window the unweighted zero multiplicity majorizes the narrower kernel.
On the Euler half-plane the completed logarithmic derivative splits into the logarithmic derivatives of the gamma factor and the finite continuation.
An imaginary norm twist translates the completed logarithmic derivative throughout the half-plane of absolute convergence.
In the shifted Euler half-plane each term of the renormalized completed logarithmic derivative is analytic.
Adding the two polar corrections in the normalized trivial chart cancels its simple poles at zero and one. In every chart the remaining residues are the positive part of the completed divisor.
Circle residues depend only on the germ on a punctured neighborhood.
Complex conjugation of both the parameter and the value preserves a local meromorphic normal form and its order.
Fixed affine changes of height preserve the logarithmic bound on a positive vertical line.
The real digamma main term along an affine vertical line retains the logarithm of its positive height scale.
On an affine vertical line the imaginary translation produces the reciprocal-height term in the real digamma asymptotic.
The digamma function commutes with complex conjugation.
After its first Stirling correction, the digamma remainder has quadratic decay in the height on the entire open right half-plane.
The difference between the vertical and real Gauss digamma kernels is bounded by two positive Laplace kernels, one of Frullani type.
A fixed vertical line in the right half-plane has an explicit logarithmic digamma bound, uniform in both signs of the imaginary part.
On each positive vertical line the digamma correction tends to zero at both height ends, by the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for its Laplace density.
For a character and its inverse the imaginary anchor terms cancel across the two symmetric height truncations, with their multiplicities.

The two imaginary anchor corrections cancel in each common height cutoff; a locally uniform limit for each compensated series thus gives the ordinary joint height limit for a character and its inverse.
Multiplicity-weighted reciprocal heights are summable precisely when the masses of successive dyadic height shells, divided by their lower endpoints, form a summable numerical series.

Patel's disk factorization rescaled by `d ≥ 1`: some height in `(H, H + 1)` avoids the ordinates of the zeros, and the logarithm of `‖f‖` is bounded below on that height in the disk of radius `3 * d`. Adapted from the `_disk` helper of PR #6071.

The statement of `introTrace_finiteL_inv_horizontal_growth` for any continuation.
The continuation has finitely many poles, all of order at most one. Copied from the private helper of PR #6071 (AppB Sec6) with `S = ∅`.
The finite Hecke continuations for inverse unitary characters have the same order at conjugate points.
Conjugating a finite Euler product on the half-plane of absolute convergence replaces the character by its inverse and conjugates the parameter.
Absolute convergence of the ideal logarithmic-derivative series gives a uniform bound on every fixed vertical line in the Euler half-plane.
The odd-kernel pairing with the real finite logarithmic derivative converges under symmetric truncation on every Euler line for every unitary character.
The positive completed divisor has finite support below any fixed height.
The positive Frullani kernel for a change of the real Laplace parameter is integrable, and its mass is the logarithm of the ratio of the parameters.
On the shifted Euler half-plane the full reference-difference series, normalized at two, equals the corrected completed logarithmic derivative.
Every positive-order completed zero belongs to every full window.
The positive Gauss kernel is the centered Binet kernel plus one half.
Removing the simple singularity in the Gauss kernel leaves a positive factor bounded by one on the positive real axis.
The Laplace transform of the bounded Gauss remainder has norm at most the reciprocal of the real part of its argument.
On the positive half-plane the Hecke gamma factor has logarithmic derivative equal to the sum of the local logarithmic derivatives.
The finite sum of all archimedean logarithmic derivatives has a convergent symmetric odd-kernel integral on every positive vertical line.
Conjugating a positive zero of a completed Hecke character gives a zero of the inverse character with the same multiplicity.
The inverse character has the opposite norm frequency.
A normalized meromorphic function admits a holomorphic continuation of its logarithmic derivative from a right half-plane exactly when its divisor vanishes in the larger half-plane.
The logarithmic derivative of a translated and scaled gamma function includes the contribution from its exponential prefactor.
Evaluate the local Hecke gamma logarithmic derivative on its positive half-plane.
A logarithmic derivative has principal part equal to the order divided by the local coordinate. This also covers a locally zero meromorphic function.
The linear Taylor approximation of the height logarithm has a quadratic error whenever the height dominates the fixed translation.
Uniformly in the frequency, an oscillatory difference is bounded by a positive exponentially damped difference at the absolute frequency.
Away from the unshifted trivial pole, a chart character has no poles in the positive half-plane.
On the positive half-plane the reciprocal gamma factor is regular and nonzero.
A nontrivial chart representative must already be nontrivial on the norm-one classes.
The unshifted pole of the completed trivial character has order minus one.
Each affine shift of the real digamma profile has a symmetric odd-kernel pairing on every fixed positive vertical line.
Translating an even continuous profile of logarithmic growth has a convergent symmetric pairing with the odd Cauchy kernel.
The odd Cauchy kernel paired with a translated Poisson kernel increases its width by one.
The symmetric odd pairing with the real part of a pure-imaginary translate of the two rational corrections is absolutely convergent, with an explicit value.
An odd Cauchy kernel pairs convergently with a derivative whose primitive grows at most as the square root of the absolute height.
The polar factors have order one at the exceptional point of the trivial chart and order zero everywhere else in the right half-plane.
A short positive profile samples the real part of the gamma kernel near its singularity. Its integral is at most `-C` once the support is sufficiently close to zero.

Apply the one-character explicit formula of Theorem B.4.2.2, p. 616, to a profile below the first prime-power logarithm. The prime and conductor terms vanish. Each infinite place then contributes less than a uniform lower bound for any finite signed divisor.
A unit-mass positive profile supported in the unit interval has a uniform Mellin bound at each fixed point.
A completed Hecke function has at most two poles, so finitely many positive orders force a finite signed divisor.
A nonnegative smooth profile of mass one fits inside any sufficiently short positive interval.
The polar correction with pole at a fixed point contributes residue one precisely there.
The narrow resolvent, the regularized archimedean integrals, and the translated Euler logarithmic derivative are analytic on the entire open chart.
A resolvent on a bounded set separated from its pole decays uniformly like the reciprocal of one plus the height of the pole.
A reference-difference expansion determines the positive-real-part regularization exactly by the real anchor value.
The real part of the resolvent at a real point to the right of the window decays quadratically in the height of its pole.

Along symmetric height truncations a self-dual character's imaginary parts cancel at every real anchor. The compensated finite sums therefore have exactly the same locally uniform limit as the bare finite sums.
A self-dual character is trivial along any norm section: every positive scale is a square and every value of the character squares to one.
The completed functional equation and conjugation of the finite Euler product reflect the order across the critical line for this same character.

The one-character explicit formula of Theorem B.4.2.2, p. 616, for a smooth compact logarithmic profile supported above one in the multiplicative coordinate. The conductor term vanishes and the prime samples agree with the geometric prime-power terms.
Vanishing at one removes the conductor term from the signed explicit formula. The two radial prime shells give the positive and negative samples of the logarithmic test.
The difference of the resolvents at two parameters in a compact set is bounded by a constant times the reciprocal square of the imaginary height weight.
A resolvent on a bounded set separated horizontally from its pole decays uniformly like the reciprocal of one plus the height of the pole.
A cutoff-uniform inverse-square Mellin estimate exchanges the cutoff limit with the full spectral sum on the right of a window.
Restricting the zero sum to an open window preserves its value if the window contains each positive-order zero.

Removing the norm frequency shifts both the argument and the reference point. Subtracting the two reference expansions cancels their common anchoring constant and translates the exceptional poles in the trivial normalized isotype.
Termwise integration of an absolutely summable Fourier series keeps the primitive uniformly bounded when its nonzero frequencies are bounded away from zero.
Separate all other poles from one fixed point using local finiteness of the divisor.
The singular part of the resolvent germ is a single term, weighted by its multiplicity.
Shifted poles lie to the left of this domain, so they contribute no residue here.
Removing the summand at the center leaves a normally convergent analytic sum on a ball.
There are finitely many window zeros below any fixed absolute imaginary height. The resulting finite sets exhaust the window.
Translation by the norm frequency reindexes any multiplicity-weighted sum over the full completed zero divisor.
Removing the gamma factor gives a continuation of the finite L-function. The entire reciprocal gamma factor can only increase the order at a zero.
For a test odd under inversion, inverting the quasi-character negates the Mellin value.
The product of the omitted unit masses at the archimedean-only stage is the reciprocal square root of the absolute discriminant.
The closed disc around two lies in the right half-plane used in §1.4.3.
On the support of a nonnegative radial test the printed denominator is bounded away from zero and is at most the denominator of the corrected real-place integrand.
For the trivial rational character, the printed moment of a radial approximant is its radial Mellin transform multiplied by the norm-one Tamagawa volume.
For the trivial rational character the actual real-place kernel gives a lower bound on the printed real-place term at parameter two.
At parameter two the radial approximant has real values between zero and one. Its support lies in a compact interval strictly above one.
Additive form of compact-subgroup containment in a finite completion.
If open subgroups form a neighbourhood base at the identity, every structural quotient of the group is discrete, so the associated elementary stage is finite-dimensional.
Each stage over a compact structural quotient with discrete quotient is finite-dimensional.
For a totally disconnected group whose compact sets fit in compact subgroups, each elementary stage is realized by locally constant functions with compact support.

If every compact subset of a Hausdorff topological group is contained in a compact subgroup, then every open compactly generated subgroup is compact (its generating compact set lies in a compact subgroup, and the subgroup is the closure of that subgroup's image).
A strict LF presentation gives completeness for the compatible additive uniformity.
Tensoring a complete space with a countably generated space carrying the finest locally convex topology gives a strict union of finite powers of the complete space.
In dimension one, the elementary weighted bound is the supremum of the corresponding classical weighted derivative norms.
The one-dimensional elementary stage with trivial other factors is the classical Schwartz space, with the same seminorms.
A strong-bidual functional belongs to the bipolar of evaluations on a compact disk of Schwartz functions. This disk already has weakly closed evaluation image.

In positive dimension, the Hermite functions form a Hilbert basis of complex L² consisting of Schwartz functions. Enumerating the multi-indices in order of total degree gives an indexing by ℕ with polynomial growth of the basis seminorms and rapid decay of the coefficients. For each decay order the bound is uniform on the unit ball of a suitable continuous Schwartz seminorm.
A series of Euclidean Schwartz functions is summable if it is absolutely summable in every defining seminorm.
A finite linear combination can be enumerated by a nonempty finite interval even when it represents zero.
The compact open subgroup indicator is the constant function on its trivial structural quotient, extended by zero.
Each mixed partial with its coordinate weight is dominated pointwise by an ordinary Schwartz function, depending continuously and linearly on the input.
Every seminorm is continuous in the finest locally convex topology, so that topology is barrelled.
With the finest locally convex topology, a countable-dimensional space has Fréchet strong dual, via evaluation on a basis.
A countable spanning set gives a rank-one expansion with geometrically bounded coefficients for the finest locally convex topology.
Finite spans of a countable generating set give a strict LF presentation for the finest locally convex topology.

decls.deviation: Nuclearity of the strong dual holds without the countability hypothesis.
decls.summary: The strong dual of a space with its finest locally convex topology is nuclear. Each bounded set of the primal space lies in a finite-dimensional subspace, so uniform convergence on that set follows from convergence on finitely many basis vectors.
Reindexing the empty tail induces a linear homeomorphism of test functions.
The empty-tail reindexing transports the countable rank and continuity of all seminorms to the finite adele ring.
Finite adelic test functions are finite sums of indicators of translated product subgroups. The coordinates of each translate are integral almost everywhere.
Compact sets in the tail have a common finite set of possibly nonintegral coordinates. Bound those coordinates by compact additive subgroups.
The integral elements of a finite adelic tail form a compact set.
Every compact subset of a finite adele tail lies in a compact subgroup.
The tail is covered by the open stages with integral coordinates outside a finite set. Each of these stages embeds into the ordinary countable product.
Open subgroups form a neighbourhood base at the identity of a finite adele tail.
Finite adelic test functions are locally constant with compact support.
A zero neighborhood in the finite adeles contains a compact open product subgroup whose local factors are integral away from a finite set.
Compact sets in a finite product fit in products of compact additive subgroups.
Every compact subset of a finite product of finite completions lies in a compact subgroup.
Open subgroups form a neighbourhood base at the identity of a finite product of finite completions.
The indicator of a compact open subset of a finite completion is a local test function.
The local Schwartz–Bruhat space is spanned by the countable family of indicators of compact open subsets of the completion.
Every elementary quotient in a structural pair for the additive completion is discrete.
Each elementary Schwartz stage of the additive finite completion is finite-dimensional because its structural quotient is compact and discrete.
Each realized stage on the additive completion is locally constant and compactly supported.
The open subgroup of a structural pair for the additive completion is compact.
The compact sets of the additive completion are contained in compact open subgroups.
A character on a finite quotient of a compact open subgroup, extended by zero, is Schwartz–Bruhat because its image is cyclic.
Every function on a finite cyclic structural quotient realizes a Schwartz–Bruhat function.
A compactly supported, locally constant function descends to a finite quotient on a compact open subgroup. Extending the Fourier expansion on that quotient by zero gives Bruhat membership.
Finite places form a countable set because their ideals are finitely generated over the countable ring of integers.
On a fixed compact set of inputs, only finitely many dilates of a locally constant function occur as the multiplier varies in a compact set.
All unit translates with the unit and inverse in a compact set have common compact support. Restriction to that support distinguishes their finite orbit.
A continuous image of a Fréchet space lies in one member of a countable closed subspace cover, by the Baire category theorem on the source.
A linear homeomorphism transports a Fréchet structure, including completeness for the additive uniformity.
The subspace topology on the range of an embedded Fréchet stage is Fréchet.
Integration by parts makes the Schwartz oscillator symmetric in complex L².
Changing a tensor factor by a linear homeomorphism preserves the inductive tensor topology.
An absolutely summable rank-one expansion of a normed-space map induces an integral evaluation form.
Transport a product kernel along a linear equivalence from a finest-topology factor.
Transport a product kernel along a linear equivalence from a finest-topology factor.
A summable coefficient bound and a uniform vector bound in each continuous seminorm suffice for nuclearity.
A split quotient of groups gives an open quotient of their test spaces by coset integration.
Splitting off a newly inserted index sends a pure tensor to the old tensor times its factor at the new index.
Restrict a projection to an embedded intermediate space containing its range.
The sole coordinate of the one-dimensional Euclidean space.
A compact identity neighborhood generates a connected locally compact group.
A real structural pair has full open subgroup and trivial kernel, so its quotient map identifies it with the real group.
In any elementary presentation of a real structural quotient, the torus and discrete factors are trivial, and the real coordinate is a continuous real-linear equivalence.
Every elementary stage of the real group is continuously linearly equivalent to the classical Schwartz space by pointwise realization.
The full real group with trivial kernel has a one-dimensional elementary presentation.
A rectangle integral off S extends from the product of its S-local factors.
Split the coordinates of a larger finite stage into the old and new places.
The global additive group is the product of the selected stage and its restricted tail.
Pullback is a linear homeomorphism. Continuity is tested on each structural stage, where pullback factors through the transported presentation.
Each elementary global stage factors continuously through one finite-place stage.
Second-countable totally disconnected groups whose compact sets fit in compact subgroups have countable-dimensional Schwartz–Bruhat spaces.
If every structural stage is finite-dimensional, every seminorm restricts continuously to each stage, so the Schwartz–Bruhat topology is the finest locally convex topology.

Continue Tate's equation from the strip of simultaneous convergence by the meromorphic identity theorem.

Scalar meromorphic functions on the plane agreeing on a punctured germ agree off a discrete set.
A continuous function periodic in the imaginary direction is bounded on closed strips.
The complex parameter is additive under successive norm twists.

Inserting a finite local unit through the S-ideles gives its full idele insertion.
Inserting an infinite local unit through the S-ideles gives its full idele insertion.
The archimedean epsilon factors have norm one, and periodicity of each finite factor gives a bound for their product on every closed strip.

Along a homomorphic section of the S-idelic norm, homogeneous theta weighted by a complex exponential of positive real part decays exponentially at both ends of the logarithmic axis.
