primes and zeros of L-functions*, Duke Math. J. 127 (2005), arXiv:math/0311468 (page numbers
are those of the preprint), Corollary 4.17, p. 34, and Lemma 4.20, p. 36, at α = 1: the
direction from bounds on the Mellin transforms to bounded classes, in the cases that Lean does
not prove.
For a sequence of tests whose θ-classes have one conductor level and lie in one Fréchet
subspace of the θ-quotient: if the Mellin transforms of the θ-functions of the tests, and of
their additive Fourier transforms, are bounded on every line of real part greater than one
(supported on a finitely generated subgroup of the discrete factor of the dual, with every
polynomial weight bounded uniformly in the index), then the θ-classes form a bounded set.
Deviation: This is what remains of the criterion `sLocalMellinSchwartzBounds_meyer`, which is
proved from it below. Proved in Lean, and excluded here by hypothesis: the case in which the
classes span a finite-dimensional space (`hS`), and the case in which they are given by even
real Schwartz profiles (`hreal`; it covers ℚ with no finite place). The other direction of the
criterion is proved in Lean as well (`sLocalMellinSchwartzBounds_meyer_general_forward`). The
hypotheses `hk`, `hM` and `hm` follow from the bounds and are proved before this statement is
applied. The bounds are written without derivatives, which is equivalent
(`sLocalMellinSchwartzBounds_meyer_zeroth_iff`), and the conclusion is boundedness in the
quotient, which is equivalent to representatives in one bounded set
(`sLocalMellinSchwartzBounds_meyer_lift_iff_quotient_bounded`).
The paper states its results for bornological spaces and in the variable of the idele
classes. Writing them for this library is the project's work and is not proved in Lean:
that the bounded sets of the Schwartz–Bruhat space here are the paper's, that the kernel of
the S-unit sum is the closed span the paper divides by, the normalizations of the Fourier
transform and of the Haar measures, and the seminorms on the dual group. The integrator and
an independent reviewer checked these steps against the paper for the whole criterion (#7346);
no specialist in the paper's framework has.

decls.summary: Subadditivity controls every integer multiple by the corresponding absolute coefficient.
A Haar-integrable function and its Haar-integrable, continuous derivative along a real group flow satisfy integration by parts without compact support.
On a theta stage realized by even real Schwartz profiles compatibly with Fourier and Mellin, the weighted estimates imply boundedness.
Finite uniform differentiations of a physical test bound every power of one plus the sum of the associated real frequency magnitudes.
The topological bornology of the theta quotient is exactly its bounded-lift bornology.
A continuous real one-parameter subgroup lifts homomorphically through a covering homomorphism. Both preservation of products and normalization at 1 come from uniqueness of based lifts.
The actual raw S-ideles lift any prescribed norm section, including the one over which the angular/radial boundedness condition quantifies.
Positive-line Mellin evaluation factors through a continuous linear functional on the theta quotient, with the normalization of the integral.
Vanishing on a vertical line extends to the entire positive half-plane.
The angular support of a Mellin-bounded sequence implies invariance of all theta classes at one fixed principal congruence level.
Continuous linear evaluations that are pointwise bounded on a nonmeagre set are uniformly bounded on every bounded set, for an arbitrary index family.
Divisibility and self-duality realize the unnormalized frequency through a compact group.
A single finitely generated subgroup supports every positive Mellin line.

The actual S-principal-congruence quotient is locally Euclidean in all number fields. The finite congruence conditions form an open subgroup; on it the complex embeddings of the archimedean units detect the level.
Principal congruence subgroups of a finite product of nonarchimedean unit groups form a neighborhood base at one.
A compact level at which finitely many continuous archimedean characters separate the remaining points of an open subgroup yields a Lie quotient.
Lift the scalar comparison to a given Fréchet stage using representatives of its points. All changes of coordinates in the weighted estimates are made before the Baire-category argument.
The lift of the specified section realizes the pure radial exponent.
At a fixed angular character the polynomially weighted vertical-strip estimates are simultaneous over a bounded family of theta classes.
At a fixed angular character the polynomially weighted Mellin integral of a single test stays bounded on each closed positive strip.
The full bounded-lift equivalence holds for arbitrary families on the rational archimedean stage, including those with infinite-dimensional theta span.
The inverse comparison on the rational stage with no finite places holds for arbitrary spans of theta classes.

Over the rational field with no finite places, all weighted trivial Mellin lines of a family and of its additive Fourier transforms suffice even when the theta classes span an infinite-dimensional subspace.
The trivial Mellin coefficient, ordinary additive Fourier transform, and theta class have a common even real Schwartz model over ℚ with no finite places.
Over ℚ with `S = ∅` the homogeneous theta function is the theta function on classes times the total norm-one mass.
Adjoining the integer indicators multiplies the rational theta Mellin coefficient by the product of the ordinary local Gaussian zeta integrals.
If every rational theta class comes from the archimedean stage, the inverse comparison holds after adjoining any finite set of places.

On the rational empty-place quotient the trivial Mellin coefficients are the classical Mellin values of the even profile up to the fixed positive norm-one mass. This normalization is independent of the sequence of tests.

Uniform derivative bounds at the origin and all weighted ray estimates at infinity give boundedness in the actual real Schwartz space. The missing zeroth-order estimate on the unit interval follows from the first derivative and the single value at the endpoint.
Every homomorphism on a subgroup of the discrete dual of a compact group is the restriction of a real logarithmic frequency of a one-parameter flow.
A single weighted absolute Fourier moment bounds the corresponding ordinary derivative everywhere. This includes the origin, which Mellin ray inversion itself does not control.

A uniform quadratic bound on one Mellin line controls the original functions with the corresponding radial weight. The estimate holds down to every positive radius and does not require derivatives of Mellin values.
All polynomial height weights for a family of Mellin transforms pass to ordinary derivatives, after translating the positive line once.
A Schwartz function is `O(x^(-a))` at infinity for every `a`.
A Schwartz function is bounded near zero.
On the positive ray, Re(s)=3/2 controls every positive-order additive moment near zero. An arbitrarily large positive line makes the same moment integrable at infinity.
Reflection commutes with the real Fourier transform and averaging the two reflected tests gives a representative of the original theta class.
The single-test comparison applies in particular to the higher-degree, infinite angular-support case.
A single test either has finitely many nonzero angular coefficients on the line or belongs to the higher-degree, infinite-support comparison.
In finite-dimensional spans a single line suffices for the inverse implication.
On the real logarithmic parameter, the physical S-adelic theta generator gives the derivative of its quotient function at every point of every orbit.
A positive Mellin line is bounded simultaneously in every unitary character and height.
Weighted Mellin values on all positive weight lines greater than one suffice for the full Schwartz bounds, including all radial derivatives.
On the zeta chart, line estimates at the two neighboring weights imply Cauchy's bound on each derivative at the middle weight.
Unfolding the single-test zeta integral on a positive norm-twist chart.
Away from a discrete subset of a norm chart the functional equation is a pointwise identity, the common factor is nonzero, and evaluation is allowed by the pole bound.
In a unitary chart the allowed order is nonnegative off a discrete set.
Polynomially weighted edge bounds propagate across a strip by Phragmén–Lindelöf. Rapid decay provides the preliminary unweighted bound for each individual test.
Choose a single elementary stage for the central line and both edges. The value comparison controls angular support there, and Cauchy's estimate controls each radial derivative on the central line.
Successive twists add their exponents.
Unfold the theta Mellin integral on the positive half-plane. Equality on a neighborhood of each point also identifies all the derivatives in the Schwartz bounds.
Absorb the imaginary part of a norm twist into its unitary character.

The S-local principal value commutes with translation by an S-idele, for any set of selected places: the selected factors are invariant by the local commutation and the remaining factors act by the identity on both sides.
Theta of the part removed by a single principal value is the translated unit average. Changing the uniformizer by a unit leaves this average unchanged.
On the unit-invariant theta functions the average is a single translate. Thus the uniformizer difference and principal value give the same quotient class.

On theta functions invariant under the integer units at one finite place, every continuous quotient seminorm is bounded by a continuous quotient seminorm of the difference with the uniformizer translate. The Mellin identity theorem on page 242 gives injectivity. The relative openness argument there controls seminorms before taking the theta quotient. A reconstruction of the primitive along uniformizer orbits with bounds modulo the theta kernel would give this estimate.

To descend an embedding on tests it suffices to lift small boundary values of kernel elements to small kernel elements. Subtracting such a lift gives a small test in the range of the embedding, where the inverse is continuous.
On a single finite factor the principal-value range is the kernel of evaluation at zero. Tensoring gives exactly the tests that vanish on the face `x_v = 0`.
If the one-place principal value kills a theta class, its theta function equals the removed unit-invariant term. It is then periodic under the uniformizer and hence zero.
Removing the value at zero times a fixed test of value one gives a local principal value.
The inverse one-place uniformizer has norm greater than one, since its norm is the residue cardinality.
An S-local theta function invariant under an idele of norm greater than one vanishes. Its values on the forward orbit are constant and tend to zero by the large-norm estimate.
On a pure tensor, removing its value on the face times `φ` amounts to performing the same subtraction on the single local factor.
On a unit-invariant theta function, the term removed by the principal value is the uniformizer translate.
A translation by a diagonal S-unit gives the identity on S-local theta classes.

On the stage with the selected finite place removed, take the translation by the projection of a diagonal S-unit. When its modulus changes, the difference between the identity and that translation is open onto its image on theta classes.

Sequential closedness of Mellin divisibility on Schwartz–Bruhat tests. On the line of unitary characters times the norm, divide by the nowhere-zero dilation multiplier. If a convergent sequence of tests has quotients represented by tests, the quotient for its limit is represented by a test.

If the Mellin transforms of a sequence are dominated on every nonzero weight line by the transforms of bounded tests, their theta classes are bounded. The functional equation transfers the comparison to the Fourier transforms. Bounds on neighboring lines control all Schwartz seminorms in Meyer's description of the coinvariants.
At nonzero real weight the distance of the dilation multiplier from zero has a positive lower bound independent of the unitary character.
Mellin evaluation of a dilation difference at any regular quasi-character.
The open mapping theorem on one Fréchet summand turns sequential closedness of the range into an inducing map.

Decompose theta classes by their finite unit conductors. Differences of the normalized averages over successive principal congruence subgroups give commuting projections. Each range lies in a single congruence level, which has a finite family of archimedean Schwartz generators as in the proof of Theorem 5.2.1.1(1), and is Fréchet. Each test has finite level.
The normalized Haar average projects onto the fixed vectors. It commutes with every continuous linear operator commuting with the subgroup action.
A pure adelic tensor is fixed at the maximum of the levels of its finite factors. Tests fixed at some level form a subspace and pure tensors span.
Successive compact averages telescope. Their differences are idempotent, since a finer average fixes the coarser range and all the averages commute.

At a fixed principal congruence level, finitely many archimedean Schwartz families represent all invariant theta functions. This is the finite-generation step of Theorem 5.2.1.1(1), p. 230, proved as `sLocalAdelicThetaSpace_strictLF_level_generators` in Sec2.
The principal congruence conditions define compact subgroups of the S-ideles. Their archimedean component is one.
Local constancy of the dilation orbit at the identity gives one principal congruence subgroup fixing a local test.

Each level is contained in a Fréchet stage as soon as it has finitely many archimedean Schwartz generators. Each generator map factors through one stage of the strict LF presentation, so a single stage contains their finite sum.
A closed subspace contained in a Fréchet subspace is Fréchet in the induced topology.

A convergent sequence in the theta quotient has a subsequence represented by convergent tests. Bounded lifting for nuclear strict LF quotients puts representatives in a bounded set of one Fréchet test stage, where the Montel property gives a convergent subsequence.
Fourier uniqueness for the integrable function obtained by multiplying theta by the idele norm. Mellin evaluations on the single line of real part one separate theta classes.
Add the inverse seminorm estimates on the finite conductor summands. Their sum is pointwise finite, so the supremum of its finite partial sums is continuous by barrelledness.
An open parameter map gives small parameters for all nearby compatible traces. Evaluating a continuous lift at such a parameter gives openness on the kernel.

Restrict theta-null tests to the face `x_v = 0`, giving the space of all traces the quotient topology from tests. This restriction is open onto its image. Equivalently, for each zero-neighborhood in the theta kernel, its traces contain a relative zero-neighborhood among the traces of theta-null tests.
Restriction to the face is continuous. Inserting the integer indicator in the missing coordinate gives a continuous section.

Group the radial ball coefficients of a theta-null test by their indices modulo the positive valuation generator `d` of the S-units. Subtracting consecutive theta values on the local shells and summing over residues gives an old-stage theta-null sum after translating the coefficient at `n` by the power `-(n / d)` of the generator. The sum of the untranslated coefficients is the trace at zero.
The unit-invariant part of a test has a finite expansion in valuation balls with test functions on the old stage as coefficients.
Summing on a valuation fiber is summing on its translate of the old unit group. The terms extended by zero have the same sum.
The positive generator of the valuation image divides the order of every S-unit.
Lift an old idele with any prescribed valuation at the added place.
A principal power of the prime at the selected place gives an S-unit with nonzero valuation there.
Removing the selected place from the product formula leaves a norm different from one whenever the S-unit has positive order there.
Factor a product over the enlarged stage into its old coordinates and the factor at the added place.
Radial local tests are spanned by valuation balls. After removing the value at zero times the unit ball, only finitely many shells remain.
The two shells of orders `d - 1` and `-1` select a single valuation fiber for each ball, including balls with a negative index.
The theta series indexed by the subgroup of field units has the same sum as the series indexed by the units of the ring of S-integers.
Evaluating the difference of two theta series a full valuation period apart extracts one translate of each ball coefficient.
Modulo differences for one generator, each translated shell coefficient has the same class as the original coefficient, for positive and negative powers alike.
Contract the new tensor factor against evaluation at zero.
The diagonal action on the face is the projection of the same S-unit to the remaining coordinates.

For a continuous endomorphism of a complete Hausdorff locally convex space, an inverse seminorm estimate on the vectors `x - P x` suffices. The term `P x` is already controlled, and an inducing additive map has complete image.
Translating the removed part by an integer unit has the same effect in the averaging formula as making another choice of uniformizer. Its theta function is therefore invariant.

Through a stage containing the selected places, the global principal value of an inserted test is the insertion of the S-local principal value. The integer tail indicator is obtained by slicing the inserted test `k₀` at a point `p` where its value is one.

On test functions, insertion of an S-local stage intertwines the S-local and the global principal values. A nonzero test, normalized at a point where it does not vanish, supplies the slice that identifies the integer tail indicator.

No countable family of seminorms on `ℂ[X]` makes every seminorm continuous. Scale the weights on `Xⁿ` past `(n + 1)` times the first `n + 1` family members at `Xⁿ`; a continuous seminorm is bounded by finitely many members, which fails for large `n`.
For nonnegative weights `w`, the weighted sum of the absolute values of the coefficients is a seminorm on `ℂ[X]` taking the value `w n` on `Xⁿ`.

The derivative at zero along a unit vector `e` has exact order one and is supported at zero. Its order-one bound is the operator norm of the derivative. The tests `χₙ(x)⟪e, x⟫`, with `χₙ` a bump equal to one near zero and supported in the ball of radius `1/(n + 1)`, have sup norm at most `1/(n + 1)` but derivative one along `e`.
On a one-point space every distribution has order zero: each test is its value times the constant test one.
Evaluation at zero is a distribution of order zero supported at zero.
The derivative at zero along `e` is a distribution.
There is a test function equal to `x ↦ ⟪e, x⟫` near zero.

A nonzero multiple of the derivative at zero along a unit vector `e` has order at most one, not order zero, and support in the origin. The tests `χₙ(x)⟪e, x⟫`, with `χₙ` a bump equal to one near zero and supported in the ball of radius `1/(n + 1)`, have sup norm at most `1/(n + 1)` while the functional takes the fixed value `c` on them.

At any finite place with a uniformizer, the printed claim fails for the trivial character: every eigendistribution of the trivial character is invariant under the uniformizer, so it vanishes on the difference of a test and its translate. Stated for a general number field so that the argument is elaborated once, not at a concrete field.
A matrix of samples `Σ_{s ∈ S} F s (xₖ) G s (yₗ)` of a finite sum of products has rank at most `|S|`, so it is singular once it has more than `|S|` rows.
The samples `exp((k/n)(l/n)) = (exp(k/n²))ˡ` form a Vandermonde matrix with distinct nodes, so they are not singular.
Precomposition with a linear isometry is a continuous linear map between the complex test function spaces. On each compact stage it preserves every derivative seminorm.

The complex test functions on a real normed space form a polynormable space over `ℂ`: complex scalar multiplication is continuous, and the real convex zero-neighborhood basis is also a complex convex basis. Adapted from `polynormableSpace_realTests` in `AppD_SchwartzBruhat/Sec3b.lean`, which is the case of the real line.
Around z, use log(y/z) to lift a punctured-plane argument to the vector cover.
On every discrete fibre, translating the vector cover scales a character by a unit scalar. All derivative norms are therefore constant across that cover.
The output at weight zero gives the underlying function. The output at each other weight proves membership and continuity in the all-exponent space.
Both first derivatives, at each output weight, as continuous maps to Schwartz–Bruhat space.
Resolve a real-linear differential in the frame tangent to dilation and rotation.
Recover local differentiability by taking one positive integral power of the squared norm whose exponent belongs to the input interval.
At each output weight the derivative uses the input weight one half lower. Untwist at one such weight to construct the underlying linear map.
Both iterated derivatives act continuously on the all-exponent decay space.
Specialize the input twist to the space of all exponents.
Combine a phase multiplier and differentiability on the punctured plane with the two orbit operators.
Differentiate a weighted dilation or rotation orbit at time zero.
Multiplying by the unit phase r/z (or r/conj z) changes the input exponent b into the output exponent b + 1/2. The two derivatives act on the same twisted function.
The weighted radial and angular generators recover both first Wirtinger derivatives. Here b is the input exponent and q is the corresponding weight at z.
The whole punctured plane with trivial stage kernel gives one elementary model for every Schwartz–Bruhat function. Continuity of the inverse is tested on stages.
Composing a flat Schwartz function with a real-linear automorphism of the archimedean coordinates that keeps the coordinate walls keeps it flat.
Vanishing of all mixed Wirtinger jets implies vanishing of all real Fréchet jets.
Vanishing of all real Fréchet jets implies vanishing of all mixed Wirtinger jets.
The modulus of a quasi-character is a product of real powers of the coordinate norms.
On the all-exponent space the modulus shifts the weights, and the unitary factor acts continuously on each Schwartz–Bruhat twist.
Assemble the one-place cylinders into one elementary presentation. Real and complex logarithmic radii share the vector factor, while only the complex angles are periodic.
Each inverse coordinate norm is bounded by the maximum norm of the inverse tuple.
In the combined presentation each real unit is a signed exponential and each complex unit is the exponential of a linear combination of radius and angle.
Applying a linear vector field to a flat test preserves flatness, by the bilinear Leibniz bound and the vanishing of every derivative of the differential at a wall.
The inverse-coordinate estimate of order one forces every additive jet to vanish at a wall, by density of the tuples of units.
Iterating the Fréchet derivative of a jet gives the norm of the derivative of the combined order.
At a point where all jets vanish, the Taylor estimate applies to every derivative of a Schwartz function.
All jets decay faster than every power of the maximum of one, the coordinate norm and the inverse-coordinate norm.
A common bound on the individual coordinate norms also bounds their maximum, including the empty product.
Repeated mean-value bounds on the unit segment bound a flat function by its highest derivative.
Taylor expansion on the segment from a wall point bounds the value by a power of the distance to the wall.
The differential of an exponential chart at a translate is multiplication by the chart value followed by the differential at zero.

In logarithmic radial and angular coordinates, coordinate weights preserve Schwartz–Bruhat decay for a Schwartz function whose Euclidean jets decay rapidly in the norms of both the coordinates and their inverses.
Every derivative of a flat Schwartz function vanishes to arbitrary order in each separate coordinate.
Translating the argument preserves meromorphic normal form on the whole plane.
Continue a Fourier–Mellin identity from the fundamental strip, then translate the exponent. Here `G` is the archimedean gamma factor, `a` its shift and `ε` the Fourier phase.
The product of all partial twists induces the weighted Schwartz topology.
The points with every real and complex coordinate nonzero are dense.
The product of the squared absolute values is smooth and vanishes at every wall.
Rescaling a relative derivative back to the additive variables costs at most one inverse tuple norm per derivative. The estimate with that many extra powers absorbs it.
Uniform jet bounds for a family survive composition with a fixed local chart. Only its finitely many derivatives at the base point enter the bound.
The punctured complex plane is an open real Euclidean chart.
Tensoring two sets with dense linear spans again gives a set with dense linear span. The two density arguments use separate continuity of the product.

The sum of two twists of a decay function has dense range in the unweighted Schwartz space, even when the allowed exponents are disconnected. In logarithmic coordinates divide compact test profiles by the sum of the two exponential weights.
Separate products of one-variable dense sets generate the unweighted Schwartz space of a finite product, including the empty product.
Division by the wall product subtracts two from each real exponent and one from each complex exponent in the defining family of Schwartz twists.
A finite box of requested weights factors through the sum of the corner twists. Its pointwise multiplier is the product of sums of the endpoint weights.
Repeated division by a smooth wall factor forces every jet of the ordinary Schwartz zero extension to vanish at every coordinate wall.
An all-exponent weighted function on the punctured lines admits an ordinary Schwartz extension in additive coordinates.
A finite power of a compactly generated group with an open Euclidean chart is again elementary: compact generating neighborhoods and charts both multiply.
Componentwise exponentiation has a smooth logarithm near the identity.
Bounding all coordinate twists controls any power of the largest coordinate or inverse coordinate. Taking finite sums of constants also works with no places.
Uniform bounds on the evaluations on a finite basis bound the multilinear operator norm, including the zeroth derivative.
The positive product of coordinate powers, with exponents measured relative to the ordinary real and complex norms.

Near the multiplicative identity use the same logarithm for every translate. Untwisting in these relative coordinates costs a fixed smooth exponential. Thus every coordinate power times any relative derivative is bounded uniformly.
On a one-point group, the constant functions identify Schwartz space with the scalars.

Evaluation on two independent sets of coordinates separates algebraic tensors. Evaluating the left coordinate recovers a vector in the right factor, and taking its basis coordinates recovers the coefficients of the original tensor.
A densely embedded algebraic tensor has precisely the completion of its image.

The approximation estimate in Lemma 5.3.3.3(2), p. 252: finite sums of separate products approximate every weighted test simultaneously in the partial Schwartz seminorms. This assertion involves only the function spaces.
Over the empty set of factors the pure tensor is one and the projective topology is the scalar topology.
Two linear maps on the tensor product agree if they agree on the separate products.
Continuous seminorms on the individual factors define a continuous projective seminorm on the finite tensor.
Iterating the binary coordinate embedding realizes the finite projective tensor in the Schwartz spaces on the product group.
For nuclear factors embedded by families of Schwartz tests, tensoring their coordinates and applying the ordinary Schwartz kernel theorem yields an embedding on the product.
Lift the coordinate product through the two finite tensors and then their binary tensor. The range lies in any submodule containing all separate products.
A bound on the pure tensors of seminormed spaces extends to their projective tensor seminorm.
When the trivial subgroup is a Bruhat stage, the one-place twists induce the topology for any nonempty set of weights. The inverse on their image reconstructs that stage.
Separate-coordinate evaluation is injective on a finite algebraic tensor, including the scalar tensor on an empty family. Split off one coordinate at a time.
Every separate product belongs to the simultaneously weighted Schwartz space. For each tuple of weights, twist each factor before applying the unweighted kernel theorem.
Joint continuity on pure tensors gives a product bound by continuous seminorms on the factors.
Splitting off one coordinate preserves the projective topology. To bound the inverse, apply the finite projective seminorm to the remaining coordinates.
The projective tensor universal property applied to the identity gives joint continuity of the pure tensor map.

The topology estimate in Lemma 5.3.3.3(2), p. 252: the projective tensor topology is induced by its maps to the unweighted Schwartz space, one for each tuple of exponents. This is an estimate on the algebraic tensor only.

All derivatives at the identity of the translates of a Schwartz–Bruhat function in exponential coordinates have uniform bounds. Each fixed directional derivative is the realization of another Schwartz–Bruhat function.
A quadratic bound in distance to a wall point gives zero differential there.
A family on an elementary group with no lattice factor is Schwartz if it is smooth on the cover, absorbs its directional derivatives, and has bounded polynomial weights.
Removing an analytic multiplier periodic in height preserves boundedness on closed vertical strips when the quotient is entire.
For an entire chart, the high-height estimate on the cleared product extends across exceptional gamma values by continuity.
Once the finite Euler denominators are cleared, reflection bounds the left half of a strip by a positive-strip zeta estimate.
Absolute integrability permits angular integration before the radial Mellin transform.
Angular averaging preserves rapid decay on the positive ray.
Integral angular weights have unit norm.
Integral angular weights are smooth.
Changing the angular interval and substituting the squared radius gives the complex Mellin profile.
Uniqueness of continuation identifies the complex Mellin transform with the local zeta function.
Polar coordinates express the complex local integral as twice a radial Mellin transform.
Multiplicative Tamagawa integration in complex coordinates uses twice Lebesgue measure divided by the squared norm.
The complex coordinate model of a local Schwartz–Bruhat function is a Schwartz function.
Euclidean coordinates identify Schwartz–Bruhat functions with classical Schwartz functions.
The local Tate equation on the fundamental strip uses the trace-pairing Fourier transform and reverses the angular weight.
The squared complex absolute value on the units is a surjective modulation.
In exponential coordinates, the realization of a Schwartz–Bruhat stage is smooth along every translate of a continuous homomorphism from a real vector space.
Dividing a positive weighted Schwartz–Bruhat twist by its smooth nonzero weight recovers the original function on the punctured field.
The local inverse of the Banach-algebra exponential transfers smoothness in multiplicative coordinates to smoothness in the punctured field.
Radial logarithm and angle give a cylinder, whose vector cover is the ordinary complex exponential with angular period one.
A positive exponential absorbs powers of the logarithm at the puncture. On the other end of the cylinder an ordinary Schwartz seminorm absorbs both weights.
On the cylinder the weighted Euler derivatives of a restricted test are again weighted restrictions. Each derivative is a linear vector field on the additive plane.
A nonzero analytic function is bounded away from zero on a sufficiently small circle around each point, even if it vanishes at the center.
The local standard Gaussian realizes the archimedean Euler factor on the entire positive half-plane.
A preimage of the inverse unit character contributes the positive unit mass at every exponent.
Shifted real and complex Gamma factors have no zeros. Their orders therefore equal their negative parts.
A function with an entire reciprocal which is nonzero somewhere has meromorphic order at most zero.
Extend the inverse unit character by zero as an additive Schwartz–Bruhat test.
An inverse finite Euler factor is entire and has a positive imaginary period.
A norm twist at a finite place has the imaginary period of its discrete value group.
Along a norm-twist chart, the Euler factor at a complex place is half a translate of the complex Gamma factor.
Along a norm-twist chart, the Euler factor at a real place is a translate of the real Gamma factor.
The inverse Euler factor at a finite place is periodic with respect to an imaginary translation. It is entire and not identically zero.
Every output weight of the derivative comes from the input weight one lower; the initial topology of all twists makes this a continuous endomorphism.
Assemble independently prescribed logarithmic profiles by realizing them in the full elementary stage with trivial kernel.
Elementary logarithmic coordinates on the two components of the punctured line.
Stagewise restriction assembles into a continuous linear map, since the source has the final seminorm topology and each stage is Fréchet.
Glue two elementary real-line functions on the two fibres. Each output seminorm is controlled by the maximum of the corresponding input seminorms.
If the trivial subgroup gives an admissible stage, its inclusion is surjective, so the ambient topology is induced by the joint Schwartz–Bruhat twists.
On the two logarithmic profiles of the twist at exponent \(b\), the twist of the ordinary derivative at exponent \(b+1\) acts by \(\pm(\partial_t-b)\).
Continuous forward realization from an elementary presentation; only the stage inclusion is needed, not its inverse.
Pulling back along a translate of the exponential gives an ordinary Schwartz function, continuously and linearly in the Schwartz–Bruhat test.
Exponential coordinates on either component restrict an elementary Bruhat stage of the real units to the elementary Schwartz space of a line.
Construct the derivative by untwisting at one output exponent; the coordinate identities at all exponents give both membership and continuity.
Integration by parts relates successive moments on each component of the punctured line.
Integrating from the puncture gives a compactly supported primitive when the two half-line integrals vanish.
The reciprocal Gamma function has at most a simple zero at each point.
The reciprocal Gamma function satisfies the order recursion coming from `1 / Γ(u) = u / Γ(u + 1)`.
For orders bounded below by minus one, the negative parts sum to minus the number of negative orders.
Every pole of the Gamma function is simple.
Every pole of the complex Gamma factor is simple.
Every pole of the real Gamma factor is simple.
Along a norm-twist chart, every pole of an archimedean Euler factor is simple.
Take the real and complex unit coordinates of the archimedean part.
Forgetting the units gives exactly the canonical mixed coordinates.
On finite integer units the mixed archimedean weight of exponent one is the full S-norm.
Inserting a compact shape into all weighted twists gives an archimedean flat Schwartz extension.
Compactly supported unit factors separate the archimedean lift from the finite coordinates, which contribute norm one on the support.
A nonnegative compact shape on a locally compact group can be made one at its unit.
Project the canonical norm section to the S-ideles.
Invert the scalar Fourier–Mellin transform, lift its profile, and twist the lift.
The indicator of integer units has a zero extension at a finite place.
A flat archimedean profile times the finite integer-unit indicators is polar-free.
A continuous section identifies the group with norm-one elements times positive reals.
Decompose the log of a second positive character on a norm section.
A tensor of a compact norm-one shape and an exponential-decay profile remains Schwartz after multiplying by any positive continuous character.
On a compactly supported shape, a positive weight is implemented by a compact smooth multiplier in logarithmic coordinates.
A polar-free test with trivial homogeneous theta given by a log profile has trivial-component zeta transform equal to the profile's Mellin transform.
Twisting the test by the inverse character cancels the unitary part of the zeta integral.
Uniqueness of continuation identifies the Mellin transform with the local zeta function.
Splitting the real local integral into its positive and negative rays gives the Mellin integral.
Multiplicative Tamagawa integration in real coordinates is integration against dx/|x|.
Two functions in meromorphic normal form on the plane that agree on the right half-plane agree everywhere.
A Schwartz function is `O(x^(-a))` at infinity for every `a`.
A Schwartz function is bounded near zero.
On the fundamental strip the real Tate factor has the phase and gamma quotient of (5.3.3.24), for the ordinary Euclidean Fourier transform.
The real absolute value on the units is a surjective modulation.
The positive units give a Bruhat stage. They lie in every open stage subgroup, while their intersection with each compact stage kernel is trivial.
Restrict an arbitrary stage to the positive component and realize the result in the positive stage, extending by zero on the other component.
Twice the projection onto the positive component minus the identity multiplies Schwartz–Bruhat functions by the sign.
A positive weight controls powers of the logarithmic coordinate near zero. At infinity one additional integer Schwartz weight controls the same powers.
In exponential coordinates the derivative of the weighted profile is the weighted profile of the Euler derivative plus the weight times the input.
Applying a linear map in one factor of a tensor power, conjugated by the identification, acts on pure tensors by updating that factor.
Every test with finite-coordinate vanishing at the places of `T` lies in the span of the pure tensors whose factors vanish at zero at the places of any `T' ⊆ T`.

At a selected place, subtracting the value at zero times the integer indicator gives a linear map that fixes every test vanishing where that coordinate is zero, and on a pure tensor replaces the factor by one vanishing at zero.
A submodule containing every pure tensor of an inductive tensor product with a tensor power contains the whole space.
Changing the archimedean field identifications changes each slice by a real-linear automorphism of the coordinates that keeps the walls.
In archimedean coordinates the chosen models differ from the mixed-space coordinates by a continuous real-linear equivalence.
The additive archimedean test in the chosen real and complex models is its ordinary Schwartz realization after precomposition with the model equivalence.
Multiply finite tests vanishing at zero on their compact support in the units. An algebraic projection permits using the resulting map on the ambient finite tensor factor.
In mixed coordinates the first factors in the spanning tensors are exactly the image of the embedded flat Schwartz space.

A local quasi-character is constant on a neighborhood of each finite unit. All powers of a sufficiently small principal unit lie in a neighborhood whose image in the complex units contains no nontrivial cyclic group.
An action on a spanning family restricts to its span. The multiplication identity for evaluations extends from the family by linearity.
Pull the quotient character back to the product of the archimedean units and the individual finite unit groups and take its restrictions to the factors.

On a subspace spanned by tensors with first factor in an embedded subspace, the tensor action of an endomorphism of that subspace is continuous for the inherited topology when the second factor has its finest locally convex topology.

Tensoring an inducing map with a space carrying its finest locally convex topology still detects continuity. Expand in a Hamel basis of the second factor and extend the seminorms on the first factor one coordinate at a time.
Restricting an S-adelic Schwartz–Bruhat function to an archimedean slice gives a classical Schwartz function, continuously in the S-adelic topology.
The zeta transform of a polar-free representative is Schwartz on every closed vertical strip. Translate that strip into the positive half-plane using a norm power.
Two functions in meromorphic normal form on the plane that agree on the right half-plane agree everywhere.

Agreement of two zeta functions on one chart gives agreement of their homogeneous theta functions by Lemma 5.1.2.2. The chart covers every quasicharacter with the prescribed restriction to the norm-one subgroup.
Removing the unitary character from a homogeneous theta function leaves a function of the logarithmic norm.
The S-idele quotient has the separation and countability properties used by the Schwartz–Bruhat projector on a split locally compact group.
The inverse Mellin profile of an entire Schwartz–Bergman function lifts through the trivial theta map and can then be twisted to the chosen component.
The logarithm identifies the positive-real Haar integral with the usual Mellin integral.
A character-homogeneous function has all-exponent decay exactly when its radial logarithmic profile, after removing the unitary character, does.
Schwartz–Bruhat membership of a function depending only on the norm can be checked on the positive-real norm quotient. The projector to the trivial character fixes such a function.
A homogeneous theta function with a scalar logarithmic profile has that profile’s Mellin transform on the right half-plane.
Apply the split-group decay criterion to the S-idele quotient with its proper norm.
An idelic norm section through one archimedean place gives the radial integration formula for the S-local zeta integral.

Multiplication of a polar-free representative by an S-idelic real norm power translates its entire zeta chart. On the common half-plane this follows on the integrands, and the identity theorem extends it to the whole plane.
Twisting a test by the inverse of a unitary character transports its trivial homogeneous theta function to the restricted character isotype.
Multiplication of a test by a character of the idele quotient factors that character out of the S-unit sum, since every projected diagonal S-unit has class one.
Unitary character multiplication preserves ordinary Schwartz–Bruhat membership in each direction.
An integral of a test times a unitary weight times a complex power of a positive function is entire when it converges absolutely at every exponent.
A finite-place Schwartz–Bruhat function vanishing at zero is integrable on the units against every norm power.
The zeta integrand of a polar-free test is absolutely integrable at every norm twist.
A logarithm times a power with exponent within one of σ is bounded by the powers with exponents σ - 2, σ and σ + 2.
The modulus of a norm twist of a unitary character is the corresponding real norm power.
A product over the infinite places splits into the real and the complex places.
A Schwartz–Bruhat function on a group, pulled back along a topological group isomorphism, is integrable for every Haar measure.
A ring isomorphism that is a homeomorphism has a continuous inverse.
On a pure tensor with a flat archimedean factor and finite factors vanishing at zero, the zeta integrand is absolutely integrable at every norm twist.
The reciprocal of a finite Euler factor is entire along a norm chart.
Assemble the archimedean product in the test space of the infinite adeles.
Mellin integration turns a compact unit average followed by dilation into the average of the character times the scalar dilation.
Restricting the global norm chart to a finite component gives the local norm chart.
Equality on the positive half-plane continues to equality away from a discrete set.
The local principal value multiplies the zeta integral by the inverse Euler factor.
The product of finitely many local tests belongs to the Schwartz–Bruhat space of the product group.
Tate's product formula and the tensor action of principal value give the identity on pure tests.
The integral of a character over the integer units is zero unless the character is trivial there.
Along a norm-twist chart, the restriction to an archimedean place is the restriction at exponent zero times the complex power of the local module.
Normalizing a translation difference preserves its image in a character quotient.
If representatives can be made to vanish at one additional place without changing their class, they can be made to vanish at every remaining place.
A normalized translation difference enforces vanishing on one additional ramified hyperplane while preserving the homogeneous theta class.
Finite zero-coordinate conditions can be checked one hyperplane at a time.
On a homogeneous theta class, translation by a norm-one idele acts by its character.
At a ramified place there is a norm-one unit with nontrivial character. Its dilation fixes the entire coordinate hyperplane at that place.
If multiplying an entire function by a finite Euler denominator produces rapid decay on all strips, the original function has that same strip property.
The product of the real and complex unit groups is compactly generated and locally Euclidean, so its Schwartz–Bruhat space has a full stage.
Norm-one Haar averaging removes the dependence on the representative of the fiber.
The section through a single infinite place changes no finite coordinates.
Pull the radial factor through the S-unit sum.
On finite integer units, the S-norm is the product of the real radii and squared complex radii.
A common nonnegative fiber profile produces a positive normalization independent of the radial test.
A test nonnegative on the norm-one fiber and positive at its identity has strictly positive real homogeneous theta value at the identity.
The diagonal S-units preserve each norm fiber of the S-ideles.
If all geometric moments vanish, the integral of the geometric series vanishes wherever its ratio is uniformly smaller than one on the support.
Apply Cauchy–Pompeiu at zero to the test multiplied by the next Laurent monomial. The multiplier is holomorphic on the support.
The Cauchy transform of a test annihilating the Laurent monomials vanishes near both ends of the punctured plane. Expand its kernel in the two complementary annuli.
For `c > 0`, the profile `exp(cx − eˣ)` decays polynomially at both ends of the line.
The derivative of `exp(cx − eˣ)` is `c exp(cx − eˣ) − exp((c + 1)x − eˣ)`.
Every derivative of `exp(cx − eˣ)`, for `c > 0`, decays polynomially.
The profile `exp(−x − eˣ)`, i.e. `t⁻¹ exp(−t)` in `t = eˣ`, decays at every exponent above `1`.
For `c > 0`, the profile `exp(cx − eˣ)` is a Schwartz function on the line.
Transport along a map with a right inverse, stated for bare functions so that no instance of the decay spaces has to be unified.
At the exponent `1/2` the profile `exp(−x − eˣ)` has the weighted profile `exp(−x/2 − eˣ)`, which is unbounded as `x → −∞` and so is not a Schwartz function.
The profile `exp(−x²) sin(exp(2x²))` has derivative `4x exp(x²)` wherever `exp(2x²)` is a multiple of `2π`.
For every bound there is a point beyond it where `exp(2x²)` is a multiple of `2π`.
The S-local Z-function of the zero test vanishes.
Over `ℚ` with no finite places, the trivial norm-twist line has a positive archimedean pole multiplicity at `0`.
Over `ℚ` with no finite places, the Euler factor of the twisted trivial character at the real place has a pole at `0`.
At a real place the twisted trivial S-local character has Euler factor `Γℝ`.
Over `ℚ` with no finite places, the local unit `-1` at the real place is the diagonal S-unit `-1`, so every S-local quasi-character restricts to `1` there.
A real place carries the sign quasi-character, which is `-1` at `-1`.
Every Schwartz–Bruhat function on the complex units is bounded.
The Wirtinger derivative of `|z|² exp(−|z|²)` at a real point `t` is `t (1 − t²) exp(−t²)`.
For every bound there is a small positive `t` with `t^(−1/2) (1 − t²) exp(−t²)` above it.
Nontrivial circle powers cannot all have real part greater than one half.
An elementary group has an identity neighborhood containing no nontrivial cyclic group.
A structural stage gives a common additive period in each nonarchimedean direction.
Inverse Mellin of the right-hand zeta datum recovers the actual homogeneous theta function, first on the norm section and then on every compact fiber.
Equality of absolutely convergent Mellin integrals on one vertical line determines a continuous radial profile, also after twisting by a fixed unitary character.
Evaluation is continuous by the Schwartz line description of Appendix D.
A multiplier from the left half-plane to the overlap has polynomial growth on compact substrips, by testing it on vertical translates of a Gaussian.
A holomorphic factor with polynomial growth on compact substrips acts continuously after reflection. Point evaluations give the closed graph.

A compact log profile, transported to the chosen isotype, is represented by a polar-free theta test. This is the lift used for the zero pole bound in Chapter 7, with the compact profile supplied directly.
Transport Appendix D's density of compactly supported profiles by logarithmic coordinates.
Construct the extension in the two shifted Mellin coordinates using the S-local Čech commutation and the zeta functional equation.
Restrict the family of weighted Schwartz–Bruhat conditions to a smaller interval.
The dual Tate factors are reciprocals throughout the overlap. Use the character chart calculation from the S-local zeta functional equation above.
Twisting a test by the inverse of a unitary character transports its trivial homogeneous theta function to the restricted character isotype.
Multiplication of a test by a character of the idele quotient factors that character out of the S-unit sum, since every projected diagonal S-unit has class one.
Transport an exact pair through two linear homeomorphisms; separating observations ensure uniqueness.
An isotypic function is determined by its values on the section.
Two continuous linear maps that are inverse to each other on a submodule give a continuous linear equivalence of that submodule.
The positive real with logarithm `x`.
Two functions on the S-idele classes that agree on every norm-one translate of the section agree.
An isotypic function on the S-idele classes, on the norm-one translate of a section point.
Restriction to a norm section identifies a norm-one isotype of the S-local decay space with the decay space of the positive reals.
On the S-idele classes, restriction to a norm section and the conjugate-character lift are continuous linear maps between the decay space and the decay space of the positive reals.
A function on the idele classes given on the section by the conjugate character lies in the isotype.
Reflection `p ↦ (u ↦ exp(-u) p(-u))` between decay spaces whose exponent intervals are exchanged by `a ↦ 1 - a`.

A modulated decay space with a norm section maps continuously to the decay space of the positive reals by restriction to the section, and back by tensoring with the conjugate of a compact-kernel character.
Every idele class is a norm-one class times a point of the norm section.
The value of the composite of the section equivalences and the profile reflection.
The Mellin formula for the composite of the section equivalence and the shifted Mellin equivalence, with absolute convergence.
For a decay profile and an exponent in its strip, the Haar integral of the profile against `t ^ z` converges and equals the Mellin transform of the profile.
On an open exponent interval, twisting the logarithmic profile by the frequency `x` followed by the Mellin equivalence gives the vertically shifted Mellin transform.
An automorphism preserving the norm of a dense linear image extends uniquely to a linear isometry equivalence on the completion.

Plancherel on the S-idele quotient identifies the norm in (5.4.2.1) with the Mellin norm on the critical line. The correcting factor has modulus one there, and dualizing the character preserves the Plancherel measure.
Fourier transforms with equal moduli after inversion have equal L² norms.
The Fourier transform is a linear automorphism of the S-adelic tests. Its fourth power is the identity by Fourier inversion.
Weighting the theta function by the square root of the idelic norm gives an integrable function whose ordinary L² norm is the weighted theta norm.
Holomorphic multipliers with polynomial bounds on closed substrips give continuous maps into the Schwartz–Bergman space of the overlap.
The S-local correcting factor has polynomial growth on every closed substrip of the overlap. The degree may depend on the substrip and the character.
Multiplication by the functional-equation factor and restriction to the overlap still detect a left component, by the holomorphic identity theorem.
Reflecting a closed substrip preserves rapid decay since the polynomial weights at `z` and `1 - z` bound each other up to a constant and a weight of degree zero.
On a closed positive strip, rapid decay controls the tails and continuity controls the remaining compact rectangle.
The multiplier action on one Schwartz–Bergman space is jointly continuous.
For each class, multiplication by its norm-twisted character preserves one Schwartz–Bergman space and is a continuous linear map.
A continuous linear map into a Schwartz–Bergman space given pointwise on the strip by a difference vanishes exactly where the two terms agree on the strip.
The archimedean epsilon factors have norm one, and periodicity of each finite factor gives a bound for their product on every closed strip.
On a positive half-plane both the finite Euler product and its reciprocal are bounded.
The norm powers of a nonarchimedean local character are periodic in height.
A continuous function periodic in the imaginary direction is bounded on closed strips.
On each vertical trace the strip reflection is the continuous Schwartz pullback by negation.
Reflection exchanges the two half-plane spaces, including their vertical-trace topologies.
A homogeneous function times its character is constant on norm fibers.
Compare an arbitrary quotient norm section with the canonical idelic section.
A submodule cut out by the coordinate translation law is the isotype of any action realizing inverse translation on coordinates.

A closed submodule containing every isotype of a compact abelian group is the whole space. Apply uniqueness of Fourier coefficients to a separating functional. The separation argument is the one used for the isotype sum in Chapter 6, §2.
Recover the continuous representative by dividing a Schwartz twist by its weight.
Compact radial profiles lift to tests, so homogeneous theta functions are dense in each isotype of an interval decay space.
On a pure ordinary representative, the defining identity for decay Fourier has the same Haar mass on its two sides. This recovers the ordinary Fourier representative.
Averaging an ordinary theta function already in the required isotype multiplies it by the total mass of the norm-one group.
Evaluating the ordinary Pettis average gives the unnormalized homogeneous theta function. This is the evaluation argument of Chapter 10, §1.
The square root of the norm changes the weighted L² norm to the Haar L² norm.
A nuclear Fréchet space is separable. The instances are implicit arguments, so that they are read off the hypotheses instead of being unfolded through the quotient.

A nuclear space is separable for each of its continuous seminorms (as in the private `seminorm_separable_of_nuclear` of Appendix D §1b): a totally bounded zero-neighbourhood spans the space and has separable span.
On the left half-plane the pole cancellation conditions are closed in the Bergman topology, since each is a finite collection of vanishing jets.
The Schwartz-line realization of a Bergman function makes each complex jet continuous.

A continuous injection from the quotient of a closed submodule of a strict LF-space into a Fréchet space is a closed embedding when its range is closed. The open mapping theorem is applied using the closed intersections with the Fréchet stages.
In normal form, agreeing on the right half-plane with an entire function forces the meromorphic continuation to equal that function everywhere.
Agreement on the convergence half-plane identifies an entire extension with the zeta function in meromorphic normal form.

The polar-free range is exactly the part of the ordinary zeta range with the left pole cancellation conditions. This uses the polar-free representative theorem of §5.3 for the entire normalized continuation.
On a test the two ordinary zeta components agree by the Tate relation on the overlap.
The real vertical trace differentiates by one factor of I at each step.
A continuous function on the S-idele class group that vanishes almost everywhere for the norm-weighted Tamagawa measure vanishes identically.
A continuous linear map into the weighted L² space that represents every theta class kills the theta kernel.
The continuous linear map induced on a quotient by a continuous linear map whose kernel contains the subspace.
The induced map agrees with the original one on representatives.
A continuous linear map out of a quotient is determined by its values on representatives.
The half-weight theta function is integrable by absolute convergence of its Mellin integral. The two theta estimates bound it pointwise, hence it is also in L².
The L² norm for a measure with a real density is the square root of the weighted integral of the squared absolute value of any representative.
The theta test map is continuous into the weighted L² space, and its class is the almost-everywhere class of the theta function of the test.
The S-local theta kernel is exactly the kernel of the theta class function.
A linear map between Fréchet spaces is continuous if it is continuous after a continuous linear injection into a Hausdorff function space.
Every matching pair has its first Bergman datum realized by an S-local test. Realize the principal parts using the reflected Fourier datum, then lift the entire remainder by Fourier–Mellin inversion.
Rescale the gamma multiplier for the affine argument of a real or complex Euler factor.

At large height on the left of the critical line, clearing the finite Euler denominators bounds the Tate factor. The reflected gamma ratio has nonpositive growth exponent there. The estimate holds away from its discrete exceptional set.
Outside a compact transition interval, each weighted smooth cutoff is either zero or a decaying exponential. All its derivatives are bounded.

Clear the archimedean factors with the periodic gamma multipliers and the finite factors with their Euler polynomials. The resulting multiplier is bounded on strips, bounded away from zero on positive strips, and cancels the full pole divisor of ρ.

Fourier–Mellin inversion and the radial lift of Lemma 5.3.4.3 realize an entire Schwartz–Bergman datum on any unitary chart. The radial integral calculation is from `polarFree_zeta_of_radial` and `polarFree_zeta_twist` in §5.3.
The finite Euler denominators used to estimate a pole-free remainder have imaginary periods. This is the periodicity calculation of §5.3, `finiteEulerInverse_periodic`.
Assemble the finitely many periodic multipliers and their holomorphic products with the local Euler factors. Bounds multiply even for incommensurable periods.
At every nonpositive integer the gamma recurrence removes the pole after multiplication by the local coordinate.

The entire function `1/Γ(1-2⁻ᵘ)` clears every gamma pole. At `u = -n` its argument is the nonpositive integer `1-2ⁿ`. In the positive half-plane `|2⁻ᵘ| < 1`, so it has no zeros there. Its imaginary period supplies bounds on vertical strips.

A bounded entire multiplier without small values on closed positive strips allows one to interpolate left data modulo that multiplier. Split the quotient on the overlap, multiply both pieces back, and glue the two expressions for the interpolant.
Bounds for a single periodic denominator. Above a positive abscissa, clamp the real part before taking its reciprocal to obtain a continuous periodic function on the plane.

Interpolate the reflected Fourier datum modulo a multiplier clearing all Tate poles. Fourier inversion of the test realizing this entire interpolant matches the principal parts at every pole simultaneously.
Glue the right component to the corrected left component. Removing the poles in meromorphic normal form produces an entire function with the original right restriction.
Split the inverse Mellin profile by a smooth partition of unity in log norm. The negative tail has all positive weights and the positive tail has all weights below one.

An entire continuation of a matching pair decays rapidly even on strips crossing the poles of the Tate factor. Estimate the cleared product, then divide out each periodic denominator by the maximum modulus principle of §5.3.
A norm twist of the chosen lift reaches every character with the same restriction. This is the split-norm argument of `exists_normTwist_of_agree_on_ker` in §5.2b.
Vanishing of the first component forces vanishing on the whole character component by meromorphic uniqueness, and hence vanishing of the homogeneous theta class.

A linear bijection from an LF-space to a Fréchet space is a homeomorphism if a separating family of linear evaluations is continuous on both sides. Factor the inverse through one LF stage in the space of evaluations, then use open mapping.
The range description identifies the image with a closed kernel in a product of Fréchet spaces.
The first component separates matching pairs by the functional equation and holomorphic uniqueness on the left half-plane.
Conversely, every matching pair is the zeta pair of a homogeneous theta class.

Once the first Bergman datum of a matching pair is realized by a test, the pair is the zeta pair of that test's theta class: the second component agrees with the reflected Fourier datum on the overlap by the functional equation, hence on its whole half-plane.

A linear family of pointwise continuous evaluations gives a continuous map into L² on a Fréchet stage whenever each representative belongs to L². Fatou's lemma makes the norm lower semicontinuous, so barrelledness gives continuity.
A norm-frequency lift shifts the reflected Fourier coordinate by the positive frequency.
A Schwartz–Bergman function constant on a vertical line vanishes there.
The rational Gaussian has a strictly positive radial Mellin integral at one quarter.
A strictly positive integrable real function has nonzero complex integral.
Functions in the Schwartz–Bruhat submodule are bounded.
Exponential decay with a smooth cutoff on the left is a Schwartz bound.
The constant function one is a Schwartz–Bruhat function on a compact group (as `compact_schwartzBruhat_one` in `AppD_SchwartzBruhat/Sec2b.lean`).
The logarithmic profile of `t ↦ t⁻¹ ψ(log t)`, with `ψ` a smooth step from `0` to `1`, decays after every exponential twist with exponent below one.
A radial function with profile `t ↦ t⁻¹ ψ(log t)` lies in the decay space with exponents below one, by the tensor splitting of Theorem D.3.3.7(1).
A function in the decay space with exponents below one cannot equal `ψ(−log t)` along a section: its twist by `t⁻¹` would be unbounded.
Integration against the additive Tamagawa measure scales by the idelic norm under multiplication by an inverse idele.
The Gaussian-normalized global family vanishes on zero theta tests on the convergence half-plane, hence on every norm chart by analytic continuation.
Point-separating functionals on a Montel space span its strong dual densely, since every separating strong-bidual functional is evaluation at a vector.
Evaluating a holomorphic family of continuous functionals at a point gives an entire function.
An entire function vanishing on a set with an accumulation point vanishes identically.
Two norm charts for the same quasi-character have the same norm-one restriction, and hence the same standard Gaussian.
Every S-local quasi-character lies on the norm-twist chart of a unitary character.
Removing the real power prescribed by the abscissa leaves a unitary character.
Applying the test projection to a dense eigenfamily selects exactly the weights with the prescribed restriction to the subgroup.
A continuous projection carries a dense generating family to a dense family in its closed fixed subspace.
Normalized compact averaging on tests induces a projection on functionals with prescribed weight. Both action conventions are recorded explicitly.
Point-separating functionals on a Montel space span its strong dual densely, since every separating strong-bidual functional is evaluation at a vector.
Convergent multiplicative integrals separate finite-place tests: character uniqueness recovers the test off zero, and continuity recovers its value at zero.
A split quotient has an embedded strong transpose; composing with an already embedded transpose preserves this property.
Specialize the common-kernel criterion to the Montel space of adelic tests.
On a norm chart, the normalized functional vanishes on a test exactly when its meromorphic zeta function vanishes identically.
The homogeneous global theta kernel is the common kernel of normalized functionals whose norm-one restriction is the prescribed character.
In a Montel space, a family with common kernel `K` generates the same strongly closed subspace as the transpose of the quotient by `K`.
Norm twisting leaves the norm-one restriction of a global character unchanged.
In the convergence half-plane the global zeta function is the Gaussian zeta factor times the globally normalized functional.
On representatives, evaluation at zero is unchanged by unit translation.
On representatives, Fourier evaluation at zero scales by the idelic norm under unit translation.
An invariant surjection to two scalars stays surjective on the fixed subspace, by dividing the compact average by its nonzero Haar mass.
A functional component on a quotient scales by `c` under an action given on representatives by `t`, when it does so on representatives.
Two continuous linear maps on a quotient module are equal when they agree on the classes of all representatives.
The vanishing criterion on norm-one isotypes, for any action and pair of functionals with the weights of Lemma 5.5.2.1 and the range on the trivial isotype.
Vanishing normalized evaluations force the global zeta integral to vanish at exponent two: there it is the Gaussian factor times the normalized eigendistribution.
A continuous linear map with closed range that sends a family with dense span onto another family has the closed span of the second family as its range.
Character uniqueness on the convergent line `Re s = 2` separates global theta classes.
Global theta of a unit translate is theta at the inversely translated idele class.
Global theta is invariant under translation by a principal-class unit.
The homogeneous global theta transform multiplies by `ω g` under a unit translate representing `g`.
Applying the test projection to a dense eigenfamily selects exactly the weights with the prescribed restriction to the subgroup.
A continuous projection carries a dense generating family to a dense family in its closed fixed subspace.
Real and complex Schwartz coordinates give continuous unit-translation orbits at every infinite place.
A surjective continuous Schwartz parametrization transfers continuity of linear-change-of-variables orbits to Schwartz–Bruhat tests.
Normalized compact averaging on tests induces a projection on functionals with prescribed weight. Both action conventions are recorded explicitly.
Point-separating functionals on a Montel space span its strong dual densely, since every separating strong-bidual functional is evaluation at a vector.
Character uniqueness recovers an infinite-place test off zero, and continuity recovers its value at zero.
Vanishing on every infinite-place eigendistribution forces all convergent Mellin integrals on the line of real part one to vanish.
Pullback values along a quotient map are related by `c` when the representatives are related by `c` modulo the kernel.
Pullback along the quotient by the kernel of a linear map `θ` takes equal values on representatives with equal images under `θ`.
Pullback along the quotient by the kernel of a linear map `θ` multiplies by `c` when `θ` does.
Zero theta gives zero normalized zeta values on the convergence half-plane, and analytic continuation gives zero values on the entire norm chart.
A functional in the line generated by a kernel-annihilating functional has one continuous quotient lift, uniquely determined on representatives.
A pointwise continuous map from a Fréchet space into a strict LF-space of functions factors continuously through a stage, when the inclusion into functions is continuous.
Equality of continuous functionals on pure tests implies equality on all tests. Use the uniqueness of the convergent zeta integral applied to its translate by U − V.
Split off each local factor of a homogeneous functional. The function `b` collects the test factors at the other places and is fixed by these local units.
Haar invariance gives the weight on the convergence half-plane. Analytic continuation of the normalized zeta value gives the same equation at every point of the chart.
Varying a single factor of a product test is continuous. Point evaluations are continuous on elementary stages, and the S-local test space is strict LF.
The pure S-local test built from the placewise tests.
Along one norm chart, zero normalized evaluations imply zero convergent integrals at every positive exponent, including the discrete exceptional Euler-factor points.
The homogeneous theta kernel is the common kernel of the normalized functionals in its norm-one character component.
In a Montel space, a family with common kernel `K` generates the same strongly closed subspace as the transpose of the quotient by `K`.
Norm twisting does not change the norm-one restriction.
Pullback along a quotient map of topological vector spaces is injective on continuous linear functionals, because the quotient map is surjective.
A pointwise holomorphic family of functionals on a barrelled space consists of continuous linear functionals throughout a connected open set if it does so in a neighborhood of one point.
On a Montel space, pointwise holomorphy of a family in the complete strong dual implies strong holomorphy, since every bidual functional is an evaluation.
Vanishing normalized evaluations force the convergent Mellin integral to vanish at exponent one, using nonvanishing of the Euler product off a discrete set.
Character uniqueness applied to the convergent radial line separates theta classes before any density theorem is used.
The S-local theta function on classes of a unit translate is the theta function on classes at the inversely translated class.
S-local theta of a unit translate is theta at the inversely translated S-idele.
At a field with one complex place, the Gaussian already contradicts the first coordinate.
An archimedean test with value one at one that vanishes at every rational at distance at least `1/2` from one.
Norm twists of a fixed quasi-character along a segment form a connected set.
A rational S-integer for `S = {v}` that is integral at `v` has denominator one.
The indicator of `1 + 5𝒪` at a finite place of `ℚ`.
A rational number is integral in the completion at `v` exactly when the prime of `v` does not divide its denominator.
An S-integer whose twisted 5-adic coordinate lies in `1 + 5𝒪` and whose real coordinate is near one is one.
The free Laurent generator and the uniformizer translation give every ball indicator: the monomial of exponent n goes to the ball of exponent n.
Pointwise averages that descend to the quotient and act by a nonzero mass on fixed vectors identify the quotient with the fixed space, provided every class has a fixed representative.
The normalized sum over a finite orbit is a fixed representative of its coinvariant class.
A fixed class has a fixed lift when the orbit of a representative is finite.
Two elements of the same valuation are related by a local integral unit, including the zero fiber.
Charts for an open homomorphism on the connected components that meet its image. Unlike the open quotient charts, the homomorphism need not be surjective.
Test elementary Schwartz membership on a common source with open maps into the two elementary groups, allowing extension by zero off the second image.
If samples can be lifted continuously on each stage, injectivity of the sampling map on the target makes the lifts compatible and gives a continuous lift on the whole space.
On the finite exponent box, express each point indicator in the basis of upper-set indicators. The same coefficients interpolate the samples outside the box by stabilization.
