On zero-moment tests the principal value multiplies the global zeta function by the reciprocal Euler product at every point: both sides are entire, and they agree off a discrete set.

A zero of the reciprocal Euler product over unramified places lies on the imaginary axis: there the norm twist takes the value one on the class of a uniformizer, and the norm of that class differs from one.
In the Mellin model of the decay isotype, the homogeneous theta function of a zero-moment test has the global zeta function of the test as its transform.

The homogeneous theta function of the principal value of a zero-moment test is the difference product, over a set of unramified places carrying the same reciprocal Euler product, of the homogeneous theta function of the test: the two have the same transform in the Mellin model of the decay isotype.

Translation of an isotypic function along a right inverse of the norm multiplies its Mellin integral by the value of the Mellin character at the translating element. It repeats `strongCoprimality_bezout_translate`, which is declared after `strongCoprimality`.

A topological linear embedding with closed range into a Fréchet space induces a topological linear isomorphism of quotients, once the target quotient is Fréchet, the source denominator is the preimage of the target one, and every target class meets the range.
Applying each coordinate functional to a finite relation gives its coefficient.
Over ℚ every primary set is a singleton, and the trivial character keeps its difference.
A quotient of a closed subspace of a finite product of rapid sequence spaces is Baire.
The quotient by a single expanding difference has infinitely many Fourier modes.
At exponent zero, the reciprocal Euler factor of the trivial character vanishes.
A test nonzero at zero gives a reflected Fourier zeta function that is not analytic at one.
The trivial character has value one on every local unit.
The trivial character is unramified at every finite place.
Multiplying a Bruhat `Cᵖ` function by a smooth function of a continuous real-valued homomorphism keeps it Bruhat `Cᵖ`, with the same good subgroup.
A unitary character of the idele classes times a smooth compactly supported function of the logarithm of the norm is a compactly supported Bruhat test.
A continuous homomorphism into the reals kills every compact subgroup.
On each fiber of an elementary group, a smooth function of a real-valued continuous homomorphism is smooth in the cover coordinates.
The class of the idele equal to `-1` at one finite place and `1` elsewhere is nontrivial: a principal idele with archimedean component one is one.
The archimedean coordinates of the origin assemble to the origin.
The origin of the archimedean coordinates lies on a coordinate hyperplane.
Over ℂ, `a ⊗ y = 0` with `a ≠ 0` forces `y = 0`.

The finite-place evaluation functionals on the finite tensor factor, and the value of an S-adelic test through the tensor decomposition: it is the contraction of its finite factor at `y`, evaluated at `x`.
Contracting the right factor commutes with a linear map on the left factor.
Over ℂ, a tensor whose contractions against a separating family of functionals on the right factor all vanish is zero.

The archimedean slice of an S-adelic test at a fixed finite coordinate is a classical Schwartz function, continuously in the S-adelic topology. Same construction as the private `sAdelePolarFree_slice` of Ch05 Sec3b, here for the coordinates of §5.3.3.
A test vanishing wherever a finite coordinate in `R` is zero lies in the finite zero subspace for `R`.
On each finite fibre, a restricted test is archimedean-flat in the coordinates of §5.3.3.
A restricted test vanishes wherever a finite coordinate outside T is zero.
A flat archimedean test that does not vanish identically.
Nontrivial circle powers cannot all have real part greater than one half.

The displayed tensor inclusion fails as soon as one selected finite place carries a full multiplicative factor: a geometric shell test there has a zero extension that is not locally constant at the origin, while every S-adelic test is.
Over any number field there are a finite set of finite places with trivial Picard group, a rational prime whose whole fibre it contains, and two of its members only one of which lies over that prime.
An elementary group has an identity neighborhood containing no nontrivial cyclic group.
The geometric sequence on the nonnegative integers is a Schwartz function on ℤ.
A discrete valuation with compact open kernel carries a Schwartz–Bruhat test with geometric values on the powers of a uniformizing element.
A structural stage gives a common additive period in each nonarchimedean direction.

An S-adelic test cannot be a product whose factor at one finite place vanishes at the origin and is nonzero along a sequence tending to the origin, when the other factors are nonzero at a common point: it is invariant under small translations of that coordinate.
A finite-place multiplicative Schwartz test with geometric values on the powers of a uniformizing element, over any number field.
An S-adelic test is invariant under all small translations of a finite coordinate.
Powers staying in a small identity neighborhood force membership in the stage kernel.
A stage realization is invariant under translation by its kernel.
The trivial idele class character is unramified outside every finite set of places.
Over ℚ the difference of a bump that is one near the origin and any of its dilates is a flat archimedean test: it vanishes near the origin, the only point of the coordinate hyperplanes.
Evaluation at zero descends to the homogeneous theta space at a stage `T` for an unramified norm-one character, through the insertion into the global homogeneous space.
A test on the archimedean factor whose mixed-coordinate form is flat along the coordinate hyperplanes is a flat archimedean test.
A test in the kernel of global homogeneous theta for the trivial character vanishes at zero: after the polar term the homogeneous theta function is small at small norm.
The local principal value of a test vanishes at zero.

The repaired comparison over ℚ with one selected prime is not injective. For a test `H` with value one at the origin, the difference of `H` and its radial translate of norm `1/N(p)` is a restricted test whose theta class is the principal value of the class of `H`, so it maps to zero. Were its class zero, it would be the principal value of the class of a restricted test `g`; the principal value is injective on theta classes, so `H - g` would lie in the theta kernel, and evaluation at the origin would give `1 = 0`.

The repaired comparison over ℚ with a nonempty set of selected primes, all of them taken for the principal value, is not surjective. Evaluation at the origin vanishes on the theta kernel of the trivial character, on the restricted tests and on principal values, so the class of a test that is nonzero at the origin is missed.
On the trivial norm-one component every quasi-character is a bare norm power.
Over ℚ the S-local norm-one character of the trivial character is trivial.
On the trivial singleton-stage quotient the principal value is injective on theta classes: its Euler multiplier does not vanish on the right half-plane.
The S-local principal value vanishes at every point whose coordinate at a selected place is zero.
On a bare norm chart the singleton Euler factor is the reciprocal of the translation-difference multiplier.
The Euler multiplier identifies PV on the trivial singleton-stage quotient with the identity minus translation by any idele of norm 1/N(p).
A pure tensor with flat archimedean factor is a restricted test when every finite place is selected.
Every restricted test vanishes at the origin, because its archimedean factor is flat.
Translating a product test by an S-idele with trivial finite coordinates only translates its archimedean factor, so the difference with the translate is again a product test.
An S-adelic test with value one at the origin.

A test with value one at the origin whose difference with its translate by an S-idele with trivial finite coordinates is a restricted test: the archimedean factor is constant near the origin, so the difference of the two archimedean factors vanishes there.
Every point of the full orbit has a norm-one transporter into the half-open section.
A global idele fixes the base point at a finite place exactly when it is inserted at that place.
Two norm-one transporters into the half-open section differ by an embedded local unit.
At an infinite place the global norm-one stabilizer of an orbit point consists of the ideles inserted at that place with a unit of norm one.
A global idele fixes the base point at an infinite place exactly when it is inserted at that place.
The coordinates of a base point are zero at its own place and one elsewhere.
Two base points in the same idele orbit are equal.
The coordinates of a unit adele are nonzero.
The saturation of an open set under the norm-one orbit relation is open.

The special adeles form a closed subset of the adele ring. A point outside it either has a coordinate outside `{0, 1}` or two coordinates different from one; both conditions are open and exclude every special adele. A point with neither property is special.

The adele ring is second countable. The finite adeles are covered by countably many open sets, each consisting of the adeles that are integral outside a finite set of places, and each of these embeds into the countable product of the second countable local fields.
The finite places of a number field form a countable set, since every prime ideal is finitely generated over the countable ring of integers.

The adele ring is metrizable. The infinite part is a finite product of metrizable completions. The finite part is second countable and weakly locally compact (the integer subrings are compact open), hence regular; with T0 this gives T3, and Urysohn's metrization theorem applies.
The S-adele ring is metrizable: a finite product of metrizable completions of `F`, routed through the definition as for `t2Space_sAdeleRing`.
Every point of the full S-local orbit has a norm-one transporter into the half-open section.
The idele inserted at a finite place has the norm of the inserted unit.
The norm of a unit at a finite place is an integer power of the absolute norm.
The projection of an idele inserted at a finite place of S has the same S-norm as global norm.
An S-idele fixes the S-local base point at a finite place of S exactly when it is the projection of an idele inserted at that place.
A uniformizer at a finite place, as a unit, with norm the reciprocal of the absolute norm.
Two S-local norm-one transporters into the half-open section differ by the projection of an embedded local unit.
At an infinite place the S-local norm-one stabilizer of an orbit point consists of the projected ideles inserted at that place with a unit of norm one.
The idele inserted at an infinite place has norm one exactly when the inserted unit has norm one.
The projected idele inserted at an infinite place has S-norm one exactly when the inserted unit has norm one.
An S-idele fixes the S-local base point at an infinite place exactly when it is the projection of an idele inserted at that place.
At a real place the units of norm one are the two signs.
The S-local orbit map is continuous.
The S-local orbit map is open.
The coordinates of an S-local base point: zero at its own place and one elsewhere.
An S-adele whose coordinates are all nonzero is a unit.
The coordinates of an S-idele are nonzero.
Near any point of the orbit of a base point, every point of the S-local union is the translate of that base point by a norm-one S-idele lying in any given neighborhood of the original one.

Near a point of the orbit of the base point at an infinite place `w₀`, every point of the S-local union is the translate of that base point by a norm-one S-idele lying in any given neighborhood of the original one. The coordinate at `w₀` is rescaled by a positive real close to one, chosen to bring the S-norm back to one.

Near a point of the orbit of the base point at a finite place `v₀`, every point of the S-local union is the translate of that base point by a norm-one S-idele lying in any given neighborhood of the original one. The coordinate at `v₀` can be kept, because the norm of a finite completion changes by a factor of at least two.
Near a norm-one S-idele, every point of the S-local union is a norm-one S-idele lying in any given neighborhood: the S-ideles are open in the S-adeles, and the other orbits have a zero coordinate.
The S-idelic norm is the product of the normalized local norms.
A point of the S-local union with no zero coordinate other than at `c`, and with norm product less than one, lies in the orbit of the base point at `c`.
A point of the S-local union with no zero coordinate is a norm-one S-idele.
The S-local orbit map is surjective.
The domain of the S-local orbit map is locally compact: the norm-one S-ideles are a closed subgroup of the locally compact S-ideles, and the base points are finitely many.
The S-idelic norm is continuous: it is a finite product of powers of coordinate norms.
The norm-one subgroup of the S-ideles is σ-compact: it is closed in the S-idele group, which is locally compact and second countable.
The S-adele ring is second countable: each infinite completion embeds isometrically in the complex numbers, and each finite completion is a proper metric space.
The index `none` gives the ordinary base point, since the projection is a ring hom.

A restricted product over a countable index type, with open distinguished subsets, is second countable: the pieces where the coordinates lie in the distinguished subsets outside a fixed finite set form a countable open cover by second countable subspaces.
The S-adele ring is second countable: the archimedean completions embed isometrically into `ℂ`, and the finite completions in `S` are proper metric spaces.

The S-adele ring is Hausdorff: it is a product of Hausdorff completions of `F`. The instance has to be routed through the definition, exactly as in `AppA_AlgebraicNT/Sec1.lean` (`adeleHausdorff_ideleLocallyCompact`).
The base point with zero at an infinite place of ℚ has zero there and finite part 1.
A base point whose coordinate at the given infinite place differs from 1 has zero there and finite part 1.
The orbit map pulls the set of points with zero coordinate at the given infinite place and finite components of valuation 1 back to an open set.
Replacing the finite part of the real-zero base point by a finite adele with nonzero components, almost all of valuation 1, gives a point of the norm-one orbit union.
A neighbourhood of an integral finite adele contains every integral finite adele that agrees with it on a suitable finite set of places.
Each completion of ℚ at a finite place has a nonzero element of valuation below 1.
Every point of the norm-one orbit union over ℚ has finite components of valuation 1 at almost all places.
Evaluation of differential operators on a character's eigenline is an algebra homomorphism.
The logarithm of the positive modulation is continuous.

For a surjective modulation and any Haar measure, a continuous function of the logarithm of the module is integrable on the group exactly when it is Lebesgue integrable on the real line: the canonical Haar measure is the kernel's probability Haar measure times `dt/t`, and `dt/t` is the exponential image of Lebesgue measure.
On the real line, `|u|^(2k) (1 + |u|²)^(-s/2)` is Lebesgue integrable exactly when `2k + 1 < s`.
The Fourier transform of an integrable square-integrable function on the dual, evaluated at the canonical characters of the bidual, preserves its L² norm.
A translation of the bidual evaluation has the same Plancherel norm, since translation of a Fourier transform multiplies its input by a unit-modulus character.

The inverse Fourier integral and the forward transform are adjoint on integrable test functions. Compactly supported approximations provide a product-measurable kernel even when the product topology and product σ-algebra have different Borel sets.
For an L² element whose Plancherel transform is integrable, the inverse Fourier integral represents that element and vanishes at infinity.
Multiplication by a bounded continuous function is a bounded operator on Haar `L²`.
The powers of any nonconstant affine function of the log modulation give a topological embedding of the degree-`2N` Sobolev space into a finite product of L² spaces.
On compactly supported smooth data, differentiation on the Fourier side amounts to multiplication by the differential symbol evaluated at the inverse bidual character.
A single algebra generator on the dual has a symbol affine in the logarithm of the modulation, with nonzero slope. Its powers act by the corresponding symbol powers.
Left translation is a jointly continuous representation on a modulated Sobolev space.
Multiplication by the logarithmic bracket identifies a modulated Sobolev space with Haar `L²`.
Raising the shifted bracket to any real power costs only a constant depending on the shift.

decls.deviation: This proof assumes a second-countable group and an available Plancherel measure. The Fourier isometries on two distinct cosets would give a nonzero integrable density on their disjoint union with every character integral equal to zero.
decls.summary: Evaluation identifies the group with its bidual.
An integrable Schwartz–Bruhat function is square-integrable, since its stage bounds include the unweighted supremum norm.
Pointwise comparison with the Sobolev density bounds each power multiplier and recovers the weighted norm from the zeroth and highest powers.
The unweighted product pairing identifies the strong dual of a weighted L² space with the weighted L² space of opposite degree, for any continuous weight on a Borel space.
Cauchy–Schwarz with the density and its reciprocal controls the unweighted integral of the norm of a Fourier-side Sobolev element.
An integrable function on the real line whose Fourier transform vanishes identically is zero almost everywhere: pair it with the Fourier transforms of Schwartz functions.
The compact-interval density is continuous.
The line density is continuous.
For a nonnegative degree, the compact-interval density dominates the exponential of its upper endpoint.
The line density dominates its exponential factor.

For a Haar measure, a decaying exponential of the logarithmic module is integrable on the part of the group where the logarithmic module is bounded below: translation by an element of nontrivial module moves one compact band onto the next.

If a continuous functional on the compact-interval space evaluates the Mellin derivative of each test supported in an open set, then the squared moment kernel is integrable on that set against the reciprocal density: the functional is integration against a class of the dual space, and this class agrees with the kernel almost everywhere on the set.
A power of `|x|` times a decaying exponential of `|x|` is integrable.
Every exponential moment of an exponential-decay profile is integrable.
The square of a Schwartz function is integrable against every real power of `1 + x ^ 2`.
A class that agrees almost everywhere with a test profile vanishing outside `U` has the Mellin derivative of the profile as its moment against the kernel cut off to `U`.
The compact-interval density is positive.
On a right half-line the supremum over pairs of abscissas equals the supremum over pairs whose first abscissa is the left endpoint.
On a left half-line the supremum over pairs of abscissas equals the supremum over pairs whose second abscissa is the right endpoint.
At an abscissa of the base interval and above the critical degree, the moment kernel cut off to a measurable set gives a continuous functional on the compact-interval space.
On supported tests the Mellin derivative evaluation at an endpoint abscissa extends continuously exactly below the upper endpoint or above the critical degree.
Below the upper endpoint, the moment kernel cut off above a point gives a continuous functional on the compact-interval space.
On the open strip of a compact base interval, each moment of a weighted L² class against a real exponential is integrable.
The moment kernel, cut off to a measurable set on which the endpoint exponentials dominate it exponentially, gives a continuous functional on the compact-interval space.
Differentiation under the integral sign for exponential moments on the real line with Lebesgue measure.

Differentiation under the integral sign for the norm twists of a quasi-character: if every logarithmic moment against the real twists in an open interval is integrable, then the twisted integral is holomorphic on the strip, and its `k`th derivative is the `k`th moment.
To the left of the line, every moment kernel cut off above a point gives a continuous functional on the line space.
Two-sided exponential bounds on the tails absorb any real twist and any logarithmic moment. Properness bounds the remaining compact band.
The Mellin transform of a profile in the logarithmic coordinate is its two-sided exponential integral.
A continuous seminorm bound by an integrable majorant gives the weighted L² inclusion. The local test criterion supplies its dense range.
Cut off a Schwartz–Bruhat test in the log coordinate. Every real twist of the resulting function is again Schwartz–Bruhat.
Local tests and their character multiples determine the supported part of weighted L².
Over the full exponent line, the Fourier–Mellin integral is the integral against the quasi-character.

Above a cutoff of the logarithmic module, the moment kernel of a unitary quasi-character twisted to an abscissa below `b` gives a continuous functional on the weighted L² space of a Haar measure, for every density that dominates `exp (2 * b * x)`.
A nontrivial modulus tiles the log axis by translates of one compact band.
The squared modulus of the moment kernel.
The norm twist of a quasi-character is the quasi-character times the exponential of the logarithmic module.
On the upper tail the reciprocal weight supplies either exponential decay or an integrable power. At the critical power the latter argument requires a strict inequality.
Each fixed twist has a continuous uniform bound. At a compact-quotient stage the bound follows from the corresponding Schwartz–Bruhat seminorm on the quotient.
Below the abscissa `b`, the squared moment kernel divided by a number that dominates `exp (2 * b * x)` decays exponentially on a half-line that is bounded below.
On the half-line where the exponential of an endpoint abscissa is the larger endpoint weight, the squared moment kernel divided by the density is a quotient of powers.
For an abscissa in the base interval, the squared moment kernel divided by the compact-interval density is at most a quotient of powers.
Differentiating the real twist adds a scalar multiple of the original polar test to its adelic directional derivative. Both terms belong to the polar subspace.
The archimedean units have an identity neighborhood containing no nontrivial subgroup.
Lift an idele-class direction through the covering by ideles.
Each real or integer coordinate on the quotient is a real homomorphism. When they factor through one logarithmic coordinate, its moment bounds control every coordinate monomial.

On an elementary quotient, descend just those family members which are constant on the fibres. Differentiating the invariance identity keeps every derivative in this subfamily. The same derivative index works across all discrete fibres of the elementary cover.
Every sufficiently small finite idele fixes an adelic test under dilation.

Realize a kernel-invariant function on a single elementary stage of a group split over the positive reals. Compactness of the norm kernel controls the polynomial weights, and one - parameter subgroups lift through the compact structural kernel.
Reparametrize the positive-real theta difference quotient by exponential time.
Lift a sufficiently small compact structural kernel through a locally injective open quotient. Its lifted points can all be chosen inside the prescribed neighborhood.
Choose a compact structural kernel which acts trivially on the theta sum. Its lifts have trivial archimedean component and stabilize the finite part of the test.
The unweighted product pairing identifies the strong dual of a weighted L² space with the L² space for the reciprocal density.

The moment kernel `x ^ k * exp (z * x)`, cut off to a measurable set on which a continuous positive density dominates it exponentially, gives a continuous functional on the weighted L² space of that density.
A pointwise comparison of squared multipliers gives a contraction between weighted L² spaces, with the stated representatives in the original measure.
In weighted L², the squared norm is the integral of the squared modulus against the density.
Integration against a kernel whose square is integrable against the reciprocal density is a continuous functional on a weighted L² space, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
The abscissas `(−1)ⁿ (1 − 1/(n+2))` accumulate at both ends of `[−1, 1]`.
The abscissas `(−1)ⁿ (1 − 1/(n+2))` lie in `(−1, 1)`, left of `1`.
The Gaussian has finite L² norm on every vertical line.
The Gaussian has nonzero L² norm on every vertical line.
On the line of abscissa `σ`, the `m`-th tilted Gaussian has `exp(m(σ − 1))` times the L² norm of the Gaussian.
The tilted Gaussians `exp(m(z − 1) + z²)` are entire test functions.
If all sampled abscissas lie left of `1` and only order zero is used, the tilted Gaussians `exp(m(z − 1) + z²)` tend to zero in the sampled topology.
A modulated cutoff has compact support when the modulation is proper.
Approximate a compact kernel first by a character polynomial times a smooth log cutoff, then approximate the cutoff by band-limited log profiles in the Schwartz topology.
Operator-norm approximation of compact kernels transfers a shrinking unit-mass family to a uniformly bounded strong approximate identity.
Averaging translated kernels is contractive on operators. On matching input eigenvectors the character cancels and the average acts as the original convolution.
On a compact set of group elements a jointly continuous action carries a bounded family of vectors to a family bounded for each continuous seminorm.

Convolution with a continuous compactly supported kernel preserves each finite order of Bruhat differentiability. All translations in its support can be computed inside one larger compactly generated open subgroup.
Multiplication by a unitary character acts continuously in the character on each fixed L² vector, preserving its norm.
Uniformly approximating two kernels on a common compact support controls the difference of their integrated operators.
A compact set of frequencies with a fixed restriction to the kernel lies in a bounded interval in the corresponding real frequency line.
The scalar convolution pairing determines composition of the integrated operators by separation by the continuous dual.
A finite weighted average of translates of a Cᵖ function is Cᵖ when the translations and coefficients range over a compact parameter set.
A single twist expresses point evaluation as a continuous Schwartz evaluation.
The Hardy–Sobolev density on a compact base interval is continuous.
The logarithm of the module is continuous.

An orbitwise Pettis action is continuous for uniform convergence on bounded sets. On each fixed-support stage its mapping seminorms are controlled by the zero-order Schwartz seminorm times the Haar mass of the support.
On a compactly supported continuous representative, translation is continuous in L² for any locally finite measure. Near a fixed translate a single compact set contains all the translated supports.

Compact Fourier support is dense in the Schwartz topology on the positive real group. In logarithmic frequency coordinates this is the usual density of compactly supported Schwartz functions on the real line.
The restrictions of group characters span a dense subspace of the continuous functions on any compact subset.
On an elementary group, lift the torus parameter to a bounded fundamental cube and sum over the finitely many discrete fibers in the averaging set.
Testing a positive Pettis integral by a continuous functional gives the ordinary scalar integral.
Forgetting a larger measure preserves representatives in the smaller L² space.
Reindex a sequence with arbitrary finite bandwidths to fit the prescribed integer bandwidth, starting once the first member fits.
Character multiplication of a profile on the modulus is a continuous linear map on Schwartz–Bruhat spaces.
Point evaluations on the decay space recover the convolution represented by the orbitwise Pettis integral.
Continuous point evaluations as elements of the strong dual.
The characters trivial on the compact kernel form an open real line. Its coordinate is normalized so the character at t is exp(i t log m).
A surjective modulation admits a section over all positive reals.
Composition with inversion is an isometric isomorphism between the square-integrable classes of two measures that inversion exchanges.
The inverse base character times arbitrary Schwartz profiles of the norm gives every Schwartz–Bruhat vector of the corresponding translation isotype.
On a singleton line, division by the endpoint character leaves only the polynomial translation bound. The normalized orbits therefore act on Schwartz kernels.
Pointwise evaluation of each Pettis integral recovers a represented function.
A smooth log profile equal to one on a given compact set vanishes outside a larger compact set by properness of the modulation.
Contractive projection on the compact kernel preserves the convolution on eigenvectors and produces homogeneous kernels in a bounded frequency band.
Nonnegative continuous unit-mass kernels can be supported in an arbitrary shrinking identity neighborhood basis on which a continuous weight is small.
Compact support reduces the positive Haar integral to a finite measure. The closed convex hull of a compact orbit is compact by completeness.
A continuous positive density whose translates obey a locally uniform bound gives a strongly continuous left regular representation on weighted L².
Fourier evaluation of the compact-kernel average retains exactly the characters whose restriction gives the inverse translation eigencharacter.
Absolute Fourier inversion can be integrated against any L¹ input.
The frequency band is the compact image of a real interval in the translate of the annihilator of the kernel.
Compact generation on the original group makes the trivial subgroup of the dual good.
Passing the orbit integral through an L² representative gives Haar convolution. Positivity of the density transfers the resulting equality back to Haar measure.
Integrability of Schwartz functions persists under every polynomial weight in the logarithm of a continuous positive character.
Compactly supported L¹ kernels are Bochner integrable along each continuous orbit. The orbit norm only has to be bounded on the support of the kernel.
An absolutely integrable superposition of rank-one operators is nuclear. Its trace integrates the rank-one traces.
An absolutely integrable superposition of rank-one operators is nuclear. Its trace norm is controlled by the integrated cost of the rank-one operators.
Integrating the orbits of a strongly continuous operator family gives a continuous map into bounded operators when a continuous seminorm controls its weighted kernel integrals.
The compact-interval density of a shifted logarithmic coordinate is at most the square of the endpoint twist times the polynomial factor of the shift, times the density.
Reflecting the logarithmic coordinate exchanges the base interval with its negative.
The Hardy–Sobolev density on a compact base interval is positive.
Evaluation of the inverse singleton twist divides by the endpoint character.
The logarithm of a positive character is a Fourier multiplier on Schwartz–Bruhat functions. On the dual it is a constant multiple of a first derivative.
An isometry acting by inversion on representatives intertwines the multipliers of an inversion-invariant symbol.
A support and a uniform bound for a scalar kernel control each mapping seminorm of its Pettis operator.
An inverse Fourier integral masked on both sides by L² functions gives a nuclear kernel. Its diagonal trace separates into a Fourier mass and a pairing.
Inversion carries the measure with the reflected density to the measure with the original density, for an inversion-invariant base measure.
Under the Haar splitting, the mass of a positive module band is its logarithmic length times the mass of the compact kernel.
Translating a normalized kernel by a member of the compact kernel translates the input of its integrated operator.
After the singleton twist the translation bound has polynomial growth in the log coordinate. On kernel translates the normalizing factor cancels.

A continuous endomorphism of a weighted L² space of a left-invariant measure that acts by left translation on representatives has norm at most `C` when the translated density is at most `C ^ 2` times the density.
An integrable kernel acting by a Pettis integral on a weighted space gives ordinary Haar convolution after passage to unweighted L².
Finite character polynomials lift log profiles continuously to the group and preserve compact Fourier support.
On the positive reals, the Mellin frequency normalized by exp(−it log x) has a surjective real Schwartz Fourier chart for every choice of Haar measure.
Project a full approximate identity and reindex its spectra to obtain the prescribed bands. The zero kernel fills the finitely many initial slots.
Projecting a Schwartz kernel with compact Fourier support onto a kernel isotype cuts its spectrum down to a bounded segment of one frequency line.
A smooth bump on the real frequency line, extended by zero and translated by the starting character, gives a Schwartz cutoff on the full dual.
A weighted L¹ seminorm finite on Schwartz–Bruhat functions is continuous. On each metrizable barrelled stage its sublevel sets are closed by Fatou's lemma.
An ordinary Schwartz–Bruhat function belongs to every nonnegative logarithmically weighted L² space.
Extend a real Schwartz profile by zero from an open real line in a group whose trivial subgroup is good. This is one elementary Schwartz stage.
Fourier inversion of a smooth compactly supported kernel is absolute and pointwise for the Plancherel measure.
The order-zero seminorm of an elementary stage bounds all its realized values.
A character times a pulled-back profile has Fourier support on the corresponding translated line. On that line its transform is the transform of the profile for the pushforward Haar measure.
Haar invariance and Fubini give the convolution pairing, even against an unbounded continuous coefficient, since both kernels have compact support.
A pointwise bound for the translated density bounds translation in L².
A kernel that vanishes almost everywhere for the product measure has zero product smoothening: every average vanishes.
The Gaussian profile centred at `c`.
The indicator of a closed interval is locally constant away from its endpoints.
The difference of the Gaussian profiles at `0` and `1` against `exp(zx)`.
Integration against `dt/t` in logarithmic coordinates.
On the base `[-1, 1]` with degree zero, the supremum of the endpoint norms is the norm with endpoints `-1` and `1`.
A smooth function of the logarithmic module is Bruhat smooth. On each structural quotient, compose the descended positive quasi-character with log.
A set of logarithmic coordinates of a compact set is compact in the positive reals.
The identity is a surjective modulation of the positive reals.
The degree-two compact-interval space over the base `{0}` on the positive reals is nonzero: the indicator of `|log t| ≤ 1` has positive finite weighted mass.
On a nonzero normed space the identity has positive norm.
The multiplicative Haar measure `dt/t` gives a set of logarithmic coordinates its Lebesgue measure.
A proper modulus has a compact positive-mass log band invariant under its kernel.
Pettis convolution by a kernel of one isotype kills a vector of a different isotype.
A unitary character gives a nonzero weighted-free L² eigenvector for kernel translations.
A left-isotypic Schwartz kernel in the printed Fourier band vanishes when the character value is not its inverse.
The printed kernel conditions cannot strongly approximate the identity on a nonzero mismatched eigenspace.
If a function is locally constant with value `v` near the points of a filter, its iterated derivatives tend to those of the constant `v`.

Riemann–Roch for a theta transform, together with decay at large norm, forces the double Fourier transform of a test with two vanishing polar values to vanish at zero. Stated for abstract data, so that it elaborates without unfolding the adelic types.
If a constant is bounded by `K / r` for arbitrarily large `r`, it vanishes.
The double Fourier transform of a polar-free test has the same theta.
The Fourier transform of a polar-free test whose theta vanishes has vanishing theta.

A continuous linear map that preserves a submodule, preserves the kernel of a linear map on it, and is an involution modulo that kernel induces a unique continuous linear automorphism of the quotient. Stated for abstract modules, so that it elaborates without unfolding the Schwartz–Bruhat instances.

Riemann–Roch for a theta transform, for a test whose polar values vanish together with those of its Fourier transform: the Fourier transform preserves vanishing of theta, and the double Fourier transform has the same theta. Stated for abstract data, so that it elaborates without unfolding the adelic types.
The Tamagawa measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the weighted measure, whose density is positive.

A continuous linear map that vanishes on a submodule exactly where a linear map does descends to a unique injective continuous linear map of the quotient with a prescribed value on each class. Stated for abstract modules, so that it elaborates without unfolding the Schwartz–Bruhat instances.
Weighted theta of the polar projection is a continuous linear map from the adelic tests into the weighted L² space; on polar tests it is the weighted theta function.
A linear map from the adelic tests into a normed space that is bounded on bounded sets is continuous: each elementary stage is metrizable.
On a bounded set of polar tests, theta decays like any power of the norm at both ends with a common constant, the unit circle included.
A test whose weighted theta class is zero has vanishing theta.
The two-sided exponential of the log norm is integrable for the Tamagawa measure.
The weighted theta class of a test whose theta vanishes is zero.
A function dominated in the weighted L² sense by an integrable majorant belongs to the weighted L² space.
The weighted theta function of a test with two-sided decay is dominated pointwise by exp(-|log |g||).
A continuous linear projection of the adelic tests onto the polar subspace.
A continuous linear surjection onto ℂ² has a continuous linear projection onto its kernel. Stated for an abstract space, so that it elaborates without unfolding the Schwartz–Bruhat instances.
With enough decay, the weight |g|^a, the theta bound and the interval density together are dominated by exp(-|log |g||).
On a first-countable space, a linear map into a normed space that is bounded on the images of bounded sets under a continuous linear map is continuous after that map.
A linear family of functions that all lie in L² gives a linear map into L².
Two weighted L² classes with the same representative almost everywhere are equal.

A continuous linear map that vanishes exactly where a linear map does descends to a unique injective continuous linear map of the quotient by its kernel with a prescribed value on each class. Stated for abstract modules, so that it elaborates without unfolding the Schwartz–Bruhat instances.

A linear family of functions dominated, uniformly on bounded sets, by an integrable majorant in the weighted L² sense gives a continuous linear map into the weighted L² space, once linear maps bounded on bounded sets are known to be continuous.
S-local weighted theta is a continuous linear map from the S-local tests into the weighted L² space.
A linear map from the S-local tests into a normed space that is bounded on bounded sets is continuous: each elementary stage is metrizable.
On a bounded set of tests, S-local theta decays like any power of the norm above norm one and grows no faster than |g|^(-ε) below it, with a common constant, the unit circle included.
On a group with a modulation, exp(-δ |log |g||) is integrable for an inversion-invariant Haar measure.
The polynomial factor of the interval density grows more slowly than any exponential.
With the S-local bound, decay at large norm and growth no faster than |g|^(-(a+α)/2) at small norm, the weight |g|^a and the interval density are dominated by exp(-δ|log |g||).
The S-local Tamagawa measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the weighted measure, whose density is positive.
The density of the weighted S-local space is measurable, positive, and the interval density of the log norm.
A test whose weighted S-local theta class is zero lies in the theta kernel.
The topological facts about the S-idele quotient that the Haar measure arguments need.
The weighted S-local theta class of a test in the theta kernel is zero.
S-local theta on classes is linear in the test.
The S-idele quotient norm is a modulation.
The weighted S-local theta function of a test with the S-local bound is dominated pointwise by exp(-δ |log |g||).
In a weighted L², an element represented by a translate of a representative of another element is a scalar multiple of a third one when the representatives are proportional.
Ambient translation sends a weighted theta function to the norm factor times the weighted theta function of the translated test.
Ambient translation preserves the global theta completion.
A jointly continuous representation restricts to an invariant submodule.
The weighted theta function at an inversely translated class is the norm factor times the weighted theta function of the translated test.
A map that intertwines two maps through a surjection of their common domain sends the range of the first onto the range of the second.
Inversion intertwines the weight-a and weight-(1-a) theta embeddings with the Fourier automorphism of the polar-free theta space.
Inversion carries the weight-a theta embedding of a polar-free test to the weight-(1-a) theta embedding of its Fourier transform.
an injective dense equivariant map induces an injective dense map on isotypes.
continuous equivariant maps commute with pettis averages.
point evaluations identify the average of a representative after inversion of haar measure.
combine the isotype inclusion with the function formula on representatives.
restricting the codomain of an injective map preserves injectivity.
the modulation factor is one on the kernel of the norm.
a representative of the test-space average computes the embedded average.
equivariance restricts to a subgroup.
the test-space pettis average has the unnormalized homogeneous theta function.
twist an extended action and identify it with the ambient action on a dense image.
transfer an almost-everywhere translation identity to a weighted L² class.
lift the translation identity from representatives to a quotient realization.
real powers of a positive character form a continuous character with the inverse weight.
restrict a jointly continuous action to the closure of an invariant image.
a continuous character cancels the scalar in the intertwining identity.
translation of a weighted function extracts the inverse weight of the translating element.

A function whose derivative along every orbit of a one-parameter subgroup is again given by the same recipe is smooth along the orbit, and every iterated derivative at time zero is continuous in the base point. Stated for abstract types so that the induction does not unfold the Schwartz–Bruhat model.
Scaling a measure by a finite positive constant gives the same weighted L² space with the norm scaled by the square root of the constant.
An intertwiner of `g` with `g⁻¹` carries the isotype of a character to the isotype of the inverse character, stated for abstract spaces.
Inversion intertwines left translation by `g` with left translation by `g⁻¹`, for closed subspaces of weighted L² spaces over an abstract commutative group.
A nonnegative archimedean bump at one, times the indicator of the finite integers, vanishes at zero and has nonzero theta at one.
A rapidly decaying sequence with nonzero first value cannot have every term twice its successor.
On the norm-one subgroup the translation estimate is contractive, also after restriction to an invariant Sobolev subspace.
Pairing the raw compact-group projection with a continuous functional gives the Fourier coefficient of its orbit.
The normalized isotypic averages give the coordinates of the orthogonal Hilbert sum.
A polar-free test with nonzero theta. A dilation difference cancels the Fourier value at zero, and rapid decay shows that some translated theta value survives.
Additive Haar scaling for a unit translate, as in the norm-twist counterexample in `Ch06_LocalGlobal/Sec3_Printed.lean`.
The theta translation law, as used for the global theta action in Ch05 Sec2.
A bound from the completion at weight a to the completion at weight b on the same theta classes forces b ≤ a, by translating a nonzero test to positive log norm.
Inversion as an isometry between weighted L² spaces for reflected intervals, on an abstract group with an inversion-invariant measure.
Reflecting the logarithmic coordinate reflects the interval of the density.
Inversion carries the reflected weighted measure to the weighted measure.
The density of the weighted S-idele measure is continuous.
The S-local quotient Tamagawa measure is the canonical modulated Haar measure times the mass of the norm-one quotient. Both measures give the band of norms in [1, e] the mass of the norm-one part.
At degree zero the Sobolev measure is just the base measure. Multiplying by the square root of the modulation absorbs the density of the source L² space.
The half-weight isometry carries the closed ranges of two embeddings onto one another when it identifies their representatives on a common set of tests.

The compact Hilbert-sum coordinates for a subgroup acting on a closed subspace of a compact-interval Sobolev space. The instances are spelled as the S-local statement elaborates them, so that the statement is matched syntactically.
The kernel of a compact isotypic average is the closed span of twisted differences.
Testing the two Pettis averages on functionals only requires intertwining the orbit of the input.
The average of polar-free classes still has both polar coordinates zero.
A map from polar-free classes extends across the two finite-dimensional polar coordinates.
An ordinary isotypic average of a polar representative admits a polar representative.
The representatives of the ordinary compact average have precisely the homogeneous theta function.
On a norm-one orbit the scalar in the global Sobolev action is one.
Restrict the ordinary isotype equivalence to polar classes, then use the dense Sobolev embedding.
Lift a norm-one group element and compare the two actions on translated tests.

On the weighted L² space with weight |x|² (I = {1}, s = 0) over a commutative group with a module taking a value above one, inversion is not a bounded automorphism. It would conjugate translation by g⁻¹ into translation by g, so its norm would be at most |g|⁻² times itself.
If the Hilbert-sum norm identity holds for one nonzero continuous theta function, the norm-one group has mass at least one: Bessel bounds the components by the mass squared.
Squared L² seminorm of a continuous function as a lower integral.
A Hilbert-sum factorization of quotient maps equates the squared norm of each total function with the sum of the squared norms of its components.

`rawIsotype_factorization_norm` for a weighted measure `μ' ≪ μ`: the Hilbert-sum factorization equates the squared weighted norm of each total function with the sum of the squared weighted norms of its components.
The global statement fails over ℚ(ζ₃) with a = α = β = s = 0.
Over ℚ(ζ₃) with S = ∅, the S-ideles of norm in [1, T] have mass at least 2π(T − 1)/T.
At a complex place, the multiplicative Tamagawa measure of the annulus 1 ≤ |x|² ≤ T is at least 2π(T − 1)/T: the density 1/|x|² is at least 1/T and the measure is twice Lebesgue.

The S-local statement with a = α = β = 1, s = 0 fails as soon as the norm-one mass exceeds one and some nonzero theta function depends only on the norm: its trivial-character average is the mass times itself.
For S = ∅ and at most n units, the S-ideles of norm in [1, T] have mass at most n · vol(J₁) · log T.
The S-idele classes of norm in [1, T] have quotient mass vol(J₁) · log T.
One Hilbert-sum coordinate equal to `r • v` with `‖r‖ > 1` contradicts the norm identity `Σ ‖Θ_j‖² = ‖v‖²` for `0 < ‖v‖ < ∞`.
A continuous function that is nonzero somewhere has nonzero L² norm for a measure with everywhere positive density against an open-positive measure.
Over ℚ(ζ₃) with S = ∅, the Gaussian exp(−|z|²) in the complex coordinate is a test function equal to exp(−|g|) on every S-idele g (the idelic norm is |z|²).
The norm-one quotient of ℚ(ζ₃) with S = ∅ has mass above one (it is π/3): at T = 26/25 the two bounds on the annulus give 2π/26 ≤ 6 · vol(J₁)/25.
ℚ(ζ₃) has exactly one infinite place, and it is complex.
For S = ∅ and finitely many units, the theta function of a test that depends only on the idelic norm is the number of units times the same profile of the class norm.
The units of ℚ(ζ₃) integral at every finite place (S = ∅) are finite, at most six.
The norm-one idele classes of ℚ(ζ₃) have Tamagawa mass π/(3√3) < 1.
Weil's formula with counting measure on a finite closed subgroup of at most n elements: the preimage of a set of cosets has at most n times its quotient mass.
A test with vanishing value at zero and Fourier value one has theta bounded below near norm zero.
Every positive radius has an infinite-measure small-norm region in the idele class group of ℚ.
A rapidly decaying sequence with nonzero first value cannot have every term twice its successor.
A polar-free test with nonzero theta at positive log norm. Start with a bump that vanishes at zero and use one dilation difference to cancel its Fourier value there.
Additive Haar scaling for a unit translate, as in the norm-twist counterexample in `Ch06_LocalGlobal/Sec3_Printed.lean`.
A nonnegative archimedean bump at one, times the indicator of the finite integers, vanishes at zero and has nonzero theta at one.
If the interval contains the nonnegative half-line, a nonzero value at positive log norm forces the supremum of the weighted L² norms to be infinite.
The Gaussian theta dominates its term at the identity S-unit.
The rational Gaussian has nonzero theta at a class of norm two.
Any strict increase in strip width absorbs every nonnegative polynomial Sobolev degree.
For a zero of multiplicity `N`, the exact strip index is equivalent to a derivative below `N` extending continuously to the scalar Sobolev space.

decls.deviation: The strict boundary inequality is the correction F152. Necessity outside the strip follows by embedding a wider interval with degree zero and applying its endpoint criterion.
decls.summary: On entire exponential tests the order-`k` Mellin derivative extends continuously to the symmetric scalar Sobolev space exactly in the interior, or at an endpoint with `2 * k + 1 < s`.
The Fourier–Mellin equivalence on the whole plane. The inverse sends an entire test to its radial profile in logarithmic coordinates.

Finite analytic divisors and a strongly convergent multiplier family detect the closure using precisely the bounded Taylor functionals annihilating the whole test ideal. The exceptional finite sets can contain excess generator zeros.
An evaluation on the dense entire-symbol chart agrees with the derivative on every entire physical test profile represented in the scalar weighted space.
In any chart with the correct radial representatives, multiplication by an entire Schwartz–Bergman test extends to a continuous operator on the Sobolev space.

Contractive holomorphic cutoffs tending pointwise to one on a wider strip give operators converging strongly to the identity. On each test vector their Mellin transforms agree with pointwise multiplication by the cutoffs throughout the wider strip.

The cutoffs preserve membership of every generator times every entire test in the geometric theta space. The cutoff can be moved onto the test, after which its inverse Mellin transform supplies the radial convolution kernel.
Entire Schwartz–Bergman tests map densely into the scalar Sobolev space. Their representatives are the logarithmic inverse Fourier–Mellin transforms.

A fixed polar-free Hecke generator supplies a strongly convergent sequence of contractive strip symbols. Every symbol times an entire test killing the specified finite divisor lifts into the closed theta space; all tests retain the actual inverse Mellin formula.
A polynomial times the Gaussian can attain any prescribed exact vanishing order.
Agreement of radial profiles on Lebesgue measure transports to their inverse-character lifts for the Tamagawa measure.

In an invariant subspace of test functionals, every derivative with a nonzero coefficient in a finite linear combination of jets of a single entire generator belongs to the subspace. Only the jets on that finite set enter.
All zeros of a nonzero bounded strip generator can be exhausted by a sequence of finite sets. The complementary products are contractive on the smaller strip and tend pointwise to one.

A continuous linear combination of one finite Jordan chain can contain a highest nonzero coefficient only if every jet up to and including that degree is continuous. The lowering map models precomposition with a bounded smooth coordinate multiplier.

A bounded finite jet combination at multiple points can only use bounded individual jets. The cutoff multiplier selects a single frequency and its coordinate multiple lowers the ordinary derivative jet exactly by its integer degree.
Vanishing higher coefficients do not affect the separation of the supported terms.
Multiplying an entire Schwartz–Bergman symbol by a polar-free theta transform preserves its rapid decrease on each finite vertical strip.
The scalar test ideal generated by all polar-free theta Mellin transforms in one chart.

In a single inverse-character radial component, all bounded jets that annihilate the scalar theta ideal vanish on a vector with zero admitted arithmetic moments. This is the scalar arithmetic hypothesis of `analytic_strip_synthesis`.

An order-k derivative annihilating the theta test ideal is strictly below the actual positive completed Hecke multiplicity at its shifted point. This includes points of order zero and the canceled poles.
The Mellin transform of a polar-free theta test, shifted by the center of the target strip.
Pointwise multiplication of entire Schwartz–Bergman tests, linear in the second factor.
Starting from a biorthogonal family, the other biorthogonal families are exactly its translations by one common-kernel vector per index.
Removing some of a finite-order zero within the entire Schwartz–Bergman space preserves the orders at every other point.
A triangular collection in a linear subspace interpolates all the coordinates of one finite jet.
Gaussian damping converts an entire function bounded on closed vertical substrips to an entire Schwartz–Bergman function without changing any vanishing orders.
Exact order at one zero and the required vanishing at other zeros produce an entire Schwartz–Bergman transform with arbitrary prescribed finite jet at that point.
A two-sided Laplace integral absolutely convergent at both real endpoints is bounded uniformly across that closed complex substrip.
If a density has a fixed exponential translation bound, convolution with a faster two-sided exponential gives a uniformly comparable density.
An explicit exponential translation bound for the actual symmetric Hardy–Sobolev weight.
A weighted square norm written with a nonnegative integral.
The contractions on both vertical lines give a bound for the squared norm, uniform in the multiplier, for any continuous density with controlled translation growth.
Contractive holomorphic multipliers on a wider vertical strip act uniformly boundedly on the full Hardy–Sobolev norm. Pointwise convergence to one implies strong convergence on that whole space.
A uniform bound for translates of a nonnegative window passes to every positive mixture of those windows.
Pointwise convergence to zero under an L² envelope gives convergence in L².
The positive and negative halves of a decaying two-sided exponential have equal finite mass.
A multiplier contractive on one vertical Mellin line is contractive for the corresponding exponential square norm of logarithmic test profiles.
If the cutoff has the prescribed zero multiplicity, every lower moment of the cutoff profile vanishes.
Pull pointwise multiplication by a contractive holomorphic symbol on a strip back to its exponential test profiles by the Fourier–Mellin equivalence.
The multiplier on exponential tests is a contraction for the unweighted vertical Plancherel norms on each Mellin line. In logarithmic coordinates the squared norm has density `exp (2 * v * x)`.
The Mellin transform of a multiplied test is the product of its transform with the symbol.
A bounded holomorphic multiplier preserves the entire family of substrip bounds in the Schwartz–Bergman space.
Inverse Fourier–Mellin transform transports bounded cutoff convergence to the exponential test topology, hence to the norm on every enclosed Sobolev interval.
Every contraction on the vertical test lines extends to the symmetric Hardy–Sobolev space with a bound depending only on the widths and degree.
The smooth step is temperate. Every derivative of positive order vanishes outside the unit interval.
Multiplication by bounded, pointwise convergent analytic multipliers converges in the full Schwartz–Bergman topology on the open strip.
If the symbols are contractive on the open strip and converge to one pointwise, their inverse Fourier–Mellin multipliers converge to the identity in the test topology.
Uniform bounds on two exponential lines imply a uniform bound in every translate of the decaying two-sided exponential window.
An arbitrary family of distinct Hecke zeros inside the outer strip gives nonzero pairwise-distinct disk points and the summable multiplicity bound used by the infinite Blaschke tail products.
Positive Hecke jet orders on a vertical frequency chart are locally finite.
In a unitary chart the trivial quasi-character and the idelic norm correspond to simple poles of the completed L-function.

The positive Hecke divisor in every vertical strip centered at real part 2 satisfies the Blaschke condition after conformal transport to the disk. The test attaining the polar-free divisor minimum at the center is nonzero there.
Finite moment support gives a finite interpolant modulo the joint kernel. When such inputs are dense, the quotient images of single-coordinate interpolants have dense span.
Compact character averaging preserves density of an equivariant map.
A jointly continuous family on a compact parameter space preserves sequence convergence uniformly in the parameter.

, and Theorem 10.2.1.1, pp. 441–442. At each twist away from the trivial character and the idelic norm, one polar-free test attains the order of the completed Hecke L-function in its Mellin transform.
, and Theorem 10.2.2.1, p. 446. At every zero of the completed Hecke L-function, some polar-free theta test has a Mellin transform with exactly its multiplicity.

On a neighborhood of a prescribed closed Hecke strip, contractive analytic multipliers tend to one. Each multiplier has the full prescribed zero orders away from a finite set of distinct points in that closed strip.
A smooth compactly supported frequency profile can prescribe a single Taylor coefficient on a locally finite real set. All remaining jets vanish.
Each surviving zero jet on the a-line has a Sobolev vector pairing to one with it and to zero with every other jet. The construction prescribes a compact smooth frequency profile on one character.

For each compact character there is a sequence of bounded analytic cutoffs on the widened strip. Apart from a finite set of actual strip-jet indices, each cutoff kills the indicated order and every lower derivative on this component.
Some polar-free theta test has a transform nonzero at absolute real coordinate two.
The frequency derivative of a Fourier integral is a log moment. Only polynomial moments up to the requested order enter this real-variable formula.
Continuous representatives remain linearly independent in L² when a measure positive on open sets is absolutely continuous with respect to the L² measure.
Exponential polynomials attached to distinct characters have independent coefficients.
Multiplying distinct powers of an additive coordinate by one character preserves linear independence when the coordinate has infinite range.
Translations put the character times the mth power of an additive coordinate in the simultaneous generalized eigenspace of that character.

Compact Fourier support meets only finitely many surviving line jets. The restriction to the compact norm-one subgroup is discrete, each real chart is closed, and the positive Hecke divisor has finite support on every compact set.
A representative with compact Fourier support can have only finitely many nonzero line jet moments.
A continuous representative of a Fourier transform vanishes off the topological support of any almost-everywhere equal representative.
A bounded extension of an admitted evaluation on one isotype agrees by density with the ambient Sobolev pairing, up to the Fourier derivative phase.
On a vertical frequency line an exact complex analytic order gives a smooth nonvanishing local unit times the corresponding power of the real coordinate.
The Chapter 10 isotype approximate identity has genuine compactly supported ordinary Schwartz symbols in the normalized chart, and converges strongly in the Sobolev norm of that isotype.
Multiplication by an arbitrary real Schwartz profile in the frequency chart equals the ambient zero-line action of its inverse Fourier kernel.

A closed subspace containing all character components of a vector contains the vector itself. Testing its compact orbit against a separating functional reduces to uniqueness of Fourier coefficients on the compact abelian group.
A frequency cutoff supported on a patch where a symbol has the prescribed zero order turns local smooth division into a compactly supported multiplier.
The distribution-free chart is dense directly in the weighted norm. The surjectivity on homogeneous Schwartz tests includes the norm-dense concentrated exponential tests of §10.2.1.
On Haar-integrable representatives, the zero-line Schwartz action is exactly multiplication of Fourier transforms on every component.
Every compact Schwartz profile with full Hecke zero multiplicities in its Taylor jet gives a genuine element of the closed global weighted theta image.
In a fixed isotype the geometric theta closure contains every vector annihilated by the continuous derivatives below the Hecke zero orders.
Reverse norm-closure inclusion inside a single compact-character isotype on a zero-width spectral line. Each surviving jet of this isotype is tested.
An individual chart derivative extends to this isotype only in the exact strict range prescribed by the scalar endpoint Sobolev theorem.
At degree at most one no derivative on a frequency line is continuous in the weighted norm. Even the values at Hecke zeros impose no closed condition.
All Schwartz convolutions on the zero-width line preserve the closed weighted theta image, including the inverse transforms of arbitrary smooth compact frequency profiles.
The common zero-jet kernel lies in the global weighted theta closure once that inclusion is known on each compact-character isotype.
Canonical logarithmic Haar coordinates give the Fourier transform of a character-twisted scalar profile with the exact Tamagawa normalization.
A smooth one-variable function whose first `m` Taylor coefficients vanish is smoothly divisible by the corresponding power of the coordinate, including at the point.
The finite span of smooth symbols multiplied by compact Schwartz cutoffs maps into a submodule once its individual Schwartz generators do.

Every fixed real frequency has a neighborhood and a single polar-free theta test generating all smooth profiles there with vanishing Taylor jet through the local Hecke order. The multiplier is a compactly supported Schwartz function on the whole frequency line.

On an entire frequency component, any compactly supported smooth profile which vanishes to full Hecke order at every zero is a finite linear combination of exact theta profiles times compactly supported Schwartz multipliers.
A Schwartz profile given by a multiplier times an adelic polar-free Mellin transform belongs to the closed global theta space in the weighted isotype.
Restriction of an entire Mellin transform to the imaginary axis multiplies its kth complex derivative by the kth power of the frequency phase.
On the normalized line the ordinary Fourier transform of the centered theta representative is its global theta Mellin transform, evaluated at the shifted center.
Pullback by the log norm times the inverse character defines a bounded map of the scalar singleton Sobolev space into the Tamagawa-weighted isotype.
Two translation differences kill the polar coordinates while preserving a nonzero eigenfunctional of any distinct weight.
Distinct choices of base character, both real coordinates of a norm twist, or logarithmic degree give linearly independent functions on the idele class group.
A Fourier band defines a submodule, and its image under a linear quotient map agrees with the description using any almost-everywhere equal L² representative.
Orthogonal projections onto closures of subspaces converge strongly whenever each vector has a convergent sequence of approximants in the corresponding subspaces.
Set-valued version of the projection argument, allowing the Fourier-band submodules to be constructed independently from their concrete sets.
A surjective continuous linear image of supported approximants admits strongly convergent orthogonal projections onto the closures of the corresponding bands.
The character-weighted average of a continuous orbit belongs to its isotype. Testing this vector against a continuous functional gives the Fourier coefficient of the scalar orbit.

At width zero the separating compact-character argument assembles the local multiplier synthesis for every character into ambient norm closure.

decls.deviation: Use the strict Sobolev cutoff. Smooth profiles on one real frequency line give the individual interpolants. Compact Fourier support and the line common-kernel identity give norm density in the quotient.

The real-frequency Fourier profile of a Sobolev vector differentiates at every surviving order. With the conjugation used by the Fourier transform, its chart runs through the inverses of the Mellin characters.
The pairing of a weighted function with a line jet is the derivative of its norm-twisted Mellin integral at the shifted point.
Every function in the two-sided decay space is integrable against every quasi-character.
Every logarithmic moment of a function integrable against all quasi-characters is integrable against every real norm twist.
A logarithmic power below the strict cutoff is square-integrable for the reciprocal weight.
A Schwartz profile on one Mellin line gives exactly the corresponding Sobolev jet moments. The inverse character in the chart accounts for the conjugation in the Fourier transform.
At width zero the real offset of each strip jet is zero, and its remaining indices give exactly one line jet with the same function representative.
Transport a statement about the reindexed reciprocal-weight vectors from the interval [−0, 0] to the identical line Sobolev space.
A Hilbert quotient dual maps isometrically to the annihilator under an ambient duality.

Abstract form of `spectralSobolevIsotypeQuotient_isometry`: an action preserving a closed subspace descends to the quotient, and if a compact subgroup acts by contractions with an isotypic average, the isotype quotient is isometric to the isotype of the quotient.
Testing an isotypic Pettis average against a functional gives its scalar integral.
On the isotype the average is multiplication by the total mass.
The average maps an invariant closed subspace into itself.
The average is bounded by the mass when the subgroup acts by contractions.
The isotypic average descends to a quotient by an invariant subspace.
On the quotient, the average of a class in the quotient isotype is the mass times it.
A unit complex number times its conjugate is one.
Conjugating a weighted L² vector and multiplying by the density gives a vector of the reciprocal-weight space whose product integral with the original is its squared norm.
Dense interpolants and a total lifted dual family form a spectral Markushevich basis.
A total family of continuous functionals on a Hilbert space has norm-dense span.

decls.deviation: Finite moment support is dense by the preceding cutoff argument. The reverse common-kernel inclusion then gives density of the single interpolants themselves.

multiple-zero line strictly to the right of the centre has a representative at bounded

Reconstruction: This isolates the single-character part of the strip margin.

Choose a witness component for each abscissa, then one abscissa representing each component so chosen. A single choice of ordinates sees all the representatives.
For one character, a bounded height interval contributes only finitely many multiple-zero abscissae in the closed right half of the critical strip.

The finite-line assertion for every section is equivalent to two tests in the open right half of the strip. One tests each component separately over unbounded heights. The other uses a single real segment for all components, allowing every choice of section.
A multiple zero with real part greater than one half lies in the open critical strip.
Reflect a multiple zero into the opposite half of the strip by the completed functional equation. Reflection negates the ordinate and replaces the character by its inverse.

Near any real number there are only finitely many distinct pairs of real part and multiplicity among multiple completed Hecke zeros, over all ordinates and chosen characters. The norm integral on p. 447 gives no such restriction. It would suffice to bound the multiplicities on the line with that real part and exclude multiple zeros on all other sufficiently nearby vertical lines.

The multiple zeros of the chosen completed Hecke L-functions lie on finitely many vertical lines, over all components of the norm-one dual and all ordinates. This is the half of `spectralStripJet_order_and_margin_locally_finite_multiple_zeros` that keeps the jets of high order away from the edges of a strip.
