This is the half of `spectralStripJet_order_and_margin_locally_finite_multiple_zeros` that bounds the orders of the strip jets.
For a jet whose order is at least the boundary threshold, the norm integral is at least a fixed multiple of the logarithm of the inverse distance of its real offset from the edge.
The norm integral of a strip jet does not change when the real offset changes sign.

An admitted jet on an inverse Hecke-character component agrees with its bounded scalar Mellin derivative on the entire radial Sobolev space. The Tamagawa/canonical Haar factor is explicit. All other angular components vanish.
Translating a unitary norm chart to ordinate zero preserves its norm-one component and all completed Hecke zero multiplicities.
The reverse common-kernel inclusion on a strip follows from its matching admitted moments for each inverse-character radial Sobolev vector.

decls.deviation: At the boundary the admitted orders satisfy the strict inequality `2k+1<s`. The proof uses Mellin division and weighted Sobolev approximation.
decls.summary: Vanishing of every admitted moment places a vector in the closed span of the weighted polar-free theta tests.
Membership on a single inverse-character component follows from its continuous Taylor functionals that annihilate the whole theta test ideal.
If two norm-twist charts differ by translation, their zero multiplicities agree at the corresponding points.
Integrating scalar multiples of a commutative action preserves every eigenspace.
The canonical log pullback is an isometry even after multiplication by an arbitrary unitary character; changing Haar normalization preserves closed range.
Compact character averaging takes each pure vector back onto its character component. Totality extends this observation from pure vectors to all vectors.
A bounded analytic multiplier preserves the Schwartz–Bergman test space on a smaller strip on which the test function is defined.
A uniformly rapidly decaying analytic function on an open vertical strip gives a Schwartz–Bergman element with its original values throughout that strip.

Inside an arbitrary buffered strip, the tail times an entire test is the Mellin transform of an exponential test approximated in the full test topology by multiples of the chosen generator. The multipliers themselves are actual inverse-Mellin exponential tests on the same buffered strip.

The normalized complementary tail of the actual zeros of one strip generator takes any entire test killing the finitely many excluded multiplicities to the closure, in the exponential test topology, of products by that generator.
A pointwise-convergent, uniformly bounded family of multipliers multiplies a fixed Schwartz–Bergman test convergently in the full strip test topology.
The physical strip jet is the chosen compact character times an exponential polynomial.
Finite order strip moments of inverse profiles on a wider open interval.
An integral supported on a nontrivial compact character vanishes by Haar invariance.
On one compact-character chart every admitted jet has a Schwartz–Bergman interpolant, vanishing at every remaining admitted jet on that entire chart.
Every scalar two-sided exponential-decay profile lifts to the ambient strip Sobolev space in the inverse base-character component.
The Mellin transform of a polar-free generator is uniformly bounded on each closed vertical substrip, including after a translation of the center.
The inverse-base-character lifts of the full radial weighted Hilbert spaces are total in the arithmetic weighted Sobolev space, for every Sobolev exponent.
Every physical moment on the same chart is a scalar Mellin derivative. All other compact characters have zero pairing.
On a split group, each physical compact-character tensor is one of the given base-character lifts after a unitary radial phase correction.
Pullback from weighted radial L² with the inverse base character.
The whole radial Hilbert range in an arbitrary prescribed character is in the closure of ambient vectors with finite jet support.
The radial phase from the chosen base character lies in the same weighted L² space.
The canonical weighted Hilbert tensor map reads elementary product representatives with respect to Tamagawa measure.
A double difference of the standard Gaussian removes both polar values. At either exceptional weight its normalized Mellin factor has a simple zero.
A nonzero Fourier coefficient of a radial lift determines its restriction to the compact norm-one group.

For one polar-free generator, a normalized Blaschke tail of its full divisor times any entire rapidly decreasing test killing the complementary finite jets has a radial lift in the closed global theta Sobolev space.
A Mellin product by the centered transform of any adelic polar-free test is the Fourier transform of its radial convolution in the closed theta space.
Mellin values on the strip determine every logarithmic test profile.
The normalized eigendistribution is the entire test factor and the two orders add at every point.
The completed L-function divides each polar-free theta Mellin transform as a germ; equality of orders holds wherever the normalized eigendistribution is nonzero.
The Mellin derivatives below the completed L-function’s order vanish.
Factorization on a right half-plane determines the equality of meromorphic orders everywhere.
A character with nonzero logarithmic derivative crosses each polar weight simply.
Weighted closed theta spaces are stable under the actual Bochner integrals of radial exponential kernels with enough room for the translation norm.
The polynomial factor in the translation bound is absorbed by the available extra width. This gives a weighted L¹ norm for every inverse Mellin kernel.
The physical radial lift is continuous into the Tamagawa weighted strip space.
On the normalized line the ordinary Fourier transform of the centered theta representative is its global theta Mellin transform, evaluated at the shifted center.
The unweighted Haar integral of a weighted polar-free theta function against an admitted zero jet vanishes, including the center shift in its multiplicity.
A completed Hecke L-function has no zero with real part outside the closed interval from zero to one: to the right of one by the Euler product, and to the left of zero by the functional equation.
A spectral Markushevich basis stays one when each vector is multiplied by a nonzero scalar and its functional by the inverse scalar.
Multiplying the vectors of a family by nonzero scalars does not change its linear span.

Let `b` be a Hilbert basis indexed by `ℕ ⊕ ℕ`. Put `x (inl n) = b (inl n)` and `x (inr n) = b (inl n) + (n + 1)⁻¹ • b (inr n)`. Then `x` has a total biorthogonal family `Λ` with `‖Λ (inr n)‖ ≥ n + 1`.
A norm twist moves a critical-line zero of rational zeta to frequency zero in the trivial norm-one isotype.
A frequency set of Plancherel measure zero yields only the zero class.
At Sobolev degree three, the first logarithmic jet fails to be square integrable.

The trivial Hecke character of some number field has a completed L-function with a zero of multiplicity at least two. The intended witness is the splitting field of X³ − 2, whose Dedekind zeta function contains the square of the two-dimensional Artin factor.
The critical first-jet density has a divergent harmonic tail.
The compact-neighborhood test in `lcaFourier_isometry_surjective`, viewed here in weighted L².

The rational trivial-character chart has a positive critical-line zero isolated by a closed interval entirely above zero. The positive ordinate comes from the vendored Lince project certificate `HardyFirstZero.first_zero_on_line`. The Hecke normalization uses the comparisons in `Ch13_ZerosHecke.Targets` as in the F183 proof.
From a fixed uniform bound for the spectral parameter and the convolved blocks, the eigenvalue to the power k controls each whole block.
On a complete block of length at most k, its convolution is a finite linear combination of fixed translations, with weights given by interpolation of its moments.
A diagonal flag of jet rows annihilates the k-th power of the centered operator.
At a uniformly bounded jet length the moment interpolation matrix is fixed once and for all.
A Pettis integral of translates of a vector in a closed invariant subspace of a Hilbert space stays in that subspace, since every vector orthogonal to it kills the integrand.
A continuous endomorphism commuting with the translation action intertwines the two regularized vectors obtained from Pettis integrals of the corresponding orbits.
The regularized action of a commutative group commutes with its translations, so it preserves every isotype of a restricted translation action.
An approximant of rank at most `n` within `2⁻ⁿ` of the `n`-th approximation number; the zeroth one is zero.

An operator whose range lies in a subspace of dimension at most `r` is a sum of `r` rank-one operators whose functionals have norm at most that of the operator and whose vectors have norm at most one.
Rescaling a rank-one term by the norm bound of its functional.
If `c n ≤ e (n + 1) + e n` and `e` decays rapidly, then `c (⌊√m⌋)` decays rapidly in `m`.
Rapid decay against `n ^ k` for every `k` gives rapid decay against `(n + 1) ^ k`.
Adding two rank-n approximants gives a rank-at-most-2n approximant.
A polynomial bound on odd approximation numbers extends to all indices by monotonicity.
Equality of descended convolutions can be checked on representatives.
Compress ambient convolution to the isotype using the quotient isometry and its orthogonal projection.
An additive convolution action transports finite factorizations to compositions.
Bounded restriction and projection preserve a Banach nuclear presentation.
The quotient representative formulas identify the compression with the restricted action.
A family of trace-class operators in which every member is a finite sum of two-fold products of family members has rapidly decreasing approximation numbers.
Trace-class operators have a uniform, one-power approximation-number bound.
Every finite sum of approximation numbers is bounded by the trace norm.
Once the rectangle includes a zero, its jets reproduce the corresponding coordinates of the image of the original operator.
Trace-norm Cauchy bounds pass to each finite sum of powers of approximation numbers at an operator-norm limit. Taking their supremum controls the Schatten tail.
Rank-one insertions detect every scalar matrix entry of a single zero block. Two applications of uniform boundedness give one operator-norm bound for all blocks.

A lower semicontinuous seminorm restricts continuously to each Fréchet stage of a strict LF-space, whose topology is final locally convex. This is the Fréchet-stage argument of `IsLFSpace.barrelled` from Appendix C.
Descending a linear family of operators through a fixed quotient is linear.
A descended endomorphism has operator norm bounded by the ambient operator norm.
The Hardy–Sobolev action is continuous in operator norm, and passing to the quotient can only decrease the norm.
A linear operator-norm continuous family of nuclear endomorphisms has a trace-norm continuous lift when its domain is a strict LF-space.
The trace norm is a supremum of continuous finite sums of approximation numbers on any operator-norm continuous family of trace-class operators.

and 454. A homogeneous compactly supported Bruhat test is a finite sum of convolutions of pairs of tests of the same character. Deviation: Isolate the radial Dixmier–Malliavin factorization and its transport along the idelic norm.
The two character factors in the convolution integral multiply to `χ x`. The remaining integrand factors through the log norm, so it integrates against the pushforward Haar measure.
A character times the pullback of a real-line test by the log norm is a Bruhat test.

decls.summary: Extend a real test to the positive half-line through the logarithm. Its support lies in the exponential image of the original support, so the zero extension is smooth at zero.
Reflect the kernel of a translation integral and put the Haar normalization into it. The resulting convolution is itself a smooth compactly supported test.
Restriction to a one-parameter subgroup is smooth in the real parameter.
Haar translation forces the Mellin transform of a homogeneous test to vanish off its character.
The isometric quotient-isotype inclusion intertwines the two convolutions on representatives.
A sum on pairs supported on one character is the sum over that character's fiber.
Cyclicity identifies the trace with its restriction when the range lies in an isometric copy.
Check range containment and intertwining on quotient representatives before comparing traces.
Number the norm-one characters and, within each row, the selected zeros.
Relabeling a biorthogonal system by a bijection preserves its two dense spans.
Relabeling both zeros and their derivative indices leaves each finite rectangle unchanged.
The transpose convolution acts by the complete triangular matrix of logarithmic Mellin moments, before passing to the kernel of the lower coordinates.
A quotient jet functional evaluates on a representative by its explicit Haar moment.
On the common kernel of all lower moments at this zero, the selected jet coordinate of the convolution is the Mellin value times the same coordinate of the input.
If the lower moments vanish, translation multiplies the top moment by the norm twist.
Pointwise square-root identity from AppC_LCTVS/Sec3a, used for compression and for the contraction which attains the trace norm.

A finite block sum nearly attaining the common bound leaves little trace norm for disjoint sums. A finite span of moments detects the almost maximal sum and is orthogonal to every block outside a fixed finite set.

operator on the biorthogonal vectors, the scalar traces of the individual zero
blocks are summable. The jets at each zero are summed before testing summability.
The estimates for (10.3.2.7) involve only Mellin derivatives and give no bound for these
pairings with a compact operator. A summable majorant for the absolute block
traces, allowed to depend on the operator and test, would suffice.

it is what the author intends.

against an arbitrary compact operator, allowing clusters of zeros, is supplied or known to us.

decls.doc:
Paper: Theorem 10.3.2.1(1), pp. 453–455, after (10.3.2.7). For a fixed test,
discard the output directions of finitely many jets. The positive square root of
the remaining Gram operator should have uniformly small finite diagonal sums.
By `_hb` the Riesz vectors span densely, so the complementary projections tend strongly to
zero and compress any fixed finite-rank rectangle to zero in trace norm. In a trace-norm
Cauchy tail, contractivity bounds each later compressed trace norm, and hence each finite
diagonal sum, by the fixed rectangle's compressed trace norm plus the tail error.
Gap: The scalar Mellin estimates on p. 455 do not control this sum for an
individual rectangle, in particular when its boundary separates nearby zeros.

By `_hb` the Riesz vectors span densely, so the complementary projections tend strongly to zero and compress any fixed finite-rank rectangle to zero in trace norm. In a trace-norm Cauchy tail, contractivity bounds each later compressed trace norm, and hence each finite diagonal sum, by the fixed rectangle's compressed trace norm plus the tail error.
The two orthogonal output compressions satisfy a weighted trace-norm bound. This follows from the Pythagorean identity on each input vector and operator monotonicity of the positive square root.
Every selected block takes values in the span of its finitely many jet vectors.
A finite-rank operator attains its trace norm against a compact contraction. Use the contraction taking the operator to its absolute value and restrict it to the finite-dimensional range.
Biorthogonality identifies the blocks missed by any finite set of moments. Totality makes the complementary projections strongly null, hence small in trace norm on any fixed finite section.

For included jets the finite section has exactly the convolution coordinate. Consequently the difference of two sufficiently large sections lies in the orthogonal complement of any fixed finite span of Riesz vectors. Finite diagonal sums for a single section after this orthogonal projection bound its trace norm.
Pointwise summability of the block traces against compact operators gives one trace-norm bound for all finite selections, by uniform boundedness on the Banach space of compact operators.
Finite independent moment functionals have biorthogonal vectors in their Riesz span.
A total family of independent moment functionals computes a nuclear trace if the operator acts diagonally modulo the earlier moments of each finite block.
Linear independence passes to the conjugate Riesz representatives.
The common-kernel identity lifts the strip moments to a separating family on the quotient.
Translating by log norm plus and minus the missing order supplies the factorial and binomial factors in every term of the translated jet. Haar invariance handles both signs.
Compare lower and higher jet functionals using only their realization in the reciprocal weighted Haar space. Membership of each retained jet supplies endpoint integrability.
Along a countably generated filter, strong convergence to the identity suffices for convergence of the traces of left products with a fixed nuclear operator.
Quotient translations act on every jet at one zero by the finite binomial matrix.
A cutoff can be kept away from all sites of an arbitrary divisor by a distance depending only on the width and the number of sites in the interval.
A nonempty set of cutoffs with a prescribed clearance in a closed window has a least member. This selects one reproducible boundary from the simultaneous interval bound.
Evaluation on a biorthogonal vector reads its coefficient on the dense span of the jets.
In any normed space, the `i`th vector of a Markushevich system has norm at least the reciprocal of the distance of the `i`th functional from the span of the others.

In a space isometric to a Hilbert space the bound of `spectralSobolevQuotient_markushevich_le_norm_mul_infDist` is an equality: the orthogonal part of the Riesz vector of the `i`th functional, relative to the others, is a multiple of the `i`th vector.
In a Markushevich system every combination of the other functionals vanishes at the `i`th vector.

Bounded trace norms of the finite block sums give summable block traces after inserting any bounded operator: the trace of the inserted finite sum is at most the norm of the operator times the trace norm.
A complex family whose finite partial sums are bounded in norm is summable.
A real family whose finite partial sums are bounded in absolute value is summable.
For nonnegative blocks, simultaneous finite samples detect summability. Choose each circle maximum and a coefficient test within a factor of two of each individual norm.
Differentiation in the real frequency variable requires absolute log moments only through the requested order. This is the dominated-integral argument in §10.2.
A full set of zero-block coordinates determines the finite convolution sum.
The actual line translation acts on all admitted log jets by the binomial formula.
The rational idele class character induced by a quartic Dirichlet character modulo five is nonreal on the norm-one class of the local unit two.
The idelic character of a Dirichlet character modulo 5, at the idele with `2` at the place over 5 and `1` elsewhere, is the inverse of the character value at `2`.
A grid of width 1/(k+1) forces two distinct ordinates in the same cell.
A vanishing ordinate gap gives vanishing L² distance for unit-modulus phases. The fixed L² representative shows the constant dominator is integrable.
The L² distance of two jets can be estimated by integrating their squared pointwise distance.
Choose the trivial lift of the trivial rational norm-one character.

decls.classical: the number of distinct critical-line zeta ordinates up to height T, divided by T, is unbounded. This follows from a positive proportion of distinct critical-line zeros (Selberg 1942) and the Riemann–von Mangoldt count. Not a statement of the paper and not a gap in it: a known theorem of which this project has no formal proof. It is the arithmetic input for the refutation of (10.3.1.18), p. 451, which is proved from it by name.

decls.summary: For the rational trivial character, the order-zero jet at frequency t is the unitary phase |g|^(it). Its L² distance to the jet at u tends to zero when t-u does.
Each distinct critical-line zeta zero supplies a zeroth jet at Sobolev exponent two.
A uniform bound on the diagonal products of a biorthogonal system with normalized coordinate forms forces the forms to be uniformly separated.
At exponent two the printed and corrected jet cutoffs agree. The printed bound would therefore separate all the rational jet vectors uniformly in L².
A continuous functional given by a character pairing is an eigenfunctional for left translations, and integrating the orbit yields the test's multiplier.
The zeroth jet at a zero of the completed L-function kills the closed weighted theta subspace, by Mellin factorization on the dense polar-free tests.
A compact Bruhat cutoff times the inverse of a norm twist has the opposite translation weight to the twist's restriction, and its pairing is positive.
A weighted Sobolev class representing a compactly supported Bruhat test.
At a zero of the continued completed L-function, every adelic zeta transform vanishes on the same nontrivial norm-one component.
The critical-line ordinates in (0, 50) form a finite set containing the ten distinct certified ordinates.
A permutation of any sequence of nonzero samples can move some samples far enough out that multiplication by the index no longer tends to zero.
The trivial rational row on the critical line admits a numbering by ℕ.
Hardy's theorem supplies infinitely many ordinates of ordinary Riemann zeta zeros on the critical line.
A compact bump supported away from zero has an entire Mellin transform. A single translate of this transform avoids zero on any countable set.
A compactly supported radial test can have all its Mellin samples at a specified sequence of frequencies nonzero.
Composition with a smooth scalar function preserves Bruhat smoothness in each elementary quotient chart.
A critical-line zero of ordinary zeta has positive order for the completed L-function of the trivial rational character, and conversely.
Three ordered critical-line zeros of the ordinary Riemann zeta function suffice for the interval counterexample. This is a finite consequence of Hardy's theorem.
On the critical line the order of the trivial rational completed L-function is a finite natural number, positive exactly at the zeros of ordinary zeta.
The norm section splits the dual of the idele class group into a real line and the dual of the norm-one classes, with the kernel `exp(ixy)` in `y = log |g|`.

At a character that only sees the log norm with frequency `x`, the transform of the Gaussian `exp(−y²/2)` in `y = log |g|` has squared norm `m² · 2π · exp(−x²)`, where `m` is the mass of the norm-one classes.
In logarithmic norm coordinates the idele class measure is the mass of the norm-one classes times Lebesgue measure: Haar uniqueness on ℝ, normalized by Weil's formula.

The Plancherel measure of the compact norm-one classes gives the trivial character the reciprocal of their mass: the transform of the constant one is that mass at the trivial character and vanishes elsewhere by orthogonality.

At any prescribed compact character and frequency, the Mellin integral is nonzero for some Bruhat test. The norm section identifies the full character with the product of the compact character and the radial oscillation. The inverse of this character times a smooth bump in the log norm gives a test whose Mellin integral is the norm-one Haar mass times the positive integral of the bump. The map `τ` is a section of the idelic norm, as on p. 455; without that the statement fails (for the constant map every test has Mellin value zero, #6741).

Over ℚ, changing the basepoint of the trivial norm-one character translates its critical-line ordinates. Two distinct certified zeros have finite positive order, and at least one translated ordinate is nonzero.

Some completed Hecke L-function has a zero of order at least two on some vertical line, for some basepoint choice. Choosing the trivial lift of the trivial norm-one character realizes the multiple zero of the completed Dedekind zeta function on that line.

Approximate a square-integrable vector and keep a compactly supported representative.

The same normalized shifts for the real density in a weighted Sobolev measure.

Combine the scalar cutoff limits, exact kernel localization, fixed-window convergence, and radial Fourier range invariance on weighted Haar L².

Parseval's identity for a Hilbert basis.

An operator induced on the quotient by a closed subspace is Hilbert–Schmidt exactly when the squared norms of the adjoint of the operator on a Hilbert basis of the orthogonal complement are summable. The operator preserves the subspace, so its adjoint preserves the complement, and the adjoint of the induced operator sends the class of `e j` to the class of `T† (e j)`.
Convolution of tests is composition of their actions on the strip quotient.

Summable real sequences are square summable.
Composing a Hilbert–Schmidt operator with bounded operators on both sides gives a Hilbert–Schmidt operator.
Approximation numbers are nonnegative.

The case of `sum_sq_eq_of_orthonormal_mem` for the span of finitely many vectors, indexed by the same finite set as the orthonormal family.
Bessel's inequality for Hilbert–Schmidt sums: the squared norms of an operator on a finite orthonormal family add up to at most the sum over a Hilbert basis.

The sum of `⟪T d i, T d i⟫` over an orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional space does not depend on the basis.
The squared Hilbert–Schmidt sum over an orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional space does not depend on the basis.

A dense subspace of ℓ² need not contain its first standard basis vector.

The two-dimensional block projections would have norms at least k+1.

Two-sided polynomial growth makes a conformal group element power-bounded.

The projective gauge of the unit pure tensors controls every zero-neighborhood.

Splitting each output vector splits the rectangular kernel tensor.
A block-diagonal operator commutes with every finite sum of whole coordinate-block projections.

A strip zero's entire finite jet block annihilates convolution of a basis vector belonging to a different zero.
A quotient jet functional evaluates on a representative by its explicit Haar moment.

Each full period of a nonprincipal character sums to zero, and the remaining partial sum has norm at most its modulus.
Recover the completed L-function from its finite and archimedean factors.

On the critical line the primitive functional equation relates each value to its conjugate.
A fixed unit and the same Stirling phase approximate the archimedean factor of either parity.

Integrating a uniform error bound over a dyadic interval costs its length.
For conductor one the Dirichlet L-function is the ordinary Riemann zeta function.
The shifted Hardy modes retain curvature `1/(2t)`; beyond `B√T` their slopes have magnitude at least `K`. The two derivative estimates control both ranges on `[T,2T]`.

Removing the root-number phase and half of the conductor twist gives a real value.

Split a weighted sum at an integer threshold and sum the majorants `C/√n` on both parts.
Reindex a finite sum over the positive integers.

Normalizing a nonzero complex number near one changes its distance from one by at most a factor two.
The tail of the telescoping majorant starting at index `k` equals `(k+1)^(−d)`.
On `[T,2T]` with `T = k⁴`, a cutoff of size `(AT)²` gives uniform error at most `1/16`. The shorter cutoff `T` gives a pointwise bound of order `√T` for the L-function.
The unnormalized norm-one average multiplies a Mellin integral in the trivial component by the mass of the compact norm-one group.

On positive real arguments the gamma recurrence forces the ratio at shifts of two to grow linearly, since the Dirichlet L-series tends to one.
A zero-free entire function of order strictly less than two has constant relative shift. The disk bounds are stated at scale 6R to allow arbitrary centers in Cauchy's estimate.

The Baker–Wüstholz theorem on linear forms in logarithms, for two fixed integers: A. Baker and G. Wüstholz, *Logarithmic forms and group varieties*, J. reine angew. Math. 442 (1993), 19–62. For two fixed integers greater than one, the reciprocal of a nonzero integral linear form in their real logarithms grows at most polynomially in the coefficients. Proved here (#7362) from the classical input `baker_two_logarithms_not_liouville_of_independent`, the case of multiplicatively independent integers, which is not proved in Lean.
A rational ratio even allows degree zero, with explicit constant.

decls.classical: for multiplicatively independent integers `1 < p < q`, the ratio of their real logarithms has finite irrationality measure. This is the non-effective two-logarithm consequence of A. Baker and G. Wüstholz, *Logarithmic forms and group varieties*, J. reine angew. Math. 442 (1993), 19–62.

decls.summary: The non-Liouville estimate on a single ratio gives the exact target, including zero coefficients and both signs. Doubling denominators puts every nonzero integer slope in the range of Mathlib's definition.
The residue field of the completion at a height-one prime is finite.
Finitely many possible poles can simultaneously be removed by a polynomial. The exponents come from the defining property of meromorphicity at those points.
If the cubic zero orders are dominated throughout the strip, the quotient of the two completed functions is entire. Their two poles cancel.
The Euler products at real part two bound both the finite Dedekind zeta function and its reciprocal on the closed right half-plane.
In both possible cubic signatures, cancellation leaves two reciprocal real gamma factors.
Nonvanishing of the completed function on the Euler half-plane.
Except at its two poles, the completed Dedekind zeta function has order zero outside the open strip.

An entire quotient cannot have uniform factorial savings on both distant vertical lines, even if its known horizontal estimates hold only along two sequences depending on the strip. The point tested is the real parameter 1.
Continue the Euler factorization to every regular point of the finite quotient.
The finite continuation is regular away from the possible completed poles.
On a bounded positive strip the reciprocal real gamma factor grows at most exponentially.
Gamma recursion on integer-spaced vertical contours gives factorial decay of its inverse.
The gamma recurrence gives uniform factorial decay on the sequence of right edges.
One step of the real gamma recurrence, valid also at a zero of its reciprocal.
On every fixed vertical strip the reciprocal real gamma factor grows at most exponentially.
For fixed R the Gaussian kills any exponential in the height on horizontal edges.
Norm of the Gaussian used on a box of half-width R.
On a vertical edge, completing the square makes the Gaussian cost only an exponential in R.
Choose horizontal edges using the polynomial reciprocal bound for the finite cubic zeta function. Their heights may depend on the width of the box.
The two poles of the completed trivial character are simple.
A finite product of shifted linear factors grows at most exponentially in the width and height of the contour.
Reflection of the completed quotient costs an exponential in the real part, uniformly in the height.
The normalized meromorphic quotient agrees with ordinary division wherever the denominator is regular and nonzero.
A bound on all four sides of a rectangle bounds the value at the real point one.
The completed Dedekind zeta function has the same order at reflected points.
On the right edge the Euler factors stay bounded while both reciprocal gamma factors decay.
A cubic subfield of the splitting field of X³ − 2 detects double zeros: an excess over the rational zero order forces order at least two upstairs.
Reflection and local finiteness of the divisor turn infinitely many multiple zeros in the open strip into unbounded positive ordinates.
Reflect the right-edge bound to the left edge of the same centered box.
Prime norms over a finite set of excluded rational primes divide one of the finitely many norms of the principal ideals generated by those primes.
The regular and the two transitive S₃ permutation characters satisfy the Artin relation for every power of Frobenius.
Every prime-ideal norm is a positive power of a rational prime.
The action on the three complex roots of X³ − 2 is the full symmetric group. Complex conjugation exchanges the two nonreal roots, and the irreducible cubic has prime degree.

On some finite subset of the open critical strip, the zero count with multiplicity for ℚ(∛2) exceeds the rational zero count. The Dedekind zero-count asymptotic has leading coefficient proportional to the degree, which is three for the cubic field. Alternatively the critical-line sign change of the cubic ξ-function between heights zero and three gives a singleton, since rational ζ is zero-free there.
A local Euler denominator is nonzero whenever its argument has positive real part.
Cancel the exceptional Euler factors in two products that agree outside a finite set.
The Galois group acts transitively by postcomposition on the embeddings of a subfield. Number the embeddings using their equality in number with the degree.
A finite product of reciprocal Euler denominators is entire and nonvanishing in Re(s) > 0.
A residue field of degree d contributes d embeddings exactly when d divides the Frobenius power.
Relabeling a finite action preserves the number of fixed points.

Outside finitely many rational primes, the counts of residue-field points in an S₃ splitting field and its two subfields are fixed-point counts for one Frobenius power acting on their embeddings. The trace for E is the sum of d times the number of prime ideals of norm p ^ d over d dividing r.
Any rational prime has a prime above it in the splitting field and an arithmetic Frobenius inducing the residue-field power map.
Through reduction, composition with the r-th Frobenius power acts by raising each value to p to the r.
Outside finitely many primes, the residue-field point count equals the number of embeddings fixed by a Frobenius power. Reduction is bijective there and respects the Frobenius action.
Grouping prime ideals by their norm raises each Euler factor to the number of prime ideals of that norm.
Extending scalars bounds the number of residue maps by the rank of the integer ring.
Invert the sums of the counts of cycles with lengths dividing r, weighting each cycle by its length.
Prime ideals of norm p to the d correspond to primes over p of inertia degree d.
Group the prime-ideal count into its inertia-degree fibres.
Continue the zeta identity from its Euler products and take divisors in the open strip.
The unramified Frobenius traces determine the prime-ideal counts outside finitely many exceptional norms.
In ℚ there is one prime ideal of each rational prime norm and none of any other norm.
A rational prime ideal has norm equal to its natural prime generator.
Every positive Frobenius power has trace one for the rational zeta factor.
At good primes the degree bound and Galois normality make reduction of embeddings bijective.
Two distinct embeddings remain distinct modulo every prime outside a finite set.
A homomorphism from the integer ring to a field of characteristic p factors uniquely through the residue field at its kernel.
For a prime ideal the finite-field degree is its inertia degree over the rational prime.
A rational prime below an ideal divides the norm of every integer in that ideal.
Summing the fixed residue-field embeddings over the primes above p gives the integral point count.
The splitting field of the pure cubic contains a square root of −3. For distinct cube roots x and y, take (2x+y)/y.
In the open strip a Dedekind zeta order is finite and nonnegative.
The pure cubic and its quadratic resolvent embed into the splitting field. The resolvent has degree two, as its two conjugate roots are nonreal.

The transitive actions of S₃ on two and three points have the sign and standard permutation characters, respectively. Enumerate the six words in the two adjacent transpositions and their possible images.
After omitting finitely many prime norms, the Euler identity has only finite Euler factors as corrections. Those factors are entire and are nonzero on the open right half-plane.
If a prime splits in the intermediate field, every element of its decomposition group fixes that field pointwise.
In a Galois extension, a completely split prime accounts for exactly `[L : K]` terms. Every other unramified prime has residue degree at least two throughout its fiber.
The sum of the terms of degree at least two in the logarithmic Euler product is bounded uniformly as the real exponent decreases to one.
The sum over all prime ideals has leading term `-log (s - 1)` at one.
The Picard class of a nonzero integral ideal is represented by that ideal as a module.
Every strictly increasing sequence of finite sets that exhausts the naturals can be realized as initial segments of a single permutation.
Restricted characters separate points of the subgroup, so their complex linear span is dense.
A character of a compact group embedded in an LCA group extends to the whole group. Evaluation embeds the compact group into the compact closure of the ambient evaluation image.
Averaging the orbit of each vector gives a bounded operator depending continuously on the integrable weight.
Averages of norm at most one approximate each vector.
A strongly continuous unitary representation of an abelian group yields a continuous character detecting any element that acts nontrivially.
The double commutant of the representation is commutative and contains the representation and all its Haar averages.
A compact family of characters controls the norm of a translated Haar average.
Spectral characters on a compact level set of the average control its translates.
On the union of the sets where at least one norm-continuous translate is nonzero, the spectral characters restrict continuously to characters of the group.
If the operators with norm-continuous translates approximate the vector, its spectral measure is carried by the open set on which they detect continuous characters of the group.
Haar averaging supplies the norm-continuous translates needed by the spectral representation of a coefficient of a strongly continuous unitary action.
A positive functional on complex continuous functions on a compact space is integrated against a finite regular measure. Apply real Riesz–Markov to its real part.
The vector functional on a commutative algebra of operators has a finite regular representing measure on its Gelfand spectrum.
The left regular action on `Lᵖ` by precomposition with inverse translation.
Haar averaging is contractive as a map from integrable weights to operators.
The adjoint of a unitary group action is the action of the inverse.
For two open linear quotient maps with a common source, strictness transfers from the restriction of the first map to the second kernel to the restriction in the other direction.
The Hölder seminorm is the supremum of the difference quotients `edist (f x) (f y) / edist x y ^ r` over pairs of distinct points.
The Hölder seminorm is the supremum of the real difference quotients `dist (f x) (f y) / dist x y ^ r` over pairs of distinct points.
The Hölder seminorm is bounded by an extended constant `C` exactly when the Hölder inequality holds with constant `C`.
The Hölder inequality with the Hölder seminorm as constant.
The derivative of `expNegInvGlue` at `x` is `x⁻² expNegInvGlue x`, also for `x ≤ 0`, where both sides vanish.
On a real inner product space, the derivative of `x ↦ expNegInvGlue (‖x‖ ^ 2)` at `x` is `‖x‖⁻⁴ expNegInvGlue (‖x‖²) · 2 ⟪x, ·⟫`, also at `x = 0`, where it vanishes.
The function `expNegInvGlue` is less than `1` everywhere.
`HolderOnWith` is equivalent to the Hölder bound stated with `dist`. Compare `lipschitzOnWith_iff_dist_le_mul`.

A function bounded by `M` has oscillation at most `2 M`, which is its Hölder bound of exponent zero. Compare Mathlib's `HolderWith.holderWith_zero_of_bounded`, which bounds the oscillation of a Hölder function on a bounded space instead.
Integration of an even complex function on the real line reduces to its positive ray.
The defining characterization of a path-homotopy-trivial set.
Between distinct points `x ≠ y` of a metric space, a bound `a ≤ C * edist x y ^ r` is equivalent to the bound `a / edist x y ^ r ≤ C` on the difference quotient.
A countable `lp` sum of separable spaces is separable for finite exponent.
The Mellin transform of a Gaussian on the positive real ray.

Scalar homogeneity of the Hölder seminorm, for every map, whether or not it is `r`-Hölder. Mathlib's `MemHolder.nnHolderNorm_smul` assumes `MemHolder`; without it, both sides take the junk value `0` when `c ≠ 0`.
The headline claim, stated with Mathlib's definition only.

**The skew-adjoint elements are `-I` times the self-adjoint ones**: Mathlib's `skewAdjoint.negISMul`, `a ↦ -I • a`, is a real linear equivalence from the skew-adjoint onto the self-adjoint elements of a complex star module, with inverse `a ↦ I • a`.
A partition `0 = t₀ ≤ ⋯ ≤ tₙ = 1` of the unit interval into `n` segments.
Consecutive partition points are ordered.
A point of the unit interval has absolute value at most one.
The index of the arc containing a point `s` of the unit interval, `⌊r s⌋`, except that the end point `1` belongs to the last arc.
The point at a parameter `a < 1` of the `i`-th arc, `i < r`, lies in the `i`-th arc.
A point of the `i`-th arc lies in the `i`-th arc, or it is the common end point of the `i`-th and the `(i+1)`-th arcs and is counted in the latter.
The end point `1` lies in the last arc.
With no arcs, every point is counted in the arc of index `0`.
The position `r s - arcIndex r s` of `s` inside its arc, rescaled to the unit interval.
The point at a parameter `a < 1` of the `i`-th arc, `i < r`, is at parameter `a` in its arc.
The end point `1` is at parameter `1` in the last arc.
The point `(i + a) / r` of the unit interval: the point at parameter `a` of the `i`-th of the `r` equal arcs `[i/r, (i+1)/r]`.
A point is the point of its arc at its position in the arc.
The end of an arc is the start of the next one.
The start of the arc after the last of the `r` arcs is the end point `1`.
With no arcs, every arc point is `0`.
The first arc starts at `0`.

Given open sets `U i` into which `f` maps the consecutive segments `[t i, t (i + 1)]` of a monotone sequence in the unit interval, the path components of `f (t j)` in the intersections of the adjacent `U i` are open, path-connected vertex sets, each contained in its adjacent `U i`.
